الْجُزْءُ الْرَّابِعُ وَالْثَّلَاثُونَ
كِتَابُ الظِّهَارِ إِلَى قِتَالِ أَهْلِ الْبَغْي
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَحْدَهُ وَالصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَى مَنْ لَا نَبِيَّ بَعْدَهُ.
بَابُ الظِّهَارِ
سُئِلَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ أَحْمَد بْنُ تَيْمِيَّة - قَدَّسَ اللَّهُ رُوحَهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَالَ لِامْرَأَتِهِ:
 أَنْتِ عَلَيَّ مِثْلُ أُمِّي وَأُخْتِي؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ كَانَ مَقْصُودُهُ أَنْتِ عَلَيَّ مِثْلُ أُمِّي وَأُخْتِي فِي الْكَرَامَةِ فَلَا شَيْءَ عَلَيْهِ. وَإِنْ كَانَ مَقْصُودُهُ يُشَبِّهُهَا بِأُمِّهِ وَأُخْتِهِ فِي 
" بَابِ النِّكَاحِ "
 فَهَذَا ظِهَارٌ عَلَيْهِ مَا عَلَى الْمُظَاهِرِ فَإِذَا أَمْسَكَهَا فَلَا يَقْرَبُهَا حَتَّى يُكَفِّرَ كَفَّارَةَ ظِهَارٍ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ تَزَوَّجَ وَأَرَادَ الدُّخُولَ اللَّيْلَةَ الْفُلَانِيَّةَ؛
 وَإِلَّا كَانَتْ عِنْدِي مِثْلَ أُمِّي وَأُخْتِي وَلَمْ تَتَهَيَّأْ لَهُ ذَلِكَ الْوَقْتَ الَّذِي طَلَبَهَا فِيهِ:
 فَهَلْ يَقَعُ طَلَاقٌ؟
translated_text:
Volume Thirty-Four
From the Book of Zihār to Fighting Rebels

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

All praise belongs to Allah alone, and blessings and peace be upon the one after whom there is no prophet.

Chapter on Zihār

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked about a man who said to his wife, “You are to me like my mother and my sister.”

He answered:

If he meant, “You are to me like my mother and my sister in the respect I accord you,” then nothing is required of him. But if he intended to liken her to his mother and sister with regard to “marital relations,” this constitutes zihār, and he is subject to its requirements. If he keeps her as his wife, he must not have intercourse with her until he has offered the prescribed expiation for zihār.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked about a man who married and wanted to consummate the marriage on a particular night, saying, “Otherwise, she will be to me like my mother and my sister.” She was not ready for him at the time he had requested her. Does a divorce take effect?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
لَا يَقَعُ عَلَيْهِ طَلَاقٌ فِي الْمَذَاهِبِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ؛ لَكِنْ يَكُونُ مُظَاهِرًا فَإِذَا أَرَادَ الدُّخُولَ فَإِنَّهُ يُكَفِّرُ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ. الْكَفَّارَةَ الَّتِي ذَكَرَهَا اللَّهُ فِي 
" سُورَةِ الْمُجَادَلَةِ "
 فَيَعْتِقُ رَقَبَةً مُؤْمِنَةً فَإِنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ فَصِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ؛ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَإِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ حَنِقَ مِنْ زَوْجَتِهِ فَقَالَ:
 إنْ بَقِيت أَنْكِحُك أَنْكِحُ أُمِّي تَحْتَ سُتُورِ الْكَعْبَةِ. هَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُصَالِحَهَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 إذَا نَكَحَهَا فَعَلَيْهِ كَفَّارَةُ الظِّهَارِ:
 عِتْقُ رَقَبَةٍ مُؤْمِنَةٍ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ فَصِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَإِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا وَلَا يَمَسُّهَا حَتَّى يُكَفِّرَ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلَيْنِ قَالَ أَحَدُهُمَا لِصَاحِبِهِ:
 يَا أَخِي لَا تَفْعَلْ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ امْرَأَتِك قَبِيحٌ عَلَيْك فَقَالَ: مَا هِيَ إلَّا مِثْلُ أُمِّي.
 فَقَالَ:
 لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ قُلْت سَمِعْت أَنَّهَا تَحْرُمُ بِهَذَا اللَّفْظِ ثُمَّ كَرَّرَ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ وَقَالَ: أَيْ وَاَللَّهِ هِيَ عِنْدِي مِثْلُ أُمِّي: هَلْ تَحْرُمُ عَلَى الزَّوْجِ بِهَذَا اللَّفْظِ؟
translated_text:
He answered:

No divorce takes effect according to any of the four schools of law. However, he has pronounced zihār. If he wishes to consummate the marriage, he must first offer the expiation Allah mentioned in Surah al-Mujādalah: freeing a believing slave; if he cannot find one, fasting for two consecutive months; and if he is unable to do so, feeding sixty needy people.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked about a man who became angry with his wife and said, “If I have intercourse with you again, it is like having intercourse with my mother beneath the coverings of the Kaaba.” Is he permitted to reconcile with her?

He answered:

All praise belongs to Allah. If he has intercourse with her, he is liable for the expiation for zihār: freeing a believing slave; if he cannot find one, fasting for two consecutive months; and if he is unable to do so, feeding sixty needy people. He must not have intercourse with her until he has offered the expiation.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about two men, one of whom said to the other, “My brother, do not do these things in your wife’s presence; it is unseemly of you.” The other replied, “She is just like my mother.”

His companion said, “Why did you say that? I have heard that a wife becomes forbidden to her husband through these words.” The husband then repeated his statement, saying, “Yes, by Allah, she is like my mother to me.” Does she become forbidden to her husband through these words?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ،
 إنْ أَرَادَ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 إنَّهَا مِثْلُ أُمِّي أَنَّهَا تَسْتُرُ عَلَيَّ وَلَا تَهْتِكُنِي وَلَا تَلُومُنِي كَمَا تَفْعَلُ الْأُمُّ مَعَ وَلَدِهَا؛ فَإِنَّهُ يُؤَدَّبُ عَلَى هَذَا الْقَوْلِ وَلَا تَحْرُمُ عَلَيْهِ امْرَأَتُهُ؛
 فَإِنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ سَمِعَ رَجُلًا يَقُولُ لِامْرَأَتِهِ:
 يَا أُخْتِي فَأَدَّبَهُ - وَإِنْ كَانَ جَاهِلًا لَمْ يُؤَدَّبْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَإِنْ اسْتَحَقَّ الْعُقُوبَةَ عَلَى مَا فَعَلَهُ مِنْ الْمُنْكَرِ - وَقَالَ أُخْتُك هِيَ فَلَا يَنْبَغِي أَنْ يَجْعَلَ الْإِنْسَانُ امْرَأَتَهُ كَأُمِّهِ. وَإِنْ أَرَادَ بِهَا عِنْدِي مِثْلُ أُمِّي.
 أَيْ فِي الِامْتِنَاعِ عَنْ وَطْئِهَا وَالِاسْتِمْتَاعِ بِهَا وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يَحْرُمُ مِنْ الْأُمِّ فَهِيَ مِثْلُ أُمِّي الَّتِي لَيْسَتْ مَحَلًّا لِلِاسْتِمْتَاعِ بِهَا:
 فَهَذَا 
" مُظَاهِرٌ "
 يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ مَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْمُظَاهِرِ فَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُ أَنْ يَطَأَهَا حَتَّى يُكَفِّرَ 
" كَفَّارَةَ الظِّهَارِ "
 فَيَعْتِقَ رَقَبَةً فَإِنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ فَصِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَإِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا. وَإِذَا فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ حَلَّ لَهُ ذَلِكَ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛
 إلَّا أَنْ يَنْوِيَ أَنَّهَا مُحَرَّمَةٌ عَلَيَّ كَأُمِّيِّ:
 فَهَذَا يَكُونُ مُظَاهِرًا فِي مَذْهَبِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد.
 وَحُكِيَ فِي مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ نِزَاعٌ فِي ذَلِكَ:
 هَلْ يَقَعُ بِهِ الثَّلَاثُ؟ أَمْ لَا؟ وَالصَّوَابُ الْمَقْطُوعُ بِهِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَقَعُ بِهِ طَلَاقٌ وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُ الْوَطْءُ حَتَّى يُكَفِّرَ بِاتِّفَاقِهِمْ وَلَا يَقَعُ بِهِ الطَّلَاقُ بِذَلِكَ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He answered:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

If, by saying, “She is like my mother,” he means that she conceals his faults and neither disgraces nor reproaches him, just as a mother treats her child, then he is to be disciplined for this statement, but his wife does not become forbidden to him. For ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—heard a man address his wife as “My sister,” so he disciplined him—though if he was unaware, he would not be disciplined for this, even if he deserved punishment for the wrongdoing he had committed—and said, “Is she your sister?” A man should therefore not liken his wife to his mother.

If, however, by “She is like my mother to me,” he means refraining from intercourse, sexual enjoyment, and other acts forbidden with one’s mother—as though saying, “She is like my mother, with whom sexual enjoyment is impermissible”—then he is “one who has pronounced zihār” and is subject to the obligations this entails. He may not have intercourse with her until he offers the “expiation for zihār”: freeing a slave; if he cannot find one, fasting for two consecutive months; and if he is unable to do so, feeding sixty needy people. Once he has done this, intercourse becomes lawful for him by the consensus of the Muslims—unless he intends, “She is forbidden to me like my mother.” In that case, he is regarded as having pronounced zihār according to the schools of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad.

A disagreement has been reported within Mālik’s school as to whether a threefold divorce takes effect through these words. The unquestionably correct view is that no divorce takes effect thereby. By their unanimous agreement, intercourse is not lawful for him until he offers the expiation, and no divorce takes effect through these words. Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَالَ لِامْرَأَتِهِ بَائِنٍ عَنْهُ إنْ رَدَدْتُك تَكُونِي مِثْلَ أُمِّي وَأُخْتِي:
 هَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَرُدَّهَا؟ وَمَا الَّذِي يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
فِي أَحَدِ قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ عَلَيْهِ كَفَّارَةُ ظِهَارٍ وَإِذَا رَدَّهَا فِي الْآخَرِ لَا شَيْءَ. وَالْأَوَّلُ أَحْوَطُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَالَ فِي غَيْظِهِ لِزَوْجَتِهِ:
 أَنْتِ عَلَيَّ حَرَامٌ مِثْلَ أُمِّي.
فَأَجَابَ:
هَذَا مُظَاهِرٌ مِنْ امْرَأَتِهِ دَاخِلٌ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{الَّذِينَ يُظَاهِرُونَ مِنْكُمْ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ مَا هُنَّ أُمَّهَاتِهِمْ إنْ أُمَّهَاتُهُمْ إلَّا اللَّائِي وَلَدْنَهُمْ وَإِنَّهُمْ لَيَقُولُونَ مُنْكَرًا مِنَ الْقَوْلِ وَزُورًا وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورٌ}
 
{وَالَّذِينَ يُظَاهِرُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ ثُمَّ يَعُودُونَ لِمَا قَالُوا فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَتَمَاسَّا ذَلِكُمْ تُوعَظُونَ بِهِ وَاللَّهُ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرٌ}
 
{فَمَنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ فَصِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَتَمَاسَّا فَمَنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَإِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا}
 فَهَذَا إذَا أَرَادَ إمْسَاكَ زَوْجَتِهِ وَوَطِئَهَا فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَقْرَبُهَا حَتَّى يُكَفِّرَ هَذِهِ الْكَفَّارَةَ الَّتِي ذَكَرَهَا اللَّهُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About a man who said to his former wife, whom he had irrevocably divorced, “If I take you back, you will be like my mother and sister”: may he take her back, and what is required of him?

He answered:

According to one of the two scholarly views, he must offer the expiation for zihār if he takes her back; according to the other, nothing is required of him. The first view is more cautious.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About a man who, in anger, said to his wife, “You are as forbidden to me as my mother.”

He answered:

This man has pronounced zihār against his wife and falls under Allah’s words:

“Those of you who declare their wives as unlawful to them as their mothers—their wives are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who gave birth to them. They certainly utter an objectionable statement and a falsehood. Yet Allah is indeed Pardoning, Forgiving.”

“Those who declare their wives as unlawful to them as their mothers, then go back on what they have said, must free a slave before the two touch one another. This is what you are admonished to do, and Allah is All-Aware of what you do.”

“But whoever cannot find a slave must fast for two consecutive months before the two touch one another. Whoever is unable to do so must feed sixty needy people.”

Thus, if this man wishes to keep his wife and have intercourse with her, he must not approach her until he has offered the expiation Allah has specified.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَالَتْ لَهُ زَوْجَتُهُ:
 أَنْتَ عَلَيَّ حَرَامٌ مِثْلَ أَبِي وَأُمِّي.
 وَقَالَ لَهَا:
 أَنْتِ عَلَيَّ حَرَامٌ مِثْلَ أُمِّي وَأُخْتِي: فَهَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ طَلَاقٌ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
لَا طَلَاقَ بِذَلِكَ؛ وَلَكِنْ إنْ اسْتَمَرَّ عَلَى النِّكَاحِ فَعَلَى كُلٍّ مِنْهُمَا كَفَّارَةُ ظِهَارٍ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَجْتَمِعَا وَهِيَ عِتْقُ رَقَبَةٍ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ فَصِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ؛ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَإِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About a man whose wife said to him, “You are as forbidden to me as my father and mother.” He said to her, “You are as forbidden to me as my mother and sister.” Does this entail divorce?

He answered:

No divorce results from this. However, if he remains married to her, each of them must offer the expiation for zihār before they have intercourse. This consists of freeing a slave; whoever cannot find one must fast for two consecutive months, and whoever is unable to do so must feed sixty needy people.

original_text:
بَابُ مَا يَلْحَقُ مِنْ النَّسَبِ
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ تَزَوَّجَ بِنْتًا بِكْرًا بَالِغًا وَدَخَلَ بِهَا؛
 فَوَجَدَهَا بِكْرًا ثُمَّ إنَّهَا وَلَدَتْ وَلَدًا بَعْدَ مُضِيِّ سِتَّةِ أَشْهُرٍ بَعْدَ دُخُولِهِ بِهَا:
 فَهَلْ يَلْحَقُ بِهِ الْوَلَدُ أَمْ لَا؟
 وَإِنْ الزَّوْجُ حَلَفَ فِي الطَّلَاقِ مِنْهَا أَنَّ الْوَلَدَ وَلَدُهُ مِنْ صُلْبِهِ:
 فَهَلْ يَقَعُ بِهِ الطَّلَاقُ أَمْ لَا؟ وَالْوَلَدُ ابْنٌ سَوِيٌّ كَامِلُ الْخِلْقَةِ وَعَمَّرَ سِنِينَ أَفْتُونَا مَأْجُورِينَ؟
فَأَجَابَ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، إذَا وَلَدَتْ لِأَكْثَرِ مِنْ سِتَّةِ أَشْهُرٍ مِنْ حِينِ دَخَلَ بِهَا وَلَوْ بِلَحْظَةِ لَحِقَهُ الْوَلَدُ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ - وَمِثْلُ هَذِهِ الْقِصَّةِ وَقَعَتْ فِي زَمَنِ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.
 وَاسْتَدَلَّ الصَّحَابَةُ عَلَى إمْكَانِ كَوْنِ الْوَلَدِ لِسِتَّةِ أَشْهُرٍ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَحَمْلُهُ وَفِصَالُهُ ثَلَاثُونَ شَهْرًا}
 مَعَ قَوْلِهِ: 
{وَالْوَالِدَاتُ يُرْضِعْنَ أَوْلَادَهُنَّ حَوْلَيْنِ كَامِلَيْنِ}
 فَإِذَا كَانَ مُدَّةُ الرَّضَاعِ مِنْ الثَّلَاثِينَ حَوْلَيْنِ يَكُونُ الْحَمْلُ سِتَّةَ أَشْهُرٍ؛ فَجَمَعَ فِي الْآيَةِ أَقَلَّ الْحَمْلِ وَتَمَامَ الرَّضَاعِ وَلَوْ لَمْ يَسْتَلْحِقْهُ فَكَيْفَ إذَا اسْتَلْحَقَهُ وَأَقَرَّ بِهِ بَلْ لَوْ اسْتَلْحَقَ مَجْهُولَ النَّسَبِ؛
 وَقَالَ:
 إنَّهُ ابْنِي لَحِقَهُ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛
 إذَا كَانَ ذَلِكَ مُمْكِنًا وَلَمْ يَدَّعِ أَحَدٌ أَنَّهُ ابْنُهُ:
 كَانَ بَارًّا فِي يَمِينِهِ؛ وَلَا حِنْثَ عَلَيْهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
Chapter on the Establishment of Lineage

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

About a man who married a virgin who had reached maturity, consummated the marriage, and found her to be a virgin. She then gave birth to a child six months after the consummation. Is the child attributed to him or not? If the husband swore on pain of divorce that the child was his own biological son, does divorce take effect or not? The child is a healthy, fully formed boy who has lived for several years. Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.

He—may Allah be pleased with him—answered:

Praise be to Allah. If she gave birth more than six months after he consummated the marriage with her, even by a moment, the child is attributed to him by the agreement of the imams. A similar case occurred during the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him.

The Companions established the possibility of a child being born after six months’ gestation by citing Allah Most High’s words:

“His gestation and weaning take thirty months,”

together with His words:

“Mothers shall breastfeed their children for two full years.”

If breastfeeding accounts for two years out of those thirty months, gestation is six months. Thus, the verse combines the minimum period of gestation with the full period of breastfeeding.

The child is attributed to him even if he has not acknowledged him as his own; how much more so when he has claimed and acknowledged him! Indeed, even if he acknowledged someone of unknown lineage, saying, “He is my son,” that person would be attributed to him by the consensus of the Muslims, provided that this was possible and no one else claimed him as his son. He has therefore been truthful in his oath and has not broken it. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

About a man who purchased a virgin slave woman and had intercourse with her. She does not leave the house, and she is pregnant by him. He took her to the market, denying that the child was his and swearing to that effect.

He answered:

If he admits having had intercourse with her—for example, if he has previously acknowledged it—the child is attributed to him, and the pregnancy is deemed to be from him, provided that she gives birth within a period that makes his paternity possible. He may sell neither the unborn child nor its mother. However, if he claims to have ascertained that she was not pregnant through the prescribed waiting period, the scholars disagree over accepting his statement and requiring him to swear an oath. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About a man who married a woman who remained with him for fifteen days, after which he divorced her irrevocably. She subsequently married another man after declaring that her waiting period following the first marriage had ended. The second husband then divorced her after six years. She brought forward a daughter, claiming that she was the first husband’s child.

Is her claim valid and binding upon the first husband, even though it has not been established that she gave birth to the girl? This husband and the woman live in the same town, and nothing prevented her from asserting the claims women make, or from demanding maintenance or a fixed allowance from him.

translated_text:
He answered:

Praise be to Allah. In these circumstances, this child—the girl—cannot be attributed to him merely on the basis of her claim, according to the unanimous agreement of the imams. Indeed, even if a divorced woman claims to have given birth in circumstances in which the child, if born to her, would be attributed to him, and he denies that she gave birth, her claim to have given birth is not accepted unless she produces evidence establishing it. There is no disagreement on this.

The testimony of one woman suffices according to Abū Hanīfah and the well-known position reported from Ahmad. According to Mālik and another position reported from Ahmad, two women are required. Al-Shāfiʿī requires four women. It suffices for the husband to swear that he does not know that she gave birth to the child.

If, however, the marriage is still in effect, there are two positions within Ahmad’s school. The first is that her statement is not accepted, as in al-Shāfiʿī’s school. The second is that it is accepted, as in Mālik’s school.

If her waiting period has ended and the maximum gestation period has elapsed, and she then claims to be pregnant by the first husband who divorced her, her statement is not accepted, without disagreement. Indeed, if she declares that her waiting period has ended and then gives birth six months or more later, but within the maximum gestation period, is the child attributed to him? The scholars have two well-known positions on this. The position of Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad is that the child is attributed to him. This is also the view adopted by Ibn Surayj, one of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers. However, the well-known position in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Mālik is that the child is not attributed to him.

This disagreement applies when she has not remarried. If, however, she marries after declaring that her waiting period has ended, and then gives birth more than six months after that marriage, the child is not attributed to the first husband, without disagreement. Once you understand the imams’ positions on these two principles, how, then, can the child be attributed to him

Rather, his statement is accepted, supported by his oath that she did not give birth to the girl while married to him. He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked about a man who pronounced three divorces against his wife. A mufti advised him that the divorce had not taken effect, so the husband followed his ruling and subsequently had intercourse with his wife, who bore him a child. It was then claimed that the child was born of fornication.

He answered:

Anyone who says that is guilty of the utmost ignorance, misguidance, and defiance of Allah and His Messenger. The Muslims agree that whenever a husband has intercourse within a marriage he believes to be permissible, the child born to him within it is attributed to him, and father and child inherit from one another by unanimous agreement of the Muslims—even if that marriage is, in fact, invalid by unanimous agreement of the Muslims. This applies whether the husband is a disbeliever or a Muslim. If a Jewish man marries his brother’s daughter, the child born of that union is attributed to him and inherits from him by unanimous agreement of the Muslims, even though that marriage is invalid by unanimous agreement of the Muslims.

Likewise, if an ignorant Muslim marries a woman during her waiting period, as ignorant Bedouins do, and has intercourse with her believing her to be his wife, the child born to him through her is attributed to him and inherits from him, by unanimous agreement of the Muslims. There are many such examples. “Establishing paternity” does not require the marriage to be valid in reality. Rather, the child belongs to the marital bed, as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“The child belongs to the marital bed, and the fornicator has nothing.”

Thus, if a man pronounces three divorces against his wife and has intercourse with her believing that the divorce has not taken effect—whether through ignorance, because he followed an erroneous ruling given by a mufti, or for some other reason—the child is attributed to him, and father and child inherit from one another, by unanimous agreement. Indeed, her waiting period is not reckoned until he ceases to have intercourse with her. Since he was having intercourse with her believing her to be his wife, she remained his partner in bed; her waiting period from him therefore does not begin until she ceases to share his bed.

If a man marries a woman in an “invalid marriage,” whether its invalidity is agreed upon or disputed; acquires ownership of her under an invalid title, whether its invalidity is agreed upon or disputed; or has intercourse with her believing her to be his free wife or a slave woman whom he owns, then the child born to him through her is attributed to him, and father and child inherit from one another, by unanimous agreement of the Muslims. The child is also free, even if the woman with whom he had intercourse actually belongs to someone else and the intercourse took place without her master’s permission. As for these men who had intercourse and fathered children, even if they had done so within marriages unanimously held to be invalid, and their divorces had taken effect by unanimous agreement of the Muslims, yet they had intercourse believing that their marriages remained in force—because of a ruling someone had given them or for some other reason—the children would be attributed to them and would not be children of fornication. Rather, fathers and children would inherit from one another, by unanimous agreement of the Muslims. If this applies where the marriage is unanimously held to be invalid, how much more so where its invalidity is disputed?

This holds even when the opinion on which a man relied in having intercourse was weak, as in the case of a temporary marriage or a marriage contracted by a woman on her own behalf without a guardian or witnesses. If he has intercourse within such a union believing it to be a marriage, the child is attributed to him. How much more so, then, in a disputed marriage whose validity has been clearly supported by the Quran, the Sunnah, and legal analogy, when thorough examination has revealed the weakness of the opposing view and its proponents’ inability to defend it, for lack of any proof recognized by Islamic law?

Whoever says that a child born of this marriage, or one like it, is a child of fornication, and that the child and the father who had intercourse cannot inherit from one another, contradicts the consensus of the Muslims and has forfeited his standing in religion. If he is ignorant, he must be instructed and have it explained to him that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—his Rightly Guided Caliphs, and all the other leading scholars of the religion attributed the children of the people of the pre-Islamic era to their fathers, even though their marriages were forbidden by unanimous agreement. They did not make attribution of paternity conditional upon the marriage being permissible under Islamic law. If he persists in opposing the Messenger after

It has thus become clear that whoever rejects the fatwa that the divorce does not take effect, claims consensus that it does take effect, and declares the child to be a child of fornication is himself contradicting the consensus of the Muslims, the Book of Allah, and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, the Lord of all worlds. Anyone who issues such a fatwa or judicial ruling has done something impermissible by the consensus of the Muslims. By agreement of the Muslims, no one has the right to prohibit fatwas expressing the opinion that the divorce does not take effect or judicial decisions based on that opinion, or to rule that either is forbidden. Such judgments are invalid by the consensus of the Muslims.

All praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of all worlds. May Allah bestow abundant blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions. There is neither might nor power except through Allah, the Most High, the Almighty.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man’s former wife, six years after their divorce and after marrying another husband, brought a claim against him asserting that a girl was his daughter. A judge required him to swear an oath. The man said, “I will swear that this girl is not my daughter.”

The judge said, “You must swear that she is not her daughter.” The man refused to swear anything other than, “She is not my daughter.” Someone accompanying him said to the judge, “It is not lawful for this man to swear that she is not this woman’s daughter.” The judge struck him with a rod and treated him harshly. The man then swore the oath, and the judge recorded an order imposing financial provision for the girl upon him. Is this order valid?

translated_text:
He replied:

All praise belongs to Allah. He must swear that she did not give birth to the girl during her waiting period, or while married to him, or in his home, under circumstances in which the child’s paternity could be attributed to him. But if she married another man and could have borne the girl by the second husband, he is not required to swear that she did not give birth to her. And if she swears that she did not give birth to her before her later marriage to the second husband. If he is coerced into acknowledging paternity, his acknowledgment is invalid.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man married a woman but neither consummated the marriage nor had intercourse with her. She gave birth two months later. Is the marriage valid, and is he liable for the dower?

He replied:

All praise belongs to Allah. By agreement of the Muslims, the child’s paternity is not attributed to him. Likewise, by agreement of the Muslims, he does not become liable for the full dower. However, scholars hold “two opinions” concerning the marriage contract.

The more correct opinion is that the contract is invalid, as held by Mālik, Ahmad, and others. In that case, the couple must be separated, and he owes neither a dower, nor half a dower, nor a parting gift, just as with other invalid marriage contracts when separation occurs before consummation. However, the separation should be ordered by a judge who considers the contract invalid, so as to settle the dispute.

The “second opinion” is that the contract is valid, but he may not have intercourse with her until she gives birth, as held by Abū Hanīfah.

It has also been said that he may have intercourse with her before she gives birth, as held by al-Shāfi‘ī,

Chapter on Waiting Periods

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A woman was divorced by her husband on the twenty-eighth of Rabīʿ al-Awwal and then menstruated once. She subsequently married on the twenty-third of Jumādā al-Ākhir of the same year, claiming that she had menstruated three times, although she had menstruated only once. When the second husband learned of this, he too divorced her, issuing a single pronouncement during the first ten days of Shaʿbān of that year. She then wished to remarry the second man who had divorced her, claiming that she had reached menopause. Is her claim to be accepted, and may she be married?

He replied:

Menopause cannot be established by a woman’s assertion. However, if this woman says that her menstruation has ceased and she does not know why, she must wait a year. If she does not menstruate during that year, she may be married. If she has reached menopausal age, no such delay is required. If her menstruation is known to have ceased because of illness or breastfeeding, she remains in her waiting period until that condition ends.

This woman was required to observe “two waiting periods”: one for the first husband and another on account of intercourse with the second. Her marriage to the second man is invalid and requires no divorce to end it. Thus, if she menstruated only once and the cessation of bleeding continued,

she must observe both waiting periods in months: six months after separating from the second man, if she has reached menopause. If the reason for the cessation of her menstruation is uncertain, the period is one year and three months.

This follows the view of those who hold that the two waiting periods do not overlap, such as Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. According to Abū Hanīfa, waiting periods arising from relations with two different men overlap; however, he defines menopause by age. The view we have mentioned is the better and easier of the jurists’ two opinions, and it accords with the rulings of ʿUmar and others. According to the other opinion, a woman whose menstruation has ceased for an unknown reason remains in her waiting period until she reaches menopausal age. On their view, she would remain unable to marry until she reaches fifty or sixty years of age. This, however, entails hardship and undue difficulty in religion and undermines the interests of the Muslims.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man married a woman who has now been with him for four years without menstruating. She stated that she had also not menstruated for four years before their marriage. Her husband then pronounced three divorces upon her. How may she marry another husband, and what waiting period must she observe, given that she is fifty years old?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. According to the stronger of the scholars’ two opinions, she must observe the waiting period prescribed for women who have reached menopause: “three months.” She knows that her menstruation has ceased, and she knows that its cessation has been continuous. This is unlike a woman whose situation is uncertain and who does not know why her menstruation has ceased: whether it is a cessation

due to menopause, or to a temporary cause, such as illness or breastfeeding, after which menstruation returns? These, then, are “three categories.”

When menstruation ceases because of a temporary cause, such as illness or breastfeeding, she must undoubtedly wait until that cause has passed. When it ceases and she does not know why, the position of Mālik and Ahmad—as explicitly reported from him—and one opinion of al-Shāfiʿī is that she observes the waiting period prescribed for menopausal women after first waiting out the duration of pregnancy. This accords with the ruling of ʿUmar. The position of Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī’s later opinion is that she must wait until she reaches menopausal age and then observe the waiting period prescribed for menopausal women. This causes her great harm, for she may remain unable to marry for twenty, thirty or forty years. Such hardship has been lifted from this community. Women who have reached menopause, however, observe a waiting period of three months, according to the explicit text of the Quran and the consensus of the Muslim community.

The scholars disagree, however: is there a fixed age for menopause, after which any bleeding can only be postmenopausal bleeding? Is that age fifty or sixty, or does the matter require further distinctions? They also disagree over whether menopause can be established without reference to age.

This woman has reached menopausal age according to one of the two opinions, namely fifty, and she has not menstruated for a long time. She has also stated that she took something to stop the bleeding, and bleeding can be induced by medication. She therefore has no expectation that her menstruation will return. Thus, she is among those who have reached menopause and must observe their prescribed waiting period. And Allah knows best.

عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ فَسَخَ الْحَاكِمُ نِكَاحَهَا عَقِبَ الْوِلَادَةِ لِمَا ثَبَتَ عِنْدَهُ مِنْ تَضَرُّرِهَا بِانْقِطَاعِ نَفَقَةِ زَوْجِهَا وَعَدَمِ تَصَرُّفِهِ الشَّرْعِيِّ عَلَيْهَا الْمُدَّةَ الَّتِي يَسُوغُ فِيهَا فَسْخُ النِّكَاحِ لِمِثْلِهَا.
 وَبَعْدَ ثَلَاثَةِ شُهُورٍ مِنْ فَسْخِ النِّكَاحِ رَغِبَ فِيهَا مَنْ يَتَزَوَّجُهَا:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ تَعْتَدَّ بِالشُّهُورِ؛ إذْ أَكْثَرُ النِّسَاءِ لَا يَحِضْنَ مَعَ الرَّضَاعَةِ أَوْ يَسْتَمِرُّ بِهَا الضَّرَرُ إلَى حَيْثُ يَنْقَضِي الرَّضَاعُ وَيَعُودُ إلَيْهَا حَيْضُهَا أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، بَلْ تَبْقَى فِي الْعِدَّةِ حَتَّى تَحِيضَ ثَلَاثَ حِيَضٍ وَإِنْ تَأَخَّرَ ذَلِكَ إلَى انْقِضَاءِ مُدَّةِ الرَّضَاعِ وَهَذَا بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَبِذَلِكَ قَضَى عُثْمَانُ بْنُ عَفَّانِ وَعَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ بَيْنَ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنْصَارِ وَلَمْ يُخَالِفْهُمَا أَحَدٌ.
 فَإِنْ أَحَبَّتْ الْمَرْأَةُ أَنْ تَسْتَرْضِعَ لِابْنِهَا مَنْ يُرْضِعُهُ لِتَحِيضَ أَوْ تَشْرَبَ مَا تَحِيضُ بِهِ:
 فَلَهَا ذَلِكَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ كَانَتْ تَحِيضُ وَهِيَ بِكْرٌ فَلَمَّا تَزَوَّجَتْ وَلَدَتْ سِتَّةَ أَوْلَادٍ وَلَمْ تَحِضْ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ وَوَقَعَتْ الْفُرْقَةُ مِنْ زَوْجِهَا وَهِيَ مُرْضِعٌ وَأَقَامَتْ عِنْدَ أَهْلِهَا
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A judge annulled a woman’s marriage shortly after she gave birth, having established that she had suffered harm because her husband had ceased providing maintenance and had failed to act toward her as prescribed by Islamic law, for a period sufficient to warrant annulment in her circumstances. Three months after the annulment, someone wished to marry her. May she calculate her waiting period in months, since most women do not menstruate while breastfeeding, or must her hardship continue until breastfeeding ends and her menstruation returns?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Rather, she must remain in her waiting period until she has had three menstrual periods, even if this is delayed until the breastfeeding period ends. This is agreed upon by the four imams and others. ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān and ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib ruled accordingly among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and no one disagreed with them.

If the woman wishes to engage a wet nurse for her son so that her menstruation may return, or to drink something that will induce menstruation, she may do so. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was also asked:

A woman used to menstruate while she was still a virgin. After marrying, she bore six children and did not menstruate thereafter. She separated from her husband while she was breastfeeding and stayed with her family

original_text:
نِصْفَ سَنَةٍ وَلَمْ تَحِضْ وَجَاءَ رَجُلٌ يَتَزَوَّجُهَا غَيْرُ الزَّوْجِ الْأَوَّلِ فَحَضَرُوا عِنْدَ قَاضٍ مِنْ الْقُضَاةِ فَسَأَلَهَا عَنْ الْحَيْضِ؟
 فَقَالَتْ:
 لِي مُدَّةُ سِنِينَ مَا حِضْت.
 فَقَالَ الْقَاضِي:
 مَا يَحِلُّ لَك عِنْدِي زَوَاجٌ فَزَوَّجَهَا حَاكِمٌ آخَرُ وَلَمْ يَسْأَلْهَا عَنْ الْحَيْضِ فَبَلَغَ خَبَرُهَا إلَى قَاضٍ آخَرَ فَاسْتَحْضَرَ الزَّوْجَ وَالزَّوْجَةَ فَضَرَبَ الرَّجُلَ مِائَةَ جَلْدَةٍ وَقَالَ: زَنَيْت وَطَلَّقَ عَلَيْهِ وَلَمْ يَذْكُرْ الزَّوْجُ الطَّلَاقَ فَهَلْ يَقَعُ بِهِ طَلَاقٌ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ كَانَ قَدْ ارْتَفَعَ حَيْضُهَا بِمَرَضِ أَوْ رَضَاعٍ فَإِنَّهَا تَتَرَبَّصُ حَتَّى يَزُولَ الْعَارِضُ وَتَحِيضَ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ؛
 وَإِنْ كَانَ ارْتَفَعَ حَيْضُهَا لَا تَدْرِي مَا رَفَعَهُ فَهَذِهِ فِي أَصَحِّ قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ عَلَى مَا قَالَ عُمَرُ:
 تَمْكُثُ سَنَةً ثُمَّ تَزَوَّجُ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَحْمَد الْمَعْرُوفُ فِي مَذْهَبِهِ وَقَوْلٌ لِلشَّافِعِيِّ: وَإِنْ كَانَتْ 
" فِي الْقِسْمِ الْأَوَّلِ "
 فَنِكَاحُهَا بَاطِلٌ وَاَلَّذِي فَرَّقَ بَيْنَهُمَا أَصَابَ فِي ذَلِكَ وَأَصَابَ فِي تَأْدِيبِ مَنْ فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ. وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مِنْ 
" الْقِسْمِ الثَّانِي "
 قَدْ زَوَّجَهَا حَاكِمٌ لَمْ يَكُنْ لِغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْحُكَّامِ أَنْ يُفَرِّقَ بَيْنَهُمَا وَلَمْ يَقَعْ بِهَا طَلَاقٌ فَإِنَّ فِعْلَ الْحَاكِمِ لِمِثْلِ ذَلِكَ يَجُوزُ فِي أَصَحِّ الْوَجْهَيْنِ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ مُرْضِعٍ اسْتَبْطَأَتْ الْحَيْضَ فَتَدَاوَتْ لِمَجِيءِ الْحَيْضِ فَحَاضَتْ ثَلَاثَ حِيَضٍ وَكَانَتْ مُطَلَّقَةً:
 فَهَلْ تَنْقَضِي عِدَّتُهَا؛ أَمْ لَا.
translated_text:
for half a year without menstruating. A man other than her first husband then came forward to marry her. They went before a judge, who asked her about her menstruation.

She said, “I have not menstruated for several years.”

The judge said, “In my judgment, you may not marry.” Another judge then married her without asking her about her menstruation. When a third judge heard about her case, he summoned the husband and wife, gave the man one hundred lashes, and said, “You have committed fornication.” He also decreed a divorce, although the husband himself had not pronounced one. Does a divorce take effect thereby?

He replied:

If her menstruation has ceased because of illness or breastfeeding, she must wait until that condition ends and she menstruates, according to the consensus of the scholars.

If her menstruation has ceased for a reason unknown to her, then, according to the sounder of the scholars’ two opinions, she comes under the ruling stated by ‘Umar: “She should wait a year, then she may marry.” This is Ahmad’s established position within his school and one opinion of al-Shāfi‘ī.

If she belongs to “the first category,” her marriage is invalid. The judge who separated them was correct to do so and was also correct to discipline whoever did this. If she belongs to “the second category” and a judge married her, no other judge was entitled to separate them, and no divorce took effect, for a judge may act in such a matter according to the sounder of the two views.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was also asked:

A divorced woman who was breastfeeding found that her menstruation was slow to return, so she took medicine to induce it and then had three menstrual periods. Does her waiting period thereby end or not?

فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ إذَا أَتَى الْحَيْضُ الْمَعْرُوفُ لِذَلِكَ اعْتَدَّتْ بِهِ.
 كَمَا أَنَّهَا لَوْ شَرِبَتْ دَوَاءً قَطَعَ الْحَيْضَ أَوْ بَاعَدَ بَيْنَهُ:
 كَانَ ذَلِكَ طُهْرًا. وَكَمَا لَوْ جَاعَتْ أَوْ تَعِبَتْ؛ أَوْ أَتَتْ غَيْرَ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَسْبَابِ الَّتِي تُسَخِّنُ طَبْعَهَا وَتُثِيرُ الدَّمَ فَحَاضَتْ بِذَلِكَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ شَابَتْ لَمْ تَبْلُغْ سِنَّ الْإِيَاسِ وَكَانَتْ عَادَتُهَا أَنْ تَحِيضَ فَشَرِبَتْ دَوَاءً فَانْقَطَعَ عَنْهَا الدَّمُ وَاسْتَمَرَّ انْقِطَاعُهُ؛
 ثُمَّ طَلَّقَهَا زَوْجُهَا وَهِيَ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْحَالَةِ:
 فَهَلْ تَكُونُ عِدَّتُهَا مِنْ حِينِ الطَّلَاقِ بِالشُّهُورِ أَوْ تَتَرَبَّصُ حَتَّى تَبْلُغَ سِنَّ الْآيِسَاتِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، إنْ كَانَتْ تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الدَّمَ 
[لَا]
 
(١)
 يَأْتِي فِيمَا بَعْدُ فَعِدَّتُهَا ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْهُرٍ. وَإِنْ كَانَ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يَعُودَ الدَّمُ وَيُمْكِنُ أَنْ لَا يَعُودَ فَإِنَّهَا تَتَرَبَّصُ بَعْدَ سَنَةٍ ثُمَّ تَتَزَوَّجُ كَمَا قَضَى بِهِ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ فِي الْمَرْأَةِ يَرْتَفِعُ حَيْضُهَا لَا تَدْرِي مَا رَفَعَهُ؛
 فَإِنَّهَا تَتَرَبَّصُ سَنَةً وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ الْجُمْهُورِ:
 كَمَالِكِ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ.
 وَمَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّهَا تَدْخُلُ فِي سِنِّ الْآيِسَاتِ: فَهَذَا قَوْلٌ ضَعِيفٌ جِدًّا؛ مَعَ مَا فِيهِ مِنْ الضَّرَرِ الَّذِي لَا تَأْتِي الشَّرِيعَةُ بِمِثْلِهِ؛ أَوْ تُمْنَعُ مِنْ النِّكَاحِ وَقْتَ حَاجَتِهَا إلَيْهِ وَيُؤْذَنُ لَهَا فِيهِ حِينَ لَا تَحْتَاجُ إلَيْهِ.

translated_text:
He replied:

Yes. If she experiences the usual menstrual bleeding, she counts it towards her waiting period. Likewise, if she takes medicine that stops menstruation or lengthens the interval between periods, that interval counts as a period of purity. The same applies if hunger, fatigue, or other causes that warm her constitution and stir the blood bring on menstruation. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A woman whose hair had turned grey, but who had not reached menopause, used to menstruate regularly. She took medicine, whereupon her bleeding stopped and remained absent. Her husband then divorced her while she was in this condition. Is her waiting period to be calculated in months from the time of divorce, or must she wait until she reaches menopause?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. If she knows that her bleeding will [not] (1) return, her waiting period is three months. If it may or may not return, she should wait until a year has passed and then marry, as ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb ruled concerning a woman whose menstruation ceases without her knowing what caused it: she should wait a year. This is the position of the majority, including Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī.

As for the view that she must reach menopause, it is very weak indeed, quite apart from the harm it entails—harm of a kind the Sharia does not prescribe. Or should she be prevented from marrying when she needs to, only to be permitted to marry when she no longer needs to?

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ مَرِضَ مَرَضًا مُتَّصِلًا بِمَوْتِهِ وَلَهُ زَوْجَةٌ فَأَمَرَهَا أَنْ تَخْرُجَ مِنْ دَاخِلِ الدَّارِ إلَى خَارِجِهَا فَتَوَقَّفَتْ عَنْ الْخُرُوجِ فَقَالَ لَهَا:
 أَنْتِ طَالِقٌ. فَخَرَجَتْ وَحَجَبَتْ وَجْهَهَا عَنْهُ فَطَلَبَهَا فَدَخَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ مُحْتَجِبَةً فَسَأَلَهَا عَنْ احْتِجَابِهَا لِمَا هُوَ؟ فَأَخْبَرَتْهُ بِمَا أَوْقَعَ مِنْ الطَّلَاقِ؛
 فَأَنْكَرَ وَقَالَ:
 مَا حَلَفْت وَلَا طَلَّقْت وَمَاتَ بَعْدَ أَيَّامٍ: فَهَلْ يَلْزَمُهَا الطَّلَاقُ؟ أَمْ عِدَّةُ الْوَفَاةِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
عَلَيْهَا عِدَّةُ الْوَفَاةِ مَعَ عِدَّةِ الطَّلَاقِ؛ وَلَهَا الْمِيرَاثُ. هَذَا إنْ كَانَ عَقْلُهُ حَاضِرًا حِينَ تَكَلَّمَ بِالطَّلَاقِ؛ وَإِنْ كَانَ عَقْلُهُ غَائِبًا لَمْ يَلْزَمْهَا إلَّا عِدَّةُ الْوَفَاةِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man suffered an illness that continued until his death. He ordered his wife to leave the house, but she hesitated to leave, so he said to her, “You are divorced.” She went out and covered her face from him. He then called for her, and she came to him with her face covered. When he asked why she was covering her face, she told him of the divorce he had pronounced. He denied it, saying, “I neither swore an oath nor pronounced a divorce.” He died a few days later. Does the divorce take effect in her case, or must she observe the waiting period following his death?

He replied:

She must observe the waiting period following his death as well as the waiting period for divorce, and she is entitled to inherit from him. This applies if he was in possession of his faculties when he pronounced the divorce. If he was not in possession of his faculties, she is required to observe only the waiting period following his death. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ تَزَوَّجَ امْرَأَةً مِنْ مُدَّةِ ثَلَاثِ سِنِينَ وَرُزِقَ مِنْهَا وَلَدًا لَهُ مِنْ الْعُمْرِ سَنَتَانِ وَذَكَرَتْ أَنَّهَا لَمَّا تَزَوَّجَتْ لَمْ تَحِضْ إلَّا حَيْضَتَيْنِ وَصَدَّقَهَا الزَّوْجُ وَكَانَ قَدْ طَلَّقَهَا ثَانِيًا عَلَى هَذَا الْعَقْدِ الْمَذْكُورِ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ الطَّلَاقُ عَلَى هَذَا الْعَقْدِ الْمَفْسُوخِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ صَدَّقَهَا الزَّوْجُ فِي كَوْنِهَا تَزَوَّجَتْ قَبْلَ الْحَيْضَةِ الثَّالِثَةِ فَالنِّكَاحُ بَاطِلٌ وَعَلَيْهِ أَنْ يُفَارِقَهَا. وَعَلَيْهَا أَنْ تُكْمِلَ عِدَّةَ الْأَوَّلِ ثُمَّ تَعْتَدَّ مِنْ وَطْءِ الثَّانِي. فَإِنْ كَانَتْ حَاضَتْ الثَّالِثَةَ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَطَأَهَا الثَّانِي فَقَدْ انْقَضَتْ عِدَّةُ الْأَوَّلِ؛ ثُمَّ إذَا فَارَقَهَا الثَّانِي اعْتَدَّتْ لَهُ ثَلَاثَ حِيَضٍ ثُمَّ تَزَوَّجُ مَنْ شَاءَتْ بِنِكَاحِ جَدِيدٍ. وَوَلَدُهُ وَلَدُ حَلَالٍ يَلْحَقُهُ نَسَبُهُ؛ وَإِنْ كَانَ قَدْ وُلِدَ بِوَطْءِ فِي عَقْدٍ فَاسِدٍ لَا يُعْلَمُ فَسَادُهُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man married a woman three years ago and was blessed with a child by her, now two years old. She stated that when she married him, she had experienced only two menstrual periods, and her husband accepted her account. He had divorced her a second time under this same marriage contract. Does divorce take effect under this annulled contract?

He replied:

If the husband accepts her statement that she married before her third menstrual period, the marriage is invalid, and he must separate from her. She must complete her waiting period from the first husband and then observe a waiting period on account of intercourse with the second husband. If she had experienced her third menstrual period before the second husband had intercourse with her, her waiting period from the first husband had ended. Then, when the second husband separates from her, she must observe a waiting period of three menstrual periods on his account, after which she may marry whomever she wishes under a new marriage contract. His child is legitimate and is legally attributed to him, even if the child was born of intercourse under an invalid marriage contract whose invalidity was unknown.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

A woman observing the waiting period following her husband’s death must wait four months and ten days. She must avoid adornment and perfume on her body and clothing: she must neither adorn nor perfume herself, nor wear clothing intended for adornment. She must remain in her home, going out during the day only for a need, and at night only out of necessity.

She may eat anything Allah has permitted, such as fruit and meat, whether from male or female animals. The Muslim scholars agree that she may eat these things. Likewise, she may drink any permissible beverages. She may wear cotton, linen, and other fabrics Allah has permitted. She is not required to make white garments, or garments of any other colour, for her waiting period; rather, she may wear checked garments. However, she must not wear clothing that women use for adornment, such as red, yellow, bright green, bright blue, and similar colours. She must not wear jewellery, such as bracelets, anklets, and necklaces, nor apply henna or any other dye to herself.

She is not prohibited from undertaking any permissible work, such as embroidery, sewing, spinning, and other activities women engage in.

translated_text:
And she may do anything else that is permissible for her outside the waiting period, such as speaking to men whom she needs to address, provided she is properly covered, and other such matters.

What I have described is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which the wives of the Companions followed when their husbands died, as did his own wives. Unlike other women, his wives may never marry anyone after him, whether during the waiting period or afterwards. Muslims must honour them as a man honours his own mother. However, no man other than a mahram (unmarriageable relative) may be alone with any one of them or travel with her. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning a woman observing the waiting period following her husband’s death who has not remained in her home during it, but goes out for necessities recognized by Islamic law: must she repeat the waiting period? Does she incur sin by doing this?

He replied:

The waiting period ends once four months and ten days have elapsed from the time of death, and she does not have to make it up. If she went out for something necessary and spent the nights only in her own home, there is no blame upon her.

If, however, she went out without need and spent the night away from home without need, or spent the night away without necessity, or failed to observe the prescribed mourning, she should seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him for that. She does not have to repeat the waiting period.

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning a man who died, whose wife observed her waiting period for forty days, but was unable to disobey the sultan’s decree and then travelled to Cairo, without adorning herself with perfume or anything else: is it permissible to propose marriage to her?

He replied:

The waiting period ends after four months and ten days. If any of this period remains, she must complete it in her home and not go out by night or day except out of necessity. She must avoid adornment and perfume on her body and clothes. She may eat whatever lawful food she wishes, smell fruit, and meet anyone whom she may lawfully meet outside the waiting period. However, if someone proposes marriage to her, she must not explicitly accept his proposal. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning a woman who intended to perform Hajj with her husband, but whose husband died in Shaʿbān: is she permitted to perform Hajj?

He replied:

She may not travel for Hajj during the waiting period following her husband’s death, according to the schools of the four imams.

translated_text:
Chapter on the Waiting Period to Establish the Absence of Pregnancy

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning a man who bought a slave woman, then had intercourse with her two or three days later, before she menstruated, and sold her after ten days: may her second master have intercourse with her before she menstruates?

He replied:

By agreement of the imams, he was not permitted to have intercourse with her before ensuring that she had observed the waiting period to establish that she was not pregnant. As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“There must be no intercourse with a pregnant woman until she gives birth, nor with a woman who is not pregnant until she has observed one menstrual period to establish the absence of pregnancy.”

Likewise, by agreement of the imams, the second purchaser may not have intercourse with her until she menstruates while in his ownership. Indeed, according to one of the two scholarly opinions, the man who had intercourse with her may not sell her until he has ensured that she has observed this waiting period.

Is one waiting period required of him and another of the purchaser? Or are two waiting periods required? Or does a single waiting period suffice for both? There are two opinions. Allah knows best.

Chapter on Breastfeeding

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

As for women forbidden in marriage through breastfeeding, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“What is forbidden through blood relationship is also forbidden through breastfeeding.”

In another wording:

“What is forbidden through birth is also forbidden through breastfeeding.”

This is a matter of agreement among Muslim scholars; I know of no disagreement concerning it among the recognized scholars. If a child breastfeeds from a woman on five occasions within the first two years of life, before weaning, the child becomes hers by agreement of the imams. The man whose intercourse with her brought about her lactation likewise becomes the father of the breastfed child, by agreement of the renowned imams. This is called “laban al-fahl” (milk attributed to the male).

This is established by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“For ‘Ā’ishah had been breastfed by a woman whose husband was called Abū al-Qu‘ays. His brother came seeking permission to enter her presence, but she refused to grant him permission until she asked

He also said:

“What is forbidden through blood relationship is also forbidden through breastfeeding.”

When the man and woman become the parents of the breastfed child, all their children become that child’s siblings, whether they are children of the father alone, the woman alone, or both, or are their children through breastfeeding. All become siblings of this child through breastfeeding. Thus, even if a man has two wives, one of whom breastfeeds a boy and the other a girl, the two children become siblings and may not marry one another, according to the agreement of the four imams and the majority of Muslim scholars.

Ibn ‘Abbās was asked about this “question” and replied, “The source of conception is one and the same”—meaning that the man whose intercourse with the two women brought about their lactation is one and the same.

By the agreement of the Muslims, there is no distinction between the woman’s children who nursed alongside the child and those born to her before or after the breastfeeding. Muslims are agreed on this.

The belief held by many ignorant people—that marriage is forbidden only to someone who nursed alongside the child—is misguidance for anyone who holds it unless he abandons it. If he persists in considering such a marriage lawful, he is to be called upon to repent, just as anyone else who permits marriage between siblings through breastfeeding is called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be put to death.

Since this is so, “all the woman’s relatives are relatives of the breastfed child through breastfeeding”: her children are his siblings, her children’s children are his siblings’ children, and her male and female ancestors

However, “the daughters of his maternal uncles and aunts through breastfeeding” are lawful for him to marry, just as their counterparts through blood relationship are lawful.

The man’s relatives are likewise his relatives through breastfeeding: his siblings’ children, and their children, are his siblings’ children. The man’s brothers and sisters are his paternal uncles and aunts, whom he may not marry. He may, however, marry the daughters of his paternal uncles and aunts.

The breastfed child’s children have the same standing as he does, just as a biological child’s children have the same standing as their parent. Thus, his children, whether through blood relationship or breastfeeding, may not marry his siblings or his father’s siblings, whether related by blood or breastfeeding, because these are their paternal and maternal uncles and aunts.

As for the breastfed child’s siblings through blood relationship, or through breastfeeding by a woman other than this wet nurse, they are unrelated to her and her relatives. The siblings in question may therefore marry the wet nurse’s children. This is comparable to a man having a brother through his father and a sister through his mother, or vice versa: those two may marry one another, whereas he himself may marry neither.

Likewise, the breastfed child himself may not marry any of his wet nurse’s children or any of his own parents’ children: the former are his siblings through breastfeeding, and the latter are his siblings through blood relationship. His siblings through breastfeeding may marry his siblings through blood relationship, just as his siblings through his father may marry his siblings through his mother. The scholars agree on all of this.

Yet some who undertake to issue fatwas may take a strict approach to these matters because they are unclear to those seeking rulings, who do not describe what they are asking about using the names and distinctions relevant under Islamic law. Someone might ask, for example: “Two people have become siblings through breastfeeding. May one marry the other’s sister?” This question lacks sufficient detail. The breastfed person himself may not marry any of the other’s sisters born to the mother who breastfed him. If, however, the other has sisters born to a different mother, they are unrelated to the breastfed person, and he may marry any of them.

Likewise, someone might ask: “A boy and a girl, or two boys, have become siblings through breastfeeding. May either marry a sibling of the other, and may the sisters on either side marry into the other family?” The answer is that the brothers of either breastfeeding sibling may marry the sisters of the other, provided that the prospective husband was not breastfed by the prospective wife’s mother, nor the prospective wife by the prospective husband’s mother. The scholars agree on this.

As for the two breastfeeding siblings themselves, neither may marry any of the wet nurse’s children. Thus, neither may marry a sibling of the other who shares the mother who breastfed him or the father to whom the milk is attributed. Each may, however, marry a sibling of the other who is not a child of either of his own parents through breastfeeding. This answers the various cases in question.

The possibilities are for the breastfed child to marry a sibling of the other breastfed child through that woman or man, or to marry a sibling of the other through blood relationship or through another breastfeeding relationship. The breastfed child’s siblings, in turn, might marry someone from the first, second, or third of these groups.

and those of her husband, whether through blood or breastfeeding. The siblings of one may marry the siblings of the other; indeed, a person’s biological father may marry that person’s sister through breastfeeding. As for the wet nurse’s children, none may marry the breastfed person or his children. Nor may the breastfed person marry any children of his brothers or sisters, whether the sibling relationship is through blood or breastfeeding, since he would be their paternal or maternal uncle. All of this is agreed upon among the scholars.

Regarding the breastfeeding that establishes a marriage prohibition, there are three well-known opinions, all three reported from Ahmad.

The first is that breastfeeding establishes this prohibition whether the amount is great or small. This is the position of Mālik and Abū Hanīfa, based on the Quran’s unrestricted wording.

The second is that one or two breastfeedings do not establish the prohibition, but more than that does. This is the position of a group of scholars, based on the Prophet’s statement, blessings and peace be upon him, in an authentic hadith:

“One or two breastfeedings do not establish a marriage prohibition.”

Another version reads, “one suck or two,” and another, “one suckling or two.” Thus, he excluded these two amounts from establishing the prohibition, while all other amounts remain covered by the general wording and its implied meaning.

The third is that nothing less than five breastfeedings establishes the prohibition. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s position and the apparent position of Ahmad’s school, based on two authentic hadiths. The first is the hadith of ʿĀʾisha:

“Among what was revealed of the Quran were ten specified breastfeedings, which were then abrogated by five specified breastfeedings. The Messenger of Allah, blessings and peace be upon him, passed away while the matter remained thus.”

The other is his instruction, blessings and peace be upon him, to the wife of Abū Hudhayfa ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa to breastfeed Sālim, the freedman of Abū Hudhayfa ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, five times, so that he would thereby become her mahram—a man permanently forbidden to her in marriage.

translated_text:
Accordingly, in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, a single breastfeeding does not mean a full feeding in which the child takes the breast, releases it, then takes it again and releases it, continuing until satisfied. Rather, if the child takes the breast and then releases it voluntarily, that counts as one breastfeeding, whether it satisfies him or he needs several breastfeedings to be satisfied. If he then takes the breast again, suckles, and releases it, that counts as another breastfeeding. If he releases it involuntarily and returns shortly afterwards, there is disagreement concerning this.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Which marriages does breastfeeding prohibit, and which does it not prohibit? What is the evidence for the hadith of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her:

“The same marriages are forbidden through breastfeeding as through blood kinship”?

Please explain all the marriage prohibitions it establishes. Do the scholars differ concerning this? If they do, what is the correct and stronger opinion? Does breastfeeding an older child who has not reached puberty, or one who reaches puberty, have the same ruling as breastfeeding a young infant? Some women breastfeed their children for five years, or more or less. Can breastfeeding between some of their relatives establish a marriage prohibition between a husband and wife? Please explain this thoroughly.

Answer:

Praise be to Allah. The hadith of ʿĀʾisha is authentic, its authenticity is agreed upon, and it has been universally accepted. The imams have agreed to act upon it. Its wording is:

“The same marriages are forbidden through breastfeeding as through

blood kinship.”

The second wording is:

“The same marriages are forbidden through breastfeeding as through birth.”

Some later jurists have excluded two cases from this general rule, while others have excluded more. This is mistaken, for nothing needs to be excluded from the hadith. We explain this as follows:

If an infant receives five breastfeedings from a woman within the first two years of life, she becomes his mother, and her husband, through whose intercourse the milk was produced, becomes his father. Thus, he becomes the son of each of them through breastfeeding. All the woman’s children, whether by this man or another, and all the man’s children, whether by her or another woman, consequently become his siblings, regardless of whether they were born before or after the breastfeeding. The imams agree on this.

Since their children are his siblings, their grandchildren are his siblings’ children. He therefore may not marry any of their children or grandchildren, because they are either his siblings or his siblings’ children, and such marriages are forbidden through birth.

The woman’s brothers and sisters are his maternal uncles and aunts through breastfeeding, and her father and mother are his grandparents through breastfeeding. He therefore may not marry any of her brothers or sisters. The man’s siblings are his paternal uncles and aunts, and the man’s father and mothers are his grandfathers and grandmothers. He may therefore marry neither his paternal uncles and aunts nor his grandfathers and grandmothers. He may, however, marry the children of his paternal uncles and aunts. For all a man’s relatives are forbidden to him [except] the children of his paternal uncles and aunts and the children of his maternal uncles and aunts, as Allah states in His words:

translated_text:
“O Prophet, We have made lawful for you your wives whose dowries you have paid, those whom your right hand possesses from what Allah has granted you, and the daughters of your paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles and maternal aunts who emigrated with you.”

These “four categories” are the relatives whom one may marry, so their counterparts through breastfeeding may also be married. Since the breastfed child becomes the son of the woman and her husband, his children become their grandchildren, and the same marriage prohibitions apply to his children as apply to biological children. It is through these three lines that the marriage prohibitions arising from breastfeeding extend.

As for the breastfed child’s biological siblings, father and mother, they are unrelated to his father, mother and siblings through breastfeeding. No tie of kinship, whether through blood or breastfeeding, connects the two groups. A man may have a paternal half-brother and a maternal half-brother with no blood relationship between them. Indeed, his paternal half-brother may marry his maternal half-sister. How much more so when one is a brother through blood and the other a sister through breastfeeding: the one may marry the other, and vice versa.

This dispels a misconception that occurs to some people. The breastfed child’s brother through breastfeeding may marry his biological mother, just as he may marry his biological sister. His biological brother may also marry his sister through breastfeeding. This has no counterpart in blood kinship, for a man’s biological brother cannot marry his biological mother. His sister through breastfeeding is neither a daughter nor a stepdaughter of his biological father; she may therefore marry him.

translated_text:
Someone who has not examined the matter carefully may therefore say: “Blood kinship forbids my brother to marry my mother, whereas breastfeeding does not impose the corresponding prohibition.” This is mistaken. The breastfeeding counterpart of what is forbidden through blood kinship is for his sister or brother through breastfeeding to marry this brother’s son or his mother through breastfeeding. For example, if he and another child were breastfed by one woman, with the milk attributable to one man, his sister through breastfeeding is forbidden to marry his brother or sister through breastfeeding, since both are siblings of the breastfed child. Likewise, neither of them may marry his father or mother through breastfeeding, because they are those parents’ children through breastfeeding—not because they are siblings of their children. Whoever reflects on this and similar cases will have the confusion dispelled.

As for “breastfeeding an adult,” it does not establish marriage prohibitions according to the four imams. Such prohibitions arise only from breastfeeding a young child, such as one breastfed within the first two years. The imams disagree concerning a child breastfed close to the two-year limit, but the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad is that this does not establish marriage prohibitions.

An adult man and an adult woman do not become forbidden to one another in marriage through the breastfeeding of relatives. For example, if his wife breastfeeds his biological brother, his wife does not thereby become forbidden to him. As explained above, he may marry a woman who is his biological brother’s sister through breastfeeding, since neither blood kinship nor breastfeeding connects him to her. His wife becomes forbidden only to his brother, because she is his brother’s mother through breastfeeding, not his own. The breastfed child’s mother through breastfeeding does not become the mother of his biological siblings, because she breastfed that child alone, not the others.

translated_text:
if a man had several women with whom he had intercourse, and each breastfed a child, those children could not marry one another. Thus, when Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about this, he said: “The source of conception is the same.” This is the position of the four imams, based on the well-known hadith concerning Abū al-Quʿays, narrated by ʿĀʾishah in the two Sahīh collections.

A man is forbidden to marry his biological brother’s mother because she is either his own mother or his father’s wife, both of whom are forbidden to him. His breastfeeding brother’s mother, however, is neither his own mother nor his father’s wife, because her husband—the man to whom her milk is attributable—is not his father, either through blood kinship or breastfeeding.

If someone argues, “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Whatever is forbidden through blood kinship is also forbidden through breastfeeding.’ Since his biological brother’s mother is forbidden to him, his breastfeeding brother’s mother must likewise be forbidden,” we reply:

This is misleading and deceptive. Allah did not say, “Forbidden to you are your sisters’ mothers.” Rather, He said:

“Forbidden to you are your mothers.”

And He, Most High, said:

“And do not marry those women whom your fathers married.”

Thus, He forbade a man to marry his own mother or a woman married to his father, even if she is not his mother. The corresponding prohibition applies through breastfeeding, so he may not marry his mother through breastfeeding. As for a woman married to his father through breastfeeding, the well-known position among the imams is that she is forbidden to him. There is, however, disagreement concerning her, because this prohibition arises from affinity through marriage, not blood kinship or birth.

Whether she is forbidden is not the question under discussion here. If we say that a woman married to his father through breastfeeding is forbidden to him, we have upheld the hadith’s full general scope. Another relates that a man from Banū ‘Āmir ibn Sa‘sa‘ah said, “O Messenger of Allah, does a single feeding establish a marriage prohibition?” He replied, “No.”

Another is the report from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said:

He replied:

There is well-known disagreement on this issue within al-Shāfi‘ī’s school. According to the well-known position reported from Ahmad, nothing short of five breastfeedings establishes a marriage prohibition. This is based on the aforementioned hadith of ‘Ā’ishah and the hadith concerning Sālim, the freedman of Abū Hudhayfah, in which:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed the wife of Abū Hudhayfah ibn ‘Utbah ibn Abī Rabī‘ah to breastfeed him five times.”

This is also recorded in the Sahīh. Thus, fewer than five breastfeedings do not establish a marriage prohibition; five are required.

Another view holds that three or more establish a marriage prohibition. This is the position of a group of scholars, including Abū Thawr and others, and is also one position reported from Ahmad. They cite the following report in the Sahīh:

“Neither one suck nor two, nor one suckling nor two, establishes a marriage prohibition.”

They say that this implies that three establish a marriage prohibition. These scholars did not rely on the hadith of ‘Ā’ishah, explaining: “A passage can only be established as Quran through mass transmission, and this report has not been transmitted in that manner.”

The proponents of the first view responded: “We have two authentic hadiths affirming this ruling. One of them conveys two things: a ruling and its status as Quran. The ruling can be established through authentic reports. As for its status as Quran, we neither establish that nor regard it as Quran; rather, its text was abrogated while its ruling remained in force.”

They offered two responses to this objection:

First, there is another authentic hadith on this matter. Moreover, it has not been established that this remained part of the Quran, though its ruling remained in force.

Second, most scholars do not accept this principle; rather, it is Abū Hanīfah’s position. Indeed, Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr reported a scholarly consensus that a non-canonical reading authentically transmitted from the Companions may be used as evidence for legal rulings.

The second view on this issue is that breastfeeding establishes a marriage prohibition regardless of how little or much it involves. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik, and a weakly transmitted position from Ahmad.

Its proponents cite the apparent meaning of Allah’s words:

“And your mothers who breastfed you and your sisters through breastfeeding.”

They maintain that the term “breastfeeding” is unrestricted in the Quran. As for the hadiths, some scholars had not received them, some considered them weak, and others thought they contradicted the Quran’s apparent meaning and held that solitary reports could neither qualify the general scope of the Quran nor restrict its unrestricted wording.

Those holding the former view replied: “These reports are authentic and established according to hadith scholars. The fact that they did not reach some of the early scholars does not warrant disregarding them on the part of those who know them to be authentic.”

As for the Quran, it may be argued that, just as other evidence establishes that breastfeeding is restricted to a particular age, it likewise establishes that it is restricted to a particular amount.

Similarly, the Sunnah establishes the amount of compensation required in Allah’s words:

“Then compensation by fasting, charity, or sacrifice.”

This is so even though the transmitted report is a solitary report. Indeed, it is just as the Sunnah establishes that “a woman may not be married to a man who is already married to her paternal aunt

“Take charity from their wealth to purify and cleanse them thereby.”

The mass-transmitted Sunnah also explains matters of worship, expiation, and prescribed punishments that the Quran leaves unrestricted. The Sunnah thus explains and clarifies the Quran, indicates its meaning, and gives expression to it.

Specifying “five” has many precedents in Islamic law. Islam is built upon five pillars; the obligatory prayers are five; no zakat is due on less than five; and the intervals between zakat thresholds are five, ten, or fifteen. Righteousness comprises five matters, as Allah Most High says:

“Rather, righteousness is to believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture, and the prophets.”

Regarding disbelief, He says:

“Whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day…”

There are also the five messengers of firm resolve. In light of these and similar examples, specifying the amount of breastfeeding that establishes a marriage prohibition is not unusual within the principles of Islamic law.

If breastfeeding establishes a marriage prohibition because it causes flesh to grow and bones to develop, then the child’s growth through it is like his growth from his parents. Breastfeeding prohibits only those marriages that birth prohibits. This is why breastfeeding an adult does not establish a marriage prohibition: it is merely like food and drink.

One or two feeds have no effect. They may be disregarded, just as an amount below the minimum threshold for theft is disregarded, so that hands are not cut off for something trifling. If, however, there is doubt whether the milk entered the child’s stomach, then undoubtedly we do not rule that a marriage prohibition has been established, even if it is known that the milk entered his mouth. By the agreement of the Muslims, milk merely entering the mouth does not establish a marriage prohibition.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“Two sisters each have daughters and sons. If each sister breastfeeds the other’s daughters, do those daughters become forbidden in marriage to the sons?”

He replied:

If a woman breastfeeds a little girl five times within the girl’s first two years, the girl becomes her daughter. All the nursing woman’s children thus become siblings of the nursed girl, male and female alike, whether born before or after the breastfeeding. None of the nursing woman’s sons may therefore marry the nursed girl. The nursed girl’s brothers, however, may marry the nursing woman’s daughters, provided those daughters were not breastfed by the brothers’ mother. The underlying principle is that the nursing woman becomes the nursed girl’s mother, so her children become forbidden to the girl in marriage. The nursing woman’s brothers and sisters become the girl’s maternal uncles and aunts. The man to whom the milk is attributed becomes her father, and his children, whether by that woman or another, become her siblings. His brothers and sisters become her paternal uncles and aunts. The nursed child, his children and his grandchildren are regarded as offspring of the nursing woman and the man whose intercourse caused the milk to flow. As for the nursed child’s biological brothers, sisters, father and mother, they remain outside this kinship: no marriage prohibition arises for them from this breastfeeding. All four imams agree on this, although they differ over other matters.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“Two men were breastfed by the same woman, and one of them had a daughter. May the other marry her?”

He replied:

If a child is breastfed by a woman five times within his first two years, he becomes her son, and all her children become his siblings, whether she gave birth to them before or after the breastfeeding. Breastfeeding establishes the same marriage prohibitions as birth, according to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah

إذَا ارْتَضَعَ مَعَهَا خَمْسَ رَضَعَاتٍ فِي الْحَوْلَيْنِ صَارَ ابْنًا لَهَا؛ حَرُمَ عَلَيْهِ جَمِيعُ بَنَاتِهَا مِنْ وُلِدَ قَبْلَ الرَّضَاعِ وَمَنْ وُلِدَ بَعْدَهُ؛ لِأَنَّهُنَّ أَخَوَاتُهُ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ. وَمَتَى ارْتَضَعَتْ الْمَخْطُوبَةُ مِنْ أُمٍّ لَمْ يَجُزْ لَهَا أَنْ تَتَزَوَّجَ وَاحِدًا مِنْ بَنِي الْمُرْضِعَةِ. وَأَمَّا إذَا كَانَ الْخَاطِبُ لَمْ يَرْتَضِعْ مِنْ أُمِّ الْمَخْطُوبَةِ وَلَا هِيَ رَضَعَتْ مِنْ أُمِّهِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَتَزَوَّجَ أَحَدُهُمَا بِالْآخَرِ. بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَإِنْ كَانَ إخْوَتُهَا تَرَاضَعَا. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ اسْتَأْجَرَتْ لِبِنْتِهَا مُرْضِعَةً يَوْمًا أَوْ شَهْرًا وَمَضَتْ السُّنُونَ وَلِلْمُرْضِعَةِ وَلَدٌ قَبْلَهَا:
 فَهَلْ يَحِلُّ لَهُمَا الزَّوَاجُ؟
translated_text:
—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the agreement of the imams. Neither man may therefore marry the other’s daughter, just as he may not marry his biological brother’s daughter, by agreement of the imams.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man has two female cousins, sisters who are daughters of his maternal aunt. One was breastfed with him, while the other was not. May he marry the one who was not breastfed with him?”

He replied:

If he received five breastfeedings from the same woman as she did within his first two years, he became the nursing woman’s son. All her daughters became forbidden to him in marriage, whether born before or after the breastfeeding, because they are his sisters, by agreement of the scholars. Whenever a prospective bride has been breastfed by a woman, she may not marry any of that woman’s sons. However, if the suitor was not breastfed by the prospective bride’s mother, and she was not breastfed by his mother, they may marry one another, by agreement of the scholars, even if her siblings shared breastfeeding. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“A woman hired a wet nurse to breastfeed her daughter for a day or a month, and years have since passed. The wet nurse has a son born before the girl. Is it lawful for the two to marry?”
