If he marries her and consummates the marriage, they must be separated, without any disagreement among the imams. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man has a female companion. He and her father were not breastfed together, but their younger siblings were. Is he permitted to marry her? If he consummates the marriage and is blessed with a child by her, what is the ruling concerning them? What do the scholars say about their situation?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If he was not breastfed by her mother, nor she by his mother, but rather his siblings were breastfed by her mother and her siblings by his mother, then she is lawful for him to marry, by agreement of the Muslims. She is in the same position as the sister of his paternal half-brother.

Breastfeeding extends the prohibition of marriage to the breastfed child and his descendants, to the wet nurse, and to her husband whose intercourse with her caused her to produce milk. The wet nurse is his wife, and her children, whether born before or after the breastfeeding, become siblings of the breastfed child. The man becomes his father, and his children, whether born before or after the breastfeeding, become siblings of the breastfed child. As for the breastfed child’s biological siblings and parents, they have no kinship through breastfeeding with his parents or siblings through breastfeeding.

All of this is agreed upon among the Muslims, including the extension of the prohibition of marriage to the man. This is known as “the question of milk attributed to the husband.” What we have stated is the position of the four imams and the majority of the Companions and their successors.

Some of the early scholars held that milk attributed to the husband does not establish a prohibition of marriage. The authentic texts, however, confirm the position of the majority.

 فَهَذَا اللَّبَنُ يَنْشُرُ الْحُرْمَةَ فَإِذَا ارْتَضَعَتْ طِفْلَةٌ خَمْسَ رَضَعَاتٍ صَارَتْ بِنْتَهَا وَابْنُ بِنْتِهَا ابْنَ أُخْتِهَا وَهِيَ خَالَتُهُ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ الِارْتِضَاعُ مَعَ طِفْلٍ أَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ. وَأَمَّا أُخْتُهَا مِنْ النَّسَبِ الَّتِي لَمْ تَرْضِعْ فَيَحِلُّ لَهُ أَنْ يَتَزَوَّجَ بِهَا. وَلَوْ قَدَّرَ أَنَّ هَذَا اللَّبَنَ ثَابَ لِامْرَأَةٍ لَمْ تَتَزَوَّجْ قَطُّ فَهَذَا يَنْشُرُ الْحُرْمَةَ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَهِيَ رِوَايَةٌ عَنْ أَحْمَد. وَظَاهِرُ مَذْهَبِهِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَنْشُرُ الْحُرْمَةَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:

As for the nursed child’s biological siblings, father, and mother, they acquire no milk-kinship, and marriage to his milk-sisters is permissible for them—just as a man’s maternal half-sister may marry his paternal half-brother. All of this is agreed upon among the Muslims, without dispute. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A married woman had milk that was not due to childbirth or pregnancy. She breastfed a girl under two years old on five separate occasions. This nursing woman is the girl’s paternal aunt by blood. Later, the nursing woman’s daughter’s son wished to marry the girl she had breastfed. Is this forbidden?”

He replied:

If her husband had intercourse with her and she subsequently began producing milk, breastfeeding with this milk establishes marriage prohibitions. Thus, if a girl nurses from her on five occasions, she becomes her daughter; the woman’s daughter’s son becomes the girl’s nephew, and she becomes his maternal aunt. This applies whether or not another child was also being nursed. As for the girl’s biological sister who was not breastfed, he may marry her.

Even supposing that such milk appeared in a woman who had never married, it establishes marriage prohibitions according to the schools of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and al-Shāfiʿī. This is also one position reported from Ahmad. The apparent position of his school, however, is that it does not establish marriage prohibitions. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man proposed to a female relative, but her father said, ‘She was breastfed with you,’ and forbade him to marry her. After his own father died, he married her. Trustworthy witnesses had attested that her mother acknowledged having breastfed him. Later, however, she denied it, saying, ‘I only said that to serve a purpose.’ Is marriage to her lawful?”

He replied:

If the mother is known to be truthful and states that she breastfed him on five occasions, her statement is accepted. If he has married her daughter, the couple must be separated, according to the more correct of the two scholarly opinions. As established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī:

“The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ordered ‘Uqbah ibn al-Hārith to separate from his wife when a black slave woman stated that she had breastfed them both.”

If, however, there is doubt about her truthfulness or the number of nursing occasions, the marriage is a doubtful matter, and avoiding it is preferable. Nevertheless, no ruling separating the couple is issued without evidence requiring it.

If she retracts her testimony before the marriage, marriage to the woman is not forbidden. But if it is known that her retraction is false and that she retracted because he had prevailed upon her to conceal her testimony, then the marriage is not lawful. And Allah knows best.

 وَاَلَّذِينَ وُلِدُوا بَعْدَهُ:
 هُمْ إخْوَةٌ لِهَذَا الْمُرْتَضِعِ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ أَيْضًا.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man married a woman and had several children with her. Recently, someone who had a dispute with the wife came forward and told her husband, ‘This woman to whom you are married drank your mother’s milk.’”

He replied:

If this man is known to be truthful, knows the matter he reports, and states that she was breastfed by the husband’s mother on five occasions within the first two years of life, his statement is to be accepted in this matter. Otherwise, accepting it is not obligatory, even if he witnessed the breastfeeding. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man, when he was a small child, was breastfed by a woman alongside a daughter of hers. This daughter has younger sisters. Are any of them forbidden to him in marriage?”

He replied:

If he was breastfed by a woman on five occasions within the first two years of life, he becomes her son through breastfeeding. All her children, whether born before or after that breastfeeding, are his siblings. This, too, is a matter of consensus among Muslims.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Two sisters each have a child: one has a son and the other a daughter. The boy’s mother breastfed the girl, but the girl’s mother did not breastfeed the boy. Later, one sister had daughters and the other sons. May the brother of the breastfed child marry the girl who was nursed on the same milk as his brother? Likewise, may the children of one sister marry the children of the other, apart from the two children involved in the breastfeeding?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The girl who was breastfed may not marry any of her nursing mother’s children, whether they were born before or after the breastfeeding. As for the breastfed girl’s siblings, they may marry whichever of the nursing mother’s children they wish. Thus, someone who was not breastfed by a woman may marry one of her children, but he may not marry any of the children of a woman who breastfed him.

If a boy is breastfed by the mother in question, or a girl from among the children in question is breastfed, neither may marry any of the other woman’s children. However, the siblings of either of the two children who shared the nursing may marry the siblings of the other, provided neither prospective spouse was breastfed by the other’s mother. The marriage prohibition applies only to the child who was breastfed, not to that child’s siblings who were not breastfed by that woman. Nevertheless, all the nursing mother’s children are forbidden in marriage to the child she breastfed. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man suffered from inflammation of the eyes and washed them with his wife’s milk. Does she become forbidden to him if her milk reaches his stomach?

“Another man loves his wife and, while playing intimately with her, suckled some of her milk. Does she become forbidden to him?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Washing his eyes with his wife’s milk is permissible, and his wife does not thereby become forbidden to him, for two reasons.

First, he is an adult. If an adult suckles milk from his wife or another woman, this does not establish the marriage prohibitions arising from breastfeeding, according to the four Imams and the overwhelming majority of scholars, as indicated by the Quran and the Sunnah. They regard the hadith narrated by ‘Ā’ishah concerning Sālim, the freedman of Abū Hudhayfah, as specific to that case, because they had adopted him before adoption was prohibited.

Second, milk entering the eye does not establish these marriage prohibitions, and I know of no disagreement concerning this. Scholars have, however, differed over milk administered through the nose, following their disagreement over milk poured into the mouth without suckling. Most scholars hold that pouring milk into the mouth establishes the marriage prohibitions; this is the better-known of the two positions reported from Ahmad. Likewise, administering milk through the nose establishes these prohibitions according to one of the two positions reported from him. This is also the position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik. Al-Shāfi‘ī has two opinions on the matter.

The answer to the second question is that his suckling does not make his wife forbidden to him according to the schools of the four Imams.

فَصْلٌ:
إذَا ارْتَضَعَ الطِّفْلُ مِنْ امْرَأَةٍ خَمْسَ رَضَعَاتٍ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَتِمَّ لَهُ حَوْلَيْنِ فَإِنَّهُ يَصِيرُ وَلَدَهَا؛ فَيَحْرُمُ عَلَيْهِ كُلُّ مَنْ وُلِدَ لَهَا قَبْلَ الرَّضَاعِ وَبَعْدَهُ؛ وَيَصِيرُ زَوْجُهَا الَّذِي أَحْبَلَهَا دَرَّ لَبَنَهَا أَبَاهُ؛ فَيَحْرُمُ عَلَيْهِ جَمِيعُ أَوْلَادِ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلِ. فَإِذَا ارْتَضَعَتْ امْرَأَتُهُ طِفْلًا وَطِفْلَةً كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ خَمْسَ رَضَعَاتٍ لَمْ يَجُزْ أَنْ يَتَزَوَّجَ أَحَدُهُمَا بِالْآخَرِ؛ بَلْ هُمَا أَخَوَانِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ صَبِيٍّ أَرْضَعَتْهُ كَرَّتَيْنِ ثُمَّ حَمَلَتْ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ بِعَشْرِ سِنِينَ؛
 وَجَاءَتْ بِبِنْتٍ وَصَارَ الصَّبِيُّ شَابًّا:
 فَهَلْ لَهُ أَنْ يَتَزَوَّجَ بِتِلْكَ الْبِنْتِ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا ارْتَضَعَ مِنْهَا خَمْسَ رَضَعَاتٍ فِي حَوْلَيْنِ فَقَدْ صَارَ ابْنُهَا؛
 وَيَحْرُمُ عَلَيْهِ كُلُّ مَا وَلَدَتْهُ الْمَرْأَةُ:
 سَوَاءٌ وَلَدَتْهُ قَبْلَ الرَّضَاعِ أَوْ بَعْدَهُ: بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

If a child receives five breastfeeds from a woman before reaching two years of age, he becomes her child. He may therefore not marry any of her children, whether born before or after she breastfed him. Her husband, through whom she became pregnant and produced milk, becomes his father, and he may not marry any of that man’s children. Thus, if his wife breastfeeds a boy and a girl five times each, they may not marry one another; rather, they are siblings. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A woman breastfed a boy on two occasions. Ten years later, she became pregnant and gave birth to a girl, and the boy had become a young man. May he marry that girl or not?”

He replied:

If she breastfed him five times within his first two years, he has become her son. He may not marry any of that woman’s children, whether she gave birth to them before or after breastfeeding him, by scholarly consensus.

and a “breastfeed” consists of the child taking the breast into his mouth, drinking from it, and then letting go. This constitutes one breastfeed. If this happens five times during a single feeding session, these count as five breastfeeds. If it happens five times over two sessions, these likewise count as five breastfeeds. A breastfeed does not mean all that the child drinks during a single feeding session: she may breastfeed him in the morning and then in the evening, giving him many breastfeeds during each session. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“If a boy is breastfed by a woman other than his mother, or a girl is likewise breastfed, whom is the child thereafter forbidden to marry? What constitutes a breastfeed that establishes a marriage prohibition? Does breastfeeding after weaning have any effect in establishing such a prohibition? Does the woman remain forbidden in marriage to someone who has passed the age of breastfeeding, or not?”

He replied:

If a boy or girl receives five breastfeeds from a woman within the first two years of life, the child becomes hers through breastfeeding. The man whose intercourse caused her to produce milk becomes the child’s father through breastfeeding. The woman’s brothers and sisters become the child’s maternal uncles and aunts, and the man’s brothers and sisters become the child’s paternal uncles and aunts. Her parents become the child’s grandfathers and grandmothers, and the children of either of them become the child’s brothers and sisters. All these relatives are forbidden in marriage to the child, for breastfeeding makes marriage unlawful to the same relatives as blood kinship does. Likewise, the children of this breastfed child are forbidden in marriage to his grandfathers and grandmothers, brothers and sisters, paternal uncles and paternal aunts,

and maternal uncles and aunts through breastfeeding. All of this is agreed upon by the Muslims. Thus, the marriage prohibition arising from breastfeeding extends through both parents and through the child.

As for the breastfed child’s father, mother and grandmothers, and brothers and sisters by blood, all of these are unrelated to the nursing woman and her relatives, by agreement of the scholars. His brother by blood may therefore marry his sister through breastfeeding. All the breastfed child’s brothers may marry whichever of the nursing woman’s daughters they wish, including the daughter breastfed alongside the child as well as the others. The breastfed child himself, however, may not marry any of the nursing woman’s children, whether born before or after the breastfeeding, by agreement of the scholars.

Many people make a mistake in this matter: they fail to distinguish between the breastfed child’s siblings by blood, who are unrelated to the woman, and the nursing woman’s children, who are his siblings through breastfeeding. They treat them all as one category, but this is not so. Rather, members of the former group may marry members of the latter. The breastfed child himself, however, may not marry any of the nursing woman’s children.

If a boy and a girl are each breastfed by the other’s mother—the boy by the girl’s mother and the girl by the boy’s mother—and none of her siblings is breastfed by the other child’s mother, each child is forbidden to marry any of his or her nursing mother’s children, whether born before or after the breastfeeding. A brother by blood of either child, however, is not forbidden to marry the other child’s sister through breastfeeding.

translated_text:
And “breastfeeding that unquestionably establishes a marriage prohibition” consists of five feeds: the child takes the breast and drinks, then releases it, then takes it and drinks again, then releases it—even if this occurs within a single period, such as his morning or evening meal. Fewer than five feeds do not establish a marriage prohibition according to the school of al-Shāfi‘ī.

Another view is that any amount, whether little or much, establishes the prohibition, as held by Abū Hanīfah and Mālik. A third view is that no fewer than three feeds establish it. All three views are reported from Ahmad, but the first is the best-known position reported from him, on account of the hadith of ‘Ā’ishah in the two Sahīhs:

“Among what was revealed in the Quran was that ten feeds established a marriage prohibition. This was then abrogated by five feeds, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died while this remained the ruling.”

The Musnad and other works also report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed a woman to breastfeed a person five times so that marriage to her would become forbidden to him.

“Breastfeeding that establishes a marriage prohibition” is that which takes place within the first two years, for the full breastfeeding period is two complete years, as Allah Most High says:

“Mothers shall breastfeed their children for two full years, for those who wish to complete the period of breastfeeding.”

What occurs after the completion of the breastfeeding period does not count as breastfeeding. Thus, the majority of scholars, including the four imams and others, hold that breastfeeding an adult has no legal effect. They cite the report in the two Sahīhs from ‘Ā’ishah, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came in while a man was with me. He asked, ‘Who is this, ‘Ā’ishah?’ I replied, ‘My brother through breastfeeding.’ He said, ‘O ‘Ā’ishah, be mindful of whom you women regard as your brothers! Breastfeeding counts only when it satisfies hunger.’”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated from Umm Salamah that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

translated_text:
in the hadith:

“My son Ibrāhīm died while still a nursing infant.”

That is, while he was still of nursing age. This does not imply that there is no breastfeeding after two years, or after weaning, even if weaning occurs before two full years.

A group of earlier and later scholars held that breastfeeding an adult establishes a marriage prohibition. They cited the report in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere from Zaynab bint Umm Salamah:

“Umm Salamah said to ‘Ā’ishah, ‘An adolescent boy enters your presence whom I would not like to enter mine.’ ‘Ā’ishah replied, ‘Do you not have a good example in the Messenger of Allah?’ She said, ‘The wife of Abū Hudhayfah said, “O Messenger of Allah, Sālim enters my presence, although he is a grown man, and Abū Hudhayfah feels some unease about him.” The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Breastfeed him so that he may enter your presence.”’”

In a version narrated by Mālik in al-Muwatta’, he said:

“Breastfeed him five times.”

He thus had the status of his child through breastfeeding. ‘Ā’ishah acted upon this hadith, while the other wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declined to do so—even though ‘Ā’ishah herself narrated that he said:

“Breastfeeding counts only when it satisfies hunger.”

She nevertheless distinguished between breastfeeding intended to establish a relationship and breastfeeding intended to provide nourishment. When the latter is intended, only breastfeeding before weaning establishes a marriage prohibition. This is the breastfeeding ordinarily practised by people. As for the former, it is permissible when there is a need to establish a relationship that permanently precludes marriage. A need may render permissible what would otherwise not be permissible. This is a tenable view.

Human milk is ritually pure according to the majority of scholars. Some later scholars, however, questioned this and declared it impure.

The scholars differed over whether human milk may be sold on its own, holding three views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. One view permits its sale, as does the school of al-Shāfi‘ī. Another prohibits it, as does the school of Abū Hanīfah. A third permits the sale of an enslaved woman’s milk, but not that of a free woman. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Two women had children, one a son and the other a daughter. The daughter’s mother breastfed the son several times, then the son died. Another son was subsequently born who was not breastfed by that woman. May he marry the daughter mentioned, or is she forbidden to him because his brother was breastfed by her mother?

The answer:

If the biological brother of a breastfed child wishes to marry one of the nursing woman’s daughters, that is permissible by agreement of the imams, whether the breastfed child is alive or dead. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man has a female cousin, the daughter of his paternal uncle. Her father was breastfed by the man’s mother alongside one of the man’s brothers. The man’s mother stated that when he nursed from her, he was more than two years old. May the man marry his paternal uncle’s daughter?

He replied:

If the breastfeeding took place after two full years of age, it establishes no marriage prohibition.

He replied:

This does not prevent the boy from marrying one of this woman’s daughters, for she is not his nursing mother. According to all four imams, mere doubt does not establish a marriage prohibition. Allah knows best.

Chapter on Maintenance and Child Custody

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Concerning Allah Most High’s words:

“Mothers shall breastfeed their children for two full years, for those who wish to complete the nursing period. The father must provide them with food and clothing according to what is reasonable. No soul is burdened beyond its capacity,”

through to His words:

“And know that Allah sees all that you do,”

together with His words:

“And if they are pregnant, maintain them until they give birth. Then, if they breastfeed for you, give them their payment,”

through to His words:

“Allah will bring ease after hardship.”

These passages contain various rulings, some agreed upon and others disputed. If you reflect on Allah’s Book, it becomes clear that it settles disputes among those who know how to refer matters to it. Whoever fails to find guidance in this does so either because of an inability, for which he is excused, or because of negligence, for which he is blameworthy.

Allah Most High’s words, “Two full years, for those who wish to complete the nursing period,” indicate that this constitutes the complete nursing period, and that nursing beyond it is simply one form of nourishment. This is cited as evidence by those who hold that breastfeeding after two years is like breastfeeding an adult.

His words, “Two full years,” indicate that the expression “two years” can refer to one year and part of another. Such usage is well known in Arabic speech. It is said, “So-and-so is twenty years old,” when he has completed that span.

Al-Farrā’, al-Zajjāj and others said: “Since one may say ‘two years’ while meaning less than two—as Allah Most High says, ‘Whoever hastens to leave in two days,’ and it is known that he hastens to leave

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is reported to have said:

“The trustworthy treasurer who willingly gives what he has been instructed to give, fully and undiminished, is one of those who give charity.”

“Full” means that nothing is missing, since completeness is the opposite of deficiency. As for “made plentiful,” the expression used is “their reward made plentiful.” It can refer to something increased, or to something that has not been injured—that is, wounded. Thus, in the report narrated by Imām Ahmad in Kitāb al-Zuhd (The Book of Asceticism), Wahb ibn Munabbih relates that Allah Most High said to Moses:

“This is not because they are of little worth to Me, but so that they may receive their full share of My gracious favor, intact and undiminished, wounded neither by worldly life nor by the nat‘a of desire.”

This concerns a change in quality, whereas the earlier point concerns a reduction in quantity.

Abū al-Faraj mentioned two views on whether the verse applies generally to all mothers or specifically to divorced mothers. The latter is the view of Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, al-Dahhāk, al-Suddī, Muqātil and others. The general application is the view of Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī, al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and others. Al-Qādī said: “For this reason, we hold that she may hire herself out to breastfeed her own child, whether she is still with her husband or divorced.”

I say: The verse is evidence against them, for it requires that nursing mothers be provided with food and clothing according to what is reasonable, but nothing beyond that. Yet he says that she may hire herself out

Rather, if the verse applies generally, it indicates that she breastfeeds her child while her husband provides for her, just as he provides for her when she is pregnant. The child’s maintenance is included in the maintenance due to her as a wife, since the child is nourished through the mother’s nourishment. The same applies during breastfeeding: the maintenance provided for the unborn child is the same as that provided for the nursing infant.

On this understanding, there is no contradiction between the two views. Those who restricted the verse to divorced women required a separate provision for maintenance on account of breastfeeding, as mentioned in Surah al-Talāq. This applies specifically to a divorced woman.

As for His words, “Two full years,” it is understood that the year begins at birth and is completed at the corresponding date and time. Thus, if it begins on the tenth of Muharram, it is completed on the tenth of Muharram at the same hour. An unqualified year consists of twelve lunar months, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah.”

The same applies to the waiting period He mentions: four months and ten days. It begins at the time of death and ends when ten days have elapsed after the corresponding date. Thus, if it begins in the middle of Muharram, it ends on the fifteenth of Muharram. The same applies to stipulated terms in sales and all other periods fixed by religious law or contractual stipulation.

The jurists have two other weak views on this matter. The first is the view of those who say that, if the period begins partway through a month, all the months are calculated by counting days, so that the two years amount to three hundred and sixty days. According to this view, the period increases by twelve days, which is a clear error.

And the second view is that one month is calculated by counting days, while the remaining months are reckoned by the lunar crescents. This is closer to the correct view, but it still contains an error. On this reckoning, if the period begins on the tenth of Muharram and Muharram has only twenty-nine days, its completion would fall on the ninth. Eleven days would therefore be needed to make up the month, so the period would end on the eleventh of Muharram. This too is incorrect.

The apparent meaning of the Quran indicates that the mother is obliged to breastfeed her child, because His words, “They shall breastfeed,” are a statement conveying a command. This is a disputed issue, which is why those holding the other view interpreted the verse differently.

Al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā said: “This command is directed to fathers, because arranging for breastfeeding is their responsibility, not the mothers’. This is indicated by His words, ‘The father is responsible for their provision and clothing,’ and His words, ‘Then give them their payment.’ If breastfeeding were obligatory upon the mother, the father would not owe her payment.”

The response is that the Quran indicates that the child is entitled to breastfeeding from his mother and maintenance from his father. If no other woman is available, breastfeeding becomes her individual duty, yet she remains entitled to payment. Another woman is likewise entitled to payment even if no one else is available.

His words, “For whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding period,” indicate that it is not permissible to wish to complete breastfeeding, and that weaning before then is permissible if it serves the child’s interests. He clarified this in His words:

“If they both wish to wean the child by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them.”

This indicates that the child may be weaned only with both parents’ consent. If one wishes to complete the breastfeeding period while the other wishes to wean the child earlier, the decision rests with the one who wishes to complete it, because Allah Most High says:

“Mothers

shall breastfeed their children for two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding period. The father is responsible for their provision and clothing.”

His words, “They shall breastfeed,” are declarative in form but convey a command. The meaning is that the mother is commanded to breastfeed the child for two full years if completion of the breastfeeding period is desired. If she wishes to complete it, she is commanded to do so, and the father is responsible for her provision and clothing. If the father wishes to complete it, he has that right, since weaning is permitted only with their mutual consent. This is indicated by His words, “For whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding period.”

The word “whoever” may be understood as general, encompassing both parents, male and female alike. Thus, whichever parent wishes to complete the period, the mothers are to breastfeed on that parent’s behalf.

Alternatively, His words, “For whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding period,” may refer specifically to the father—the one for whom the child is born and breastfed. The mother gives birth and breastfeeds on his behalf, as Allah Most High says, “If they breastfeed for you.” The mother’s relationship to him is like that of a hired worker to the employer. If the father wishes to complete the period, the mothers are to breastfeed on his behalf; if he wishes not to complete it, he may do so.

On this interpretation, the verse’s explicit wording commands the mothers to breastfeed the child when the father wishes it, while its implication also permits weaning by mutual consent. The case in which the mother alone wishes to complete the period remains unaddressed. However, the implication of His words, “By mutual consent,” is that weaning is not permissible in that case, as Mujāhid and others have stated. Yet this case is covered by His words:

“If they breastfeed for you, then give them their payment.”

For if she breastfeeds for the full year, she has done so on his behalf, thereby sparing him the burden of feeding the child. Were it not for her breastfeeding, he would have to feed the child something else.

{يَهَبُ لِمَنْ يَشَاءُ إنَاثًا وَيَهَبُ لِمَنْ يَشَاءُ الذُّكُورَ}
 فَجَعَلَهُ مَوْهُوبًا لِلْأَبِ.

{وَلَا عَلَى أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَنْ تَأْكُلُوا مِنْ بُيُوتِكُمْ}

translated_text:
Thus, in this verse He explains that the mother must complete the breastfeeding period if the father wishes, while in the other He explains that the father must pay her if the woman refuses.

Mujāhid said: “Mutual consultation” concerns the period before the completion of two years. If she wishes to wean the child but he refuses, she may not do so. If he wishes to do so but she does not, he may not do so until they reach mutual agreement through consultation—that is, without harming themselves or their nursing child.

Regarding His words, Most High:

“Provided you hand over what you have agreed to pay, in a fair manner,”

the explanation given is: when you fathers hand over to the children’s mothers their payment for the breastfeeding they provided before refusing to continue. This was reported from Mujāhid and al-Suddī.

Another explanation is: when you hand over the wet nurse’s payment to her in a fair manner. This was reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Muqātil. Ibn Kathīr read (ataytum), with a short initial vowel.

In His words, Most High:

“The father is responsible for their provision and clothing in a fair manner,”

He says literally, “the one for whom the child is born,” rather than using wālid, corresponding to His use of wālidāt for “mothers.” This is because the woman is the one who gives birth to the child; the father does not give birth to him. Rather, the child is born for him. When the two are mentioned together, however, He says:

“And show kindness to both parents.”

When mentioned separately, the Quran does not call him wālid, but rather ab, “father.” This makes clear that the child is born for the father, not the mother. Hence, the father is responsible for the child’s maintenance during pregnancy and for the payment for breastfeeding him. This accords with His words, Most High:

“He grants daughters to whom He wills and grants sons to whom He wills.”

Thus, He describes the child as a gift to the father. He also treats the child’s house as the father’s own house in His words:

“Nor is there any blame upon you for eating from your own houses.”

Since the father provides for the child both in the womb and while nursing, and the woman is the vessel, the child is the father’s crop. Allah Most High says:

“Your wives are a field for you, so approach your field however you wish.”

The woman is therefore the cultivated land, and the crop within her belongs to the father. Moreover, “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade a man to irrigate with his own water

another man’s crop.”

He meant by this to prohibit intercourse with pregnant women, for the semen of the man having intercourse contributes to the fetus’s growth, just as water contributes to the growth of crops. Another authentic hadith states:

“I was about to invoke a curse upon him that would accompany him into his grave! How could he leave the child as property to be inherited from him when that is not lawful for him? And how could he enslave him when that is not lawful for him?”

Since the child belongs to the father and is his crop, this accords with the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“You and your property belong to your father.”

And his words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The best of what a man eats is from his own earnings, and his child is part of his earnings.”

The child thus results from his earnings, as this verse indicates. The crop growing in the ground is the earning of the cultivator who sowed it, watered it, and paid the rent for the land. Likewise, the man paid the woman her dowry, which is the payment for intercourse, as Allah Most High says:

“There is no blame upon you for marrying them if you give them their due dowries.”

This also accords with His words, Most High:

“His wealth will not avail him, nor what he has earned.”

“What he has earned” has been interpreted as referring to his children. The mother is therefore the cultivated land—the soil in which the crop grows—and the father has rented her through the dowry, just as one rents land. He supported the crop by providing for her during pregnancy, then provided for the nursing child, just as a tenant cultivator spends on crops and fruit both while they are concealed and after they emerge. The crop is the child, and he is part of the father’s earnings.

This indicates that a father may take from his son’s property so long as this does not harm the son, as established by the Sunnah. The son’s property is lawful for the father to use, even though it belongs to the son. The father may take ownership of it; otherwise, it remains the son’s. If the son dies without the father having taken ownership of it, it passes by inheritance from the son.

The father may also require his child to work for him, provided this does not harm him. This entails that the son must obey his father when the work is lawful and does not harm the son. For even if a man were to employ his slave in disobedience to Allah or wrong him, that would be impermissible; this applies all the more to his son.

translated_text:
The benefit of the son’s labour belongs to him unless his father takes it, unlike the benefit of a slave’s labour, which belongs to his owner. Likewise, if the slave dies, his property belongs to his owner, not to his heir.

What he mentioned also indicates that a man may not have intercourse with a woman pregnant by another man. If he does, it is like watering a crop: it increases it and fosters its growth, leaving him with a share in the child. It therefore becomes unlawful for him to enslave that child. Thus, if he acquires a slave woman who is pregnant by another man and has intercourse with her, it becomes unlawful for him to enslave her child, because he has watered him, and because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“How could he enslave him when that is not lawful for him? And how could he leave him to be inherited—that is, make him property inherited from him—when that is not lawful for him?”

Anyone who thinks the intended meaning is, “How could he make him an heir?” is mistaken. That woman was a slave belonging to the man who had intercourse with her, and a slave is not made an heir; rather, he is made property to be inherited.

Once the woman has undergone a waiting period to establish that she is not pregnant, it is known that there is no crop there. If she is a virgin, or has been in the possession of someone who does not have intercourse with her, the matter is disputed. The stronger view is that intercourse is permissible, because there is no crop there. The evidence that her womb is free of pregnancy in this case is stronger than that afforded by waiting for one menstrual period. A pregnant woman may discharge blood resembling menstrual blood, even if this is rare. Scholars have disagreed over whether this constitutes menstruation. Thus, the waiting period is not conclusive proof that the womb is free of pregnancy, but only apparent evidence. Virginity and previous ownership by a boy or a woman are stronger indications of the absence of pregnancy.

If the seller is truthful and informs the buyer that he has already had her undergo such a waiting period, the intended purpose has been fulfilled. Requiring a waiting period to establish the absence of pregnancy in a young girl who has not begun menstruating, an elderly woman, or a woman past menopause is far-fetched in the extreme.

For this reason, those who require it have disagreed: should the waiting period be one month, a month and a half, two months, or three months? All these opinions are weak.

Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, did not require a waiting period for a virgin, and no Companion is known to have disagreed with him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, only commanded such a waiting period for women taken captive, as he said concerning the captives of Awtās:

“No pregnant woman is to be approached sexually until she gives birth, nor any woman who is not pregnant until she has undergone a waiting period of one menstrual cycle.”

He did not command everyone who inherited or purchased a slave woman to have her undergo such a waiting period, although this occurred during his lifetime. It is therefore clear that he commanded the waiting period when her condition was unknown, because she might be pregnant. The same applies to an acquired slave woman whose previous master had been having intercourse with her and had not had her undergo a waiting period. However, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not mention such a case, because the Muslims did not do this. No one would consider it acceptable to sell his slave woman while she was pregnant by him. Indeed, if he had had intercourse with her, he would not sell her until she had undergone a waiting period, so the buyer would not need a second one.

For this reason, he did not prohibit intercourse with slave women pregnant by their masters when acquired through sale or gift, because this did not occur. Rather, this case was covered by his prohibition, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, against “a man watering another man’s crop with his own fluid.”

Allah Most High says:

“The father must provide for them and clothe them in a reasonable manner.”

And He, Most High, says in that verse:

“If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment.”

This indicates that this payment consists of their reasonable provision and clothing when no amount has been specified between them

translated_text:
to which they can refer.

“Customary remuneration” is assessed by reference to a specified amount only when there is such an amount to which both parties can refer. This is comparable to sales and hiring: since the commodity itself or its equivalent has a specified price, its equivalent value must be paid if it is taken without its owner’s consent. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever emancipates his share in a slave and has enough wealth to cover the slave’s price must have the slave fairly valued, pay his partners their shares, and the slave is then set free.”

Here the slave is valued because he and others like him are sold in the market, so his value—the market price at that time—can be determined. The same applies to hired workers and craftsmen. Thus, in the authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade Ali “to give the butcher anything from the sacrificial camels,” and said, “We will pay him ourselves.”

Slaughtering and distributing the meat are the responsibility of the person offering the sacrifice, so he must pay the butcher who performs this work. The butcher is entitled to the same remuneration as others doing comparable work, because butchery is a familiar trade with an established customary rate. The same applies to other crafts, such as weaving, tailoring, and building. During the Prophet’s lifetime, some people worked as tailors for payment; such a tailor is therefore entitled to what his peers receive. Likewise, a hired servant is entitled to what comparable workers receive, because this is an established custom among people.

As for the “nursing mother,” she is comparable to other mothers who breastfeed after divorce. They have no fixed customary rate; rather, their circumstances while breastfeeding are assessed in accordance with what has been mentioned. If she is pregnant by him while divorced, she is entitled to reasonable maintenance and clothing. In reality, this is maintenance for the unborn child. This is the stronger of the two scholarly views, as Allah Most High says:

“And if they are pregnant, then spend on them until they give birth.”

" أَحَدُهَا "
 أَنَّ هَذِهِ النَّفَقَةَ نَفَقَةُ زَوْجَةٍ مُعْتَدَّةٍ وَلَا فَرْقَ بَيْنَ أَنْ تَكُونَ حَامِلًا أَوْ حَائِلًا. وَهَذَا قَوْلُ مَنْ يُوجِبُ النَّفَقَةَ لِلْبَائِنِ كَمَا يُوجِبُهَا لِلرَّجْعِيَّةِ كَقَوْلِ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَالْخَلَفِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَغَيْرِهِ؛ وَيُرْوَى عَنْ عُمَرَ وَابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ؛ وَلَكِنْ عَلَى هَذَا الْقَوْلِ ل يس لِكَوْنِهَا حَامِلًا تَأْثِيرٌ فَإِنَّهُمْ يُنْفِقُونَ عَلَيْهَا حَتَّى تَنْقَضِيَ الْعِدَّةُ؛ سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ حَامِلًا أَوْ حَائِلًا. 
" الْقَوْلُ الثَّانِي "
 أَنَّهُ يُنْفِقُ عَلَيْهَا نَفَقَةَ زَوْجَةٍ؛ لِأَجْلِ الْحَمْلِ؛ كَأَحَدِ قَوْلَيْ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَإِحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْ أَحْمَد. وَهَذَا قَوْلٌ مُتَنَاقِضٌ؛ فَإِنَّهُ إنْ كَانَ نَفَقَةَ زَوْجَةٍ فَقَدْ وَجَبَ لِكَوْنِهَا زَوْجَةً لَا لِأَجْلِ الْوَلَدِ. وَإِنْ كَانَ لِأَجْلِ الْوَلَدِ فَنَفَقَةُ الْوَلَدِ تَجِبُ مَعَ غَيْرِ الزَّوْجَةِ كَمَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يُنْفِقَ عَلَى سُرِّيَّتِهِ الْحَامِلِ إذَا أَعْتَقَهَا.
 وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَقُولُونَ:
 هَلْ وَجَبَتْ النَّفَقَةُ لِلْحَمْلِ؟ أَوْ لَهَا مِنْ أَجْلِ الْحَمْلِ؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ. فَإِنْ أَرَادُوا لَهَا مِنْ أَجْلِ الْحَمْلِ. أَيْ لِهَذِهِ الْحَامِلِ مِنْ أَجْلِ حَمْلِهَا فَلَا فَرْقَ. وَإِنْ أَرَادُوا - وَهُوَ مُرَادُهُمْ -
 أَنَّهُ يَجِبُ لَهَا نَفَقَةُ زَوْجَةٍ مِنْ أَجْلِ الْحَمْلِ:
 فَهَذَا تَنَاقُضٌ فَإِنَّ نَفَقَةَ الزَّوْجَةِ تَجِبُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ حَمْلٌ. وَنَفَقَةُ الْحَمْلِ تَجِبُ وَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ زَوْجَةً. و 
" الْقَوْلُ الثَّالِثُ "
 وَهُوَ الصَّحِيحُ: أَنَّ النَّفَقَةَ تَجِبُ لِلْحَمْلِ؛ وَلَهَا مِنْ أَجْلِ الْحَمْلِ؛ لِكَوْنِهَا حَامِلًا بِوَلَدِهِ؛ فَهِيَ نَفَقَةٌ عَلَيْهِ؛ لِكَوْنِهِ أَبَاهُ
translated_text:
Scholars hold three views on this matter:

The first is that this is maintenance due to a wife observing her post-divorce waiting period, with no distinction between whether she is pregnant or not. This is the position of those who require maintenance for an irrevocably divorced woman just as they require it for a revocably divorced woman. It is held by a group of earlier and later scholars and is the school of Abū Hanīfa and others; it is also reported from Umar and Ibn Masʿūd. On this view, however, her pregnancy makes no difference, since they require that she be maintained until her waiting period ends, whether she is pregnant or not.

The second view is that she receives spousal maintenance on account of her pregnancy. This is one of al-Shāfiʿī’s two views and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. This view is contradictory: if it is spousal maintenance, then it is owed because she is a wife, not because of the child. If it is because of the child, then maintenance for the child is also obligatory when the mother is not a wife, just as a man must maintain his pregnant concubine if he emancipates her.

These scholars hold two views on the question: “Is maintenance owed to the unborn child, or to her on account of the pregnancy?” If by “to her on account of the pregnancy” they mean that it is owed to this pregnant woman because she is pregnant, then there is no difference. But if they mean—and this is what they intend—that she is entitled to spousal maintenance on account of her pregnancy, this is contradictory. Spousal maintenance is obligatory even when there is no pregnancy, and maintenance for the unborn child is obligatory even when the mother is not a wife.

The third view, which is correct, is that maintenance is owed to the unborn child, and to her on account of the pregnancy, because she is carrying his child. It is therefore maintenance for the child, owed by the man because he is its father

 فَإِنَّ وَلَدَهُ:
 إمَّا حُرٌّ وَإِمَّا مَمْلُوكٌ لِسَيِّدِ الْأَمَةِ. نَعَمْ. لَوْ كَانَتْ الْحَامِلُ أَمَةً وَالْوَلَدُ حُرٌّ مِثْلَ الْمَغْرُورِ الَّذِي اشْتَرَى أَمَةً فَظَهَرَ أَنَّهَا
translated_text:
, not for her on account of her being his wife. This is Mālik’s view and one of the two positions in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. The Quran supports this, for Allah Most High says:

“And if they are pregnant, spend on them until they give birth.”

Then He says:

“If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment.”

And here He says:

“The father must provide for them and clothe them in a reasonable manner.”

Thus, He places payment for breastfeeding upon the same person who must maintain the pregnant woman. It is well known that payment for breastfeeding is obligatory upon the father because he is the father; the same therefore applies to maintaining the pregnant woman. Moreover, the pregnant woman’s maintenance—her provision and clothing—is to be according to what is reasonable, and He has prescribed the same for the nursing woman’s payment. He also says:

“The heir bears the same duty.”

This means the child’s heir: He requires the heir to fulfil the same obligation as the father. All of this shows that maintenance during pregnancy and breastfeeding falls under “a father’s maintenance of his child,” not “a husband’s maintenance of his wife.”

Accordingly, even if she were not his wife, but had become pregnant through intercourse mistakenly believed to be lawful, with the child’s lineage attributable to him, or if she were pregnant by him and he had emancipated her, he would be obliged to provide maintenance during pregnancy, just as he must pay for breastfeeding. If, however, the unborn child belongs to someone else—as when a man has intercourse with another man’s slave woman through marriage, a mistaken belief in its lawfulness, or inheritance—the child belongs to the slave woman’s master. The man who had intercourse with her therefore owes nothing, even if he is her husband.

If a male slave marries a free woman and she becomes pregnant by him, the child’s lineage is attributed to him, but the child is free. A slave father is not obliged to maintain his free child or pay for its breastfeeding, since he has no wealth from which to maintain his child, and his master has no right over his child. His child is either free or belongs to the slave woman’s master.

However, if the pregnant woman were enslaved and the child free—as in the case of a deceived man who purchased a slave woman, only to discover that she

translated_text:
rightfully belonged to someone other than the seller, or who married a woman he believed to be free, only to discover that she was enslaved—the child in such a case is free, even though she is a slave woman owned by someone other than the man who had intercourse with her. This is because he had intercourse with her believing her to be either his own slave woman or his free wife. On this basis, the Companions ruled that the child should be purchased from the slave woman’s master; this is an analogous case. Here, then, he must maintain the pregnant woman just as he must pay the woman who breastfeeds his child. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man divorced his wife three times, and he has a daughter by her who is being breastfed. He has been required to provide maintenance during her waiting period. How long is her waiting period if she does not menstruate because she is breastfeeding?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. The majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, hold that a woman observing her waiting period after an irrevocable, threefold divorce is not entitled to maintenance. Abū Hanīfa, however, holds that she is entitled to maintenance for as long as she remains in her waiting period. If she is a woman who menstruates, she remains in her waiting period until she has had three menstrual periods. Breastfeeding generally delays the return of menstruation.

As for payment for breastfeeding, she is entitled to it by scholarly consensus, as Allah Most High says:

“If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment.”

Maintenance is obligatory only upon a man who has the means; a man without the means is not obliged to provide it.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A married woman is in need. Is her husband obliged to provide her maintenance, or should it come from her dower?

He answered:

Her husband is obliged to maintain her independently of her dower. As for her deferred dower, she may request it from him. If he pays it to her, that is good; if he refuses, he is not compelled to pay until their marriage ends through death, divorce, or the like. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked: (*)

A man has married a woman from whom he derives no benefit and who does not obey him in anything. She demands maintenance and clothing from him, yet she has made his affairs difficult. Is she entitled to maintenance and clothing from him?

He answered:

If she refuses him marital intimacy or leaves his home without his permission, she is not entitled to maintenance or clothing. Likewise, if he asks her to travel with him and she does not do so, she is not entitled to maintenance or clothing. Whenever she is in breach of her marital duties, disobeying him in matters in which she is obliged to obey him, he is not obliged to provide her with maintenance or clothing.

 وَأَصْحَابُ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ يَقُولُونَ:
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

When a woman and her husband bring a dispute over maintenance and clothing before a judge, whose word is to be accepted: hers or his? May the judge set a specific amount for maintenance and clothing? Please explain the rulings on these two questions, together with their evidence.

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. If a woman has been living in her husband’s home for some time, eating, drinking, and clothing herself in the customary manner, and the spouses then dispute this, with her saying, “You neither maintained nor clothed me; rather, someone else provided these things,” and him saying, “Rather, I provided the maintenance and clothing,” then the scholars hold two views concerning this.

“One view” is that his word is to be accepted. This is the correct view, held by the majority. A comparable case is that of a man who undertakes to teach his wife a craft as her dower. She learns it, but they then dispute who taught her. He says, “I taught her,” while she says, “I learned it from someone else.” There are two opinions on this within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

The correct position in all these cases is that the word of the person whose account is supported by customary practice is to be accepted. This is Mālik’s position. Abū Hanīfah likewise agrees that she is not entitled to anything from him, because, according to him, the obligation to pay maintenance lapses with the passage of time, as does maintenance for relatives. This is also one view within Ahmad’s school.

Those who hold this view say:

 فَإِذَا كَانَتْ الْعَادَةُ أَنَّ الرَّجُلَ يُنْفِقُ عَلَى الْمَرْأَةِ فِي بَيْتِهِ وَيَكْسُوهَا وَادَّعَتْ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ فَالْقَوْلُ قَوْلُهُ مَعَ يَمِينِهِ وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ هُوَ الصَّوَابُ الَّذِي لَا يَسُوغُ غَيْرُهُ لِأَوْجُهِ:

" الثَّانِي "
 أَنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ الْقَوْلُ قَوْلَهَا لَمْ يُقْبَلْ قَوْلُ الرَّجُلِ إلَّا بِبَيِّنَةِ فَكَانَ يَحْتَاجُ إلَى الْإِشْهَادِ عَلَيْهَا كُلَّمَا أَطْعَمَهَا وَكَسَاهَا وَكَانَ تَرْكُهُ ذَلِكَ تَفْرِيطًا مِنْهُ إذَا تَرَكَ الْإِشْهَادَ عَلَى الدَّيْنِ الْمُؤَجَّلِ وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ هَذَا لَمْ يَفْعَلْهُ مُسْلِمٌ عَلَى عَهْدِ السَّلَفِ.
translated_text:
Maintenance is due as a form of support and therefore lapses with the passage of time. The majority—including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, according to the well-known position reported from him—hold that it is due in exchange for something in return and therefore does not lapse with the passage of time.

However, if the spouses dispute whether she has received it, some scholars within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad say that the woman’s word is to be accepted, because the presumption is that she has received nothing, just as when they dispute whether she has received her dower. The correct position, however, is to refer to customary practice. If the custom is for a man to maintain and clothe his wife in his home, and she claims that he has not done so, his word is to be accepted upon his oath. This is the correct position, and no other is tenable, for several reasons:

First, in the time of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his rightly guided caliphs, no woman among the Companions and Successors is known to have had her word accepted in such a case. Had a woman’s word been accepted, there would have been ample incentive for women to bring such claims, as indeed happens. It is thus clear that it was an established principle among them that her word was not to be accepted.

Second, if her word were to be accepted, the man’s account could not be accepted without evidence. He would therefore have needed witnesses every time he fed or clothed her. His failure to do so would have constituted negligence on his part if he failed to have the deferred debt witnessed. Yet it is well known that no Muslim did this in the time of the early generations.

Third, having witnesses to this is impossible or difficult, so it is not required, just as witnesses to intercourse are not required. If the spouses dispute whether intercourse has taken place, and the woman is not a virgin, the majority do not accept her unsupported assertion that it has not, even though the presumption is that it has not occurred. Rather, either the man’s word is accepted, or he is instructed to ejaculate, or he has intercourse with her somewhere with a person nearby who can ascertain afterward that intercourse has occurred. Scholars differ over these alternatives. Here, then, her claim accords with the presumption, yet it is not accepted because producing evidence in such a matter is impossible. Providing maintenance within the home is comparable. People are not required to have witnesses when providing maintenance, for this would be an innovation in religion, a hardship for Muslims, and a departure from the way of the believers.

Fourth, scholars hold two opinions on whether a wife must be given ownership of her maintenance provisions. The stronger view is that this is not obligatory, nor must the husband assign her a fixed allowance. Rather, he feeds and clothes her according to what is reasonable. This is the position supported by the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said concerning women:

“They are entitled to their provision and clothing according to what is reasonable.”

Likewise, concerning a slave: “And his clothing according to what is reasonable.” He also said:

“Her right is that you feed her when you eat and clothe her when you clothe yourself.”

Similarly, he said concerning slaves:

“Your brothers are your servants, whom Allah has placed under your authority. Whoever has his brother under his authority should feed him from what he eats and clothe him from what he wears.”

This was the customary practice of Muslims in the time of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his caliphs. No man is ever known to have assigned his wife a fixed maintenance allowance; rather, he would feed and clothe her.

translated_text:
And since this is so, he has authority over providing for her, just as he has authority over providing for his slaves and livestock. Allah Most High says:

“Men are in charge of women.”

Zayd ibn Thābit said, “The husband is a master according to the Book of Allah,” and recited His words:

“And they found her master at the door.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb said, “Marriage is bondage, so let each of you consider to whom he gives his cherished kinswoman in bondage.” This is supported by the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Fear Allah concerning women, for they are captives in your keeping. You have taken them as a trust from Allah and made intimacy with them lawful by Allah’s word.”

He thus stated that a woman is a captive in her husband’s keeping, and that the husband has taken her as a trust from Allah: he is therefore entrusted with her care. This is why Allah has explicitly permitted a man in the Quran to strike her: only someone with authority over another may discipline that person.

Since the husband is entrusted with her care and has authority over her, his word is accepted regarding what has been entrusted to him and placed under his authority. This is just as a guardian’s word is accepted concerning expenditure on an orphan, and as the word of an agent, partner, profit-sharing investment manager, orchard sharecropper, or crop-sharing farmer is accepted concerning expenditure on partnership property—even though these arrangements involve an element of reciprocal exchange.

Marriage likewise involves partnership and reciprocal exchange, and the man holds a position of trust within it. There is therefore greater reason to accept his word in this matter than to accept the word of either partner.

Likewise, if a woman takes reasonable maintenance from his wealth and asserts that he has not provided her with maintenance, her word is accepted in this case, together with her oath, because the Lawgiver has authorized her to do so. Thus the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to Hind, “Take what suffices for you and your child according to what is reasonable,” when she said, “Abū Sufyān is a stingy man, and he does not give me enough maintenance for myself and my child.” He said, “Take what suffices for you and your child according to what is reasonable.”

translated_text:
Likewise, if the husband has been away from her on a journey for some time while she remains in her father’s house, and she claims that he neither left her any maintenance nor sent her any, her word is accepted together with her oath. The same applies to comparable cases. Thus, in this matter, distinctions must always be drawn according to the circumstances when considering past maintenance.

Whoever reflects on these considerations will understand the underlying reasoning in this question. Accepting women’s claims that they received no maintenance in the past entails harm and corruption whose extent only the Lord of all servants can count. It would mean that a woman could live with her husband for fifty years, then claim fifty years’ maintenance and clothing, alleging that, despite his wealth and her poverty, her husband had given her no food throughout that period. People can recognize with certainty that she is lying in such a case. Islamic law is far above allowing judgments based on lies and slander, injustice and aggression.

“The fifth argument”

The established principle in Islamic law is that an oath is prescribed for whichever of the two litigants has the stronger case, whether that strength rests on the original presumption of freedom from liability, actual possession, or established practice. Accordingly, when the claimant’s case is stronger, the majority—including Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad—hold that an oath is prescribed for him. Examples include the prescribed oaths in homicide cases and a financial claim supported by one upright witness: judgment is given in the claimant’s favour on the basis of that witness and his oath.

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—placed the burden of producing evidence upon the defendant when the claimant had no proof lending greater weight to his case. Hence, the majority of scholars say that when spouses dispute ownership of household belongings, each is awarded what customarily belongs to their use. Thus, the wife is awarded women’s belongings

Here, too, customary practice is that a man provides his wife with maintenance and clothing. If she has no known source from which to support herself, the matter is decided according to that customary practice.

“The sixth argument”

This woman must have had food and clothing during the period in question, and these must have come either from her husband or from someone else. The presumption is that there was no other provider, so they are attributed to him. Likewise, according to the sounder of the two views, we have stated that his word is accepted when he says that he taught her the craft and reading which he had undertaken to teach her as her dowry. This is because a newly arising condition is attributed to the known cause.

Similarly, if an impurity falls into water and the water is subsequently found to have changed, but there is doubt whether the change resulted from that impurity or something else, the sounder of the two views is that the change is attributed to the impurity. This is supported by the report established in the two Sahīh collections: the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—ruled for ‘Adī ibn Hātim that if he shot an animal while hunting, it disappeared from his sight, and he then found no mark on it other than that of his arrow, he could eat it. This is because the presumption is that no other cause brought about its death. This differs from a case in which it fell into water or his dog mingled with other dogs, for those causes also contributed to its death. A detailed discussion of these questions belongs elsewhere.

As for the judge’s assessment of maintenance and clothing, this takes place when they are disputed, just as he assesses the dowry customary for a woman of comparable standing when the spouses dispute it, and determines the extent of intercourse when the woman claims that her husband beats her. Whenever two parties dispute rights whose extent can be determined only by customary standards, the governing authority assesses them.

If, however, a man provides for his wife according to customary standards, as men of his standing ordinarily provide for women of hers, that is sufficient; no judicial assessment is needed. If the wife requests that the judge fix an allowance to be handed over to her, despite its being known that her husband provides for her according to customary standards, the correct of the two scholarly views in this situation is that the judge should not fix such an allowance, nor is the husband obliged to transfer ownership of it to her, as explained above. This is what the Quran, the Sunnah, and reasoning grounded in justice indicate.

The unquestionably correct view, held by the majority of scholars, is that a wife’s maintenance is determined by customary practice, not by a fixed amount prescribed in Islamic law. Rather, it varies according to conditions in different lands and times, the circumstances of the spouses, and their customary way of life. Allah Most High says:

“Live with them in kindness.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Take what is sufficient for you and your child according to what is reasonable.”

He also said:

“They are entitled to their provision and clothing according to what is reasonable.”

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said concerning the words of Allah Most High:

“Divorced women shall wait for three periods,”

up to His words:

“Their husbands have a greater right to take them back during that time, if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to their obligations, according to what is reasonable, but men have a degree above them,”

and up to His words:

“Divorce is twice; then either retain them on reasonable terms or release them with kindness.”

He thus made either of two courses permissible: retaining them on reasonable terms or releasing them with kindness. He stated that men have a greater right to take them back only if they desire reconciliation, and He granted women rights similar to their obligations, according to what is reasonable. Allah Most High also says:

“When you divorce women and they approach the end of their waiting period, either retain them on reasonable terms or release them on reasonable terms.”

In another verse, Allah Most High says:

“Either retain them on reasonable terms or part with them on reasonable terms.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Do not prevent them from marrying their husbands when they mutually agree on reasonable terms.”

His words here, “on reasonable terms,” indicate that if a woman agreed to something contrary to what is reasonable, her guardians would have the right to prevent the marriage. What is reasonable is marriage to a suitable match.

Those who hold that the dowry customary for a woman of her standing is part of what is reasonable may also cite this as evidence, since what is reasonable is what is customary among those concerned.

“The father is responsible for their provision and clothing according to what is reasonable.”

This standard set forth in the Quran is what justice requires in all matters relating to marriage and the rights of both spouses. The provision and clothing that a husband owes his wife must accord with what is reasonable: the customary practice recognized among people for a couple in their circumstances, in terms of kind, quantity, and quality. This varies according to their circumstances—whether they are affluent or in hardship—as well as the time—winter or summer, night or day—and the place. In each locality, he is to provide her with the food customary among its people, in accordance with their recognized practice.

The same applies to the conjugal enjoyment and companionship he owes her: he must spend the night with her and have intercourse with her according to what is reasonable. This varies with her circumstances and his. This is the sounder of the two opinions concerning obligatory intercourse: its extent is determined by what is reasonable, rather than by a fixed prescription in religious law. I have established this elsewhere.

The familiar example is “maintenance.” According to the majority of Muslims, it is determined by what is reasonable and varies with the circumstances of the spouses. Some, however, hold that religious law fixes both its kind and its quantity: one mudd (a measure of volume) of wheat, a mudd and a half, or two mudds. They base this on an analogy with the feeding required as expiation, applying the principle of analogical reasoning.

The unquestionably correct view, however, is what the Muslim community has upheld in knowledge and practice, past and present. The Quran indicates this, and in the two Sahīh collections it is reported of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

that when Hind, the wife of Abū Sufyān, said to him, “O Messenger of Allah, Abū Sufyān is a stingy man, and he does not give me enough for myself and my child,” the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—replied, “Take what suffices for you and your child according to what is reasonable.”

He thus instructed her to take what would reasonably suffice, without specifying either its kind or its quantity. Had these been fixed by religious law or otherwise, he would have explained their quantity and kind to her, just as he explained the prescribed amounts of zakah and blood money.

In Sahīh Muslim, Jābir reports that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said in his great sermon at ‘Arafāt:

“You owe them their provision and clothing according to what is reasonable.”

Since the obligation is to provide what reasonably suffices, it is clear that this varies according to the wife’s needs, the time and place, and the husband’s circumstances, whether affluent or in hardship. The clothing of a short, slight woman is not like that of a tall, large woman; winter clothing is not like summer clothing, nor is the amount of food sufficient in one season the same as in the other. Food in hot countries is not like that in cold countries, and what is customary in lands of dates and barley is not like what is customary in lands of fruit and leavened bread.

In Imam Ahmad’s Musnad and the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah, Hakīm ibn Mu‘āwiyah al-Qushayrī reports from his father, who said:

“I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what rights does the wife of any one of us have over him?’ He replied, ‘Feed her when you eat, and clothe her when you clothe yourself. Do not strike her face, do not revile her, and do not shun her except within the home.’”

These, then, are three hadiths from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In one, a wife is entitled to take what reasonably suffices for her child; and he said in the sermon he delivered on the day Allah perfected

the religion, at his largest gathering in Islam:

“You owe them their provision and clothing according to what is reasonable.”

To the man who sought his ruling concerning a wife’s rights, he said:

“Feed her when you eat, and clothe her when you clothe yourself.”

In none of these statements did he prescribe a fixed amount. Rather, he stipulated, at times, what is reasonable, and at others, sharing with her what the husband himself has. He said the same concerning the maintenance of slaves. In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Dharr reports that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“They are your brothers and servants, whom Allah has placed under your authority. Whoever has his brother under his authority should feed him from what he himself eats and clothe him from what he himself wears. Do not burden them with tasks beyond their strength; if you assign them such tasks, help them.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“A slave is entitled to his food and clothing, and must only be assigned work within his capacity.”

His instruction concerning wives and slaves is thus the same: at times, he states that food and clothing must be provided according to what is reasonable; at others, he commands that they be given a share of what one has oneself. Some scholars have held that providing what is reasonable is obligatory, whereas sharing what one has oneself is recommended. It may also be said that one instruction explains the other.

On this understanding, the obligation is to provide food and clothing according to what is reasonable in their kind, quantity, and manner of provision, although scholars have differed over this.

As for the “kind,” he is not specifically required to give her something measured by volume, such as wheat, or by weight, such as bread, or its monetary value in dirhams. Rather, custom determines this. Thus, when providing her with what reasonably suffices, if their customary food is dates and barley, for example, he gives her those.

This is the correct view, for such a transfer is not customary practice. Rather, the practice of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and of Muslims down to our own day is for a man to bring food home, from which he, his wife, and his slave eat, sometimes together and sometimes separately. Sometimes food remains, and they store it. Muslims have no established practice of a husband giving his wife ownership of dirhams each day to dispose of as an owner would. Rather, if a man conducts his married life on the basis of such a fixed allotment, Muslims would regard the couple as living together contrary to what is reasonable and harming one another in their marital life. One spouse treats the other in this way only when harm has arisen between them, not when they are living together on reasonable terms.

Moreover, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—prescribed the same obligation toward a wife as toward a slave. On one occasion he said:

“They are entitled to their provision and clothing on reasonable terms,”

just as he said concerning a slave. On another occasion he said:

“Feed her when you eat, and clothe her when you clothe yourself,”

just as he said concerning a slave. Muslims agree that one is not obliged to transfer ownership of a slave’s maintenance to him. It is therefore clear that these words do not entail an obligation to transfer ownership.

If the spouses dispute the matter, and the wife acknowledges that he feeds her when he eats and clothes her when he clothes himself, and that this accords with what is customary for a woman like her in her locality, she is entitled to nothing beyond that. If she denies this, the judge must order him to provide maintenance on reasonable terms. Indeed, the judge may not impose a fixed sum of dirhams or a fixed quantity of grain indiscriminately; rather, he must specify what is reasonable for their circumstances.

Section

Likewise, “allocating nights in the first place, intercourse, marital companionship, and sexual enjoyment” are obligatory, as we have established through more than ten proofs. Whoever doubts this obligation has failed to reflect adequately on the scriptural evidence and the ordering of human affairs.

As for the extent of the obligation, one view is that he must spend one night out of every four with her and have intercourse with her once every four months, as established in the cases of the mawlā and the man married to four wives. Another view is that he must have intercourse with her on reasonable terms, with its frequency varying according to her need and his ability, exactly as with food.

this is reasonable and she has not stipulated otherwise. She must not leave that residence without his permission unless there is a reason recognized by Islamic law. Thus, she may not relocate or travel, nor leave his home without a need, except with his permission. As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“For they are captives in your care.”

Her position is that of a slave or captive. She must allow him sexual enjoyment with her when he requests it. All of this must be reasonable, not wrongful: he may not engage in sexual enjoyment that harms her, house her in accommodation that harms her, or confine her in a manner that harms her.

Section

The scholars disagreed over whether she must serve him by performing such tasks as preparing the household bedding, serving food and drink, baking bread, grinding grain, and feeding his slaves and animals—for example, giving fodder to his mount—and similar duties.

Some said that such service is not obligatory. This view is weak, just as the view that marital companionship and intercourse are not obligatory upon him is weak. For this does not constitute living with him on reasonable terms. Indeed, even a travelling companion who is one’s equal, or a housemate, has not treated one reasonably if he does not help attend to one’s needs.

Another view—and this is correct—is that service is obligatory. For the husband is her master in Allah’s Book, and she is a captive in his care according to the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Captives and slaves are obliged to serve; moreover, this is what is customary and reasonable.

Among those who hold this view, some say that only light duties are obligatory. Others say that she must serve him in accordance with what is customary and reasonable. This is the correct view. She must therefore serve him

translated_text:
by performing the duties customarily expected of a woman like her for a man like him. These vary according to circumstances: a Bedouin woman’s duties differ from those of a townswoman, and a strong woman’s from those of a weak woman.

Section

The customary rights of each spouse are what a marriage contract without additional stipulations entails. What such a contract entails is determined by custom, just as a sale contract without additional stipulations requires payment in the customary currency. If either spouse imposes a condition upon the other that neither forbids something lawful nor permits something forbidden, then Muslims must abide by their stipulations. Contractual obligations are derived sometimes from the wording and sometimes from custom.

Both, however, are subject to the limits of what Allah and His Messenger have not forbidden. Each contracting party may undertake obligations toward the other that Allah has not forbidden that party to assume. Nor does He forbid a party to undertake, in an exchange, to provide something that may lawfully be given without compensation. In cases such as lending sexual access or assigning rights of patronage to someone other than the emancipator, no stipulation can make these obligatory. For if granting something is forbidden, how could a stipulation make it obligatory? These are comprehensive principles, presented briefly. Allah knows best.
