He replied:

If maintenance cannot be obtained from him, she is entitled to have the marriage annulled. Once her waiting period has ended, she may marry someone else. Annulment falls within the judge’s authority. If she annuls the marriage herself because annulment by the judge is unobtainable, or otherwise, the matter is disputed.

If, however, the judge did not annul the marriage, but instead testimony was given to her that her husband had died, and she married on that basis when her husband had not died, the marriage is invalid. Nevertheless, if the second husband believed it valid because he supposed that the first husband had died and the marriage had been dissolved, or for a similar reason, the child is legally attributed to him, he must pay the dowry, and he is not subject to the prescribed punishment. She must, however, complete the waiting period arising from her union with him. After that, the marriage to the first husband is to be dissolved, if possible, and she may marry whomever she wishes.

In the latter case, the right to reimbursement is disputed.

As for maintenance becoming an established debt merely because it has been assessed—even when the recipient’s needs have been met by a voluntary benefactor or through their own earnings, as is said concerning a wife’s maintenance—I know of no one who holds this view. If a ruling contradicts scholarly consensus, a judge’s judgment does not make it binding. Whoever has had money taken from him without right is entitled to recover what was taken.

According to Abū Hanīfa’s school, maintenance lapses with the passage of time, even if a judge has awarded it, unless the judge authorizes borrowing. This is because the judge has general authority, so his permission takes the place of permission from the absent person. Some scholars of that school mention two reported positions on whether a judge’s award makes maintenance a debt. However, they interpret the position affirming that it becomes due as applying when the judge directs someone to borrow and spend on those entitled to maintenance, with a right to reimbursement.

The same applies when a husband is well-to-do but defiantly refuses to provide maintenance, and the wife asks the judge to authorize her to borrow. If the judge directs her to do so, she may seek reimbursement from her husband, because the judge’s instruction has the same effect as his own. Even if the judge has awarded her maintenance, he may direct her to borrow on her husband’s account so that her entitlement to maintenance is not extinguished by the death of either spouse. Since maintenance lapses upon the death of either of them, the purpose of directing her to borrow is to secure her entitlement to maintenance. The judge is charged with ensuring that rights reach those entitled to them, and this is one means of doing so.

However, suppose the judge directs a relative to borrow, but the relative does not do so, having no need because a voluntary benefactor provides maintenance or because the relative has earnings of their own. Judge Shams al-Dīn understood that maintenance becomes an established debt in this situation, because those scholars spoke without qualification of an instruction to borrow, without stipulating that borrowing must actually take place. Others, however, understood that the purpose of the instruction to borrow was for borrowing actually to take place. Permission to borrow, without any actual borrowing, does not make the authorized amount a debt until it is borrowed.

translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a woman who died, leaving among her heirs a son who claimed from his father the dower and clothing due to her: “Is the husband liable for the clothing owed for the period before her death, given that the son is in need?”

He replied:
“If the circumstances are as stated, the father must pay him what he is entitled to. Indeed, even if the son had no inheritance, but was in need and unable to clothe himself, the father, if well-to-do, would be obliged to provide maintenance for him, his wife, and his young children who are in need and unable to earn a living.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man who married a woman and consummated the marriage, and continued to provide her maintenance despite her defiance of her marital obligations. Her father then took her away and travelled with her without the husband’s permission. What consequences do the father and daughter face?

He replied:
“Praise be to Allah. If he travelled with her without the husband’s permission, he is subject to discretionary punishment for doing so. The wife is likewise subject to discretionary punishment if she could have remained behind. She is not entitled to maintenance from the time she departed. Allah knows best.”

He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a man who had been married into a family for a year. A dispute then arose between them, and they demanded a year’s clothing from him, which they obtained. They then demanded maintenance, saying, “She is under legal guardianship, and we did not authorize you to provide for her.” Is this permissible?

He replied:
“Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. If the husband had received her into his household in accordance with Islamic law, and he, his father, or someone similar was feeding her according to customary practice, neither her father nor she herself has any right to demand maintenance. This is precisely the provision of maintenance in a reasonable manner that was practised during the time of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his Companions, and among Muslims generally in every age and land. The leading scholars have also expressly affirmed this. Indeed, anyone who requires the husband to hand over dirhams to her father so that he may buy her food each day has departed from the practice of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the Muslims, even though some people have advocated this.

How much more untenable is it, then, if he has already provided for her with her father’s acquiescence in this arrangement and his having entrusted her to them—given that she must, of course, eat—and her father then wishes to demand maintenance without counting what they have already spent on her? This is invalid under Islamic law, which affords it no basis whatsoever.

Anyone who imagines otherwise, believing that maintenance is a right owed to her like a debt, which her guardian must therefore receive, and that he has not authorized this expenditure, is mistaken on several grounds:

Third: This does not require his permission, for it is her entitlement under Islamic law. The Lawgiver has made providing for her obligatory; thus, even if her guardian forbade it, his prohibition would carry no weight.

Fourth: His acquiescence in her remaining there, when maintenance is needed, constitutes permission by custom. Nor can it be argued that he did not entrust the husband with providing maintenance, for two reasons:

First: Islamic law itself has entrusted him with this, just as it has entrusted the husband with her person, her allotted share of his time, and her other rights. Men are responsible for women, and women are like captives with men, as the Quran and Sunnah indicate.

Second: Entrusting someone by custom is equivalent to entrusting him expressly. And Allah knows best.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man whose wife had him imprisoned over her clothing and bridal due, and who remained imprisoned for some time: could she demand maintenance from him for the period of imprisonment she had caused?

He replied:

“If he was unable to pay and she had him imprisoned, she was wronging him and preventing him from exercising his marital rights with her. She is therefore not entitled to maintenance from him during that period. But if she had an enforceable right that was already due, and he was able to fulfil it but withheld it after a lawful demand, then he was the one acting wrongfully. If, despite this, she remained willing to fulfil her obligations towards him, she would be entitled to maintenance.”

عَنْ رَجُلٍ لَهُ زَوْجَةٌ وَلَهُ مُدَّةُ سَبْعِ سِنِينَ لَمْ يَنْتَفِعْ بِهَا؛
 لِأَجْلِ مَرَضِهَا:
 فَهَلْ تَسْتَحِقُّ عَلَيْهِ نَفَقَةً أَمْ لَا؟
 فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَسْتَحِقُّ وَحَكَمَ عَلَيْهِ حَاكِمٌ:
 فَهَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ إعْطَاؤُهَا أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ، تَسْتَحِقُّ النَّفَقَةَ فِي مَذْهَبِ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ طَلَّقَ زَوْجَتَهُ طَلْقَةً وَاحِدَةً وَكَانَتْ حَامِلًا فَأَسْقَطَتْ:
 فَهَلْ تَسْقُطُ عَنْهُ النَّفَقَةُ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ، إذَا أَلْقَتْ سِقْطًا انْقَضَتْ بِهِ الْعِدَّةُ وَسَقَطَتْ بِهِ النَّفَقَةُ وَسَوَاءٌ كَانَ قَدْ نُفِخَ فِيهِ الرُّوحُ أَمْ لَا إذَا كَانَ قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ فِيهِ خَلْقُ الْإِنْسَانِ؛ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَتَبَيَّنْ فَفِيهِ نِزَاعٌ.
translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a man who had been unable to have marital relations with his wife for seven years because of her illness: was she entitled to maintenance from him? If she was not entitled to it, but a judge ordered him to pay it, was he obliged to give it to her?

He replied:

“Yes, she is entitled to maintenance according to the schools of all four imams.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man who divorced his wife once while she was pregnant, after which she miscarried: did his obligation to provide maintenance cease?

He replied:

“Yes. If she miscarries a fetus, her waiting period ends and her entitlement to maintenance ceases, whether or not the soul had been breathed into it, provided that its human form had become discernible. If its human form had not become discernible, there is disagreement on the matter.”

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ طَلَّقَ زَوْجَتَهُ ثَلَاثًا وَأَلْزَمَهَا بِوَفَاءِ الْعِدَّةِ فِي مَكَانِهَا فَخَرَجَتْ مِنْهُ قَبْلَ أَنْ تُوُفِّيَ الْعِدَّةَ وَطَلَبَهَا الزَّوْجُ مَا وَجَدَهَا:
 فَهَلْ لَهَا نَفَقَةُ الْعِدَّةِ.
فَأَجَابَ:
لَا نَفَقَةَ لَهَا؛ وَلَيْسَ لَهَا أَنْ تُطَالِبَ بِنَفَقَةِ الْمَاضِي فِي مِثْلِ هَذِهِ الْعِدَّةِ فِي الْمَذَاهِبِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ مَاتَتْ زَوْجَتُهُ وَخَلَّفَتْ لَهُ ثَلَاثَ بَنَاتٍ:
 فَأَعْطَاهُمْ لِحَمِيهِ وَحَمَاتِهِ وَقَالَ: رُوحُوا بِهِمْ إلَى بَلَدِكُمْ حَتَّى أَجِيءَ إلَيْهِمْ؛ فَغَابَ عَنْهُمْ ثَلَاثَ سِنِينَ فَهَلْ عَلَى وَالِدِهِمْ نَفَقَتُهُمْ وَكِسْوَتُهُمْ فِي هَذِهِ الْمُدَّةِ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
مَا أَنْفَقُوهُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ بِنِيَّةِ الرُّجُوعِ بِهِ عَلَى وَالِدِهِمْ فَلَهُمْ الرُّجُوعُ بِهِ عَلَيْهِ إذَا كَانَ مِمَّنْ تَلْزَمُهُ نَفَقَتُهُمْ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man who divorced his wife three times and required her to complete her waiting period in her residence. She left before completing it, and her husband looked for her but could not find her. Was she entitled to maintenance during the waiting period?

He replied:

“She is not entitled to maintenance, nor may she claim maintenance for the past portion of such a waiting period according to any of the four schools. And Allah knows best.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man whose wife died, leaving him three daughters. He entrusted them to his father-in-law and mother-in-law, saying, “Take them to your town until I come to them.” He then remained away from them for three years. Was their father liable for their maintenance and clothing during that period?

He replied:

“They may recover from their father whatever they reasonably spent on the daughters with the intention of seeking reimbursement from him, provided that he was obliged to maintain them. And Allah knows best.”

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ وَطِئَ أَجْنَبِيَّةً حَمَلَتْ مِنْهُ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ تَزَوَّجَ بِهَا:
 فَهَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ فَرْضُ الْوَلَدِ فِي تَرْبِيَتِهِ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْوَلَدُ وَلَدُ زِنَا؛ لَا يَلْحَقُهُ نَسَبُهُ عِنْدَ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ؛ وَلَكِنْ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُنْفِقَ عَلَيْهِ الْمُسْلِمُونَ؛ فَإِنَّهُ يَتِيمٌ مِنْ الْيَتَامَى وَنَفَقَةُ الْيَتَامَى عَلَى الْمُسْلِمِينَ مُؤَكَّدَةٌ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ مُتَزَوِّجٍ بِامْرَأَةِ وَلَهَا وَلَدٌ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ وَلَهُ فَرْضٌ عَلَى أَبِيهِ تَتَنَاوَلُهُ أُمُّهُ وَالزَّوْجُ يَقُومُ بِالصَّبِيِّ بِكُلْفَتِهِ وَمُؤْنَتِهِ مُدَّةَ سِنِينَ وَحِينَ تَزَوَّجَ الرَّجُلُ كَانَ مِنْ الصَّدَاقِ خَمْسَةُ دَنَانِيرَ حَالَّةٍ فَشَارَطَتْهُ عَلَى أَنَّهَا لَا تُطَالِبُهُ بِهَا إذَا كَانَ يُنْفِقُ عَلَى الْوَلَدِ مَا دَامَ الصَّبِيُّ عِنْدَهُ؛
 وَلَمْ تُعَيِّنْ لَهُ كُلْفَةً وَلَا نَفَقَةً:
 فَهَلْ لَهُ مُطَالَبَةُ أُمِّ الصَّبِيِّ بِكُلْفَةِ مُدَّةِ مَقَامِهِ عِنْدَهُ؟
translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man who had intercourse with a woman to whom he was not married. She became pregnant by him, and he subsequently married her. Was he obliged to provide maintenance for the child’s upbringing?

He replied:

“The child was born of unlawful intercourse; according to the four imams, his lineage is not ascribed to that man. Nevertheless, the Muslims must support him, for he is an orphan, and the Muslims’ duty to maintain orphans is emphatically enjoined. And Allah knows best.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man married to a woman who had a son by another man. The boy’s father owed him a maintenance allowance, which his mother received, while her husband supported the boy and met his expenses and upkeep for several years. When the man married her, part of the dowry consisted of five dinars payable immediately. She stipulated that she would not demand this sum from him if he maintained the child for as long as the boy remained with him, without specifying any amount for his expenses or maintenance. Could he demand reimbursement from the boy’s mother for the expenses of the period the boy stayed with him?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا كَانَ الْأَمْرُ عَلَى مَا ذَكَرَ وَلَمْ يُوَفِّ امْرَأَتَهُ بِمَا شَرَطَتْ لَهُ فَلَيْسَ لَهُ أَنْ يُطَالِبَ بِمَا أَنْفَقَهُ عَلَى الصَّبِيِّ إذَا كَانَ الْإِنْفَاقُ بِمَعْرُوفِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَيْسَ مُتَبَرِّعًا بِذَلِكَ سَوَاءٌ أَنْفَقَ بِإِذْنِ أُمِّهِ أَمْ لَا.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ تَطْعَمُ مِنْ بَيْتِ زَوْجِهَا؛ بِحُكْمِ أَنَّهَا تَتْعَبُ فِيهِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 تَطْعَمُ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ:
 مِثْلَ الْخُبْزِ وَالطَّبِيخِ وَالْفَاكِهَةِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا جَرَتْ الْعَادَةُ بِإِطْعَامِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ عَجَزَ عَنْ الْكَسْبِ وَلَا لَهُ شَيْءٌ وَلَهُ زَوْجَةٌ وَأَوْلَادٌ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لِوَلَدِهِ الْمُوسِرِ أَنْ يُنْفِقَ عَلَيْهِ وَعَلَى زَوْجَتِهِ وَإِخْوَتِهِ الصِّغَارِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، نَعَمْ عَلَى الْوَلَدِ الْمُوسِرِ أَنْ يُنْفِقَ عَلَى أَبِيهِ وَزَوْجَةِ أَبِيهِ وَعَلَى إخْوَتِهِ الصِّغَارِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ كَانَ عَاقًّا لِأَبِيهِ قَاطِعًا لِرَحِمِهِ مُسْتَحِقًّا لِعُقُوبَةِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He replied:

“If matters are as stated, and he has not paid his wife the amount to which her stipulation related, he may not demand reimbursement for what he spent on the boy, provided the expenditure was reasonable. For he was not spending it as a voluntary gift, whether he did so with the mother’s permission or without it.”

He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a woman who gives food from her husband’s household on the grounds that she works hard there.

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah. She may give food within reasonable customary limits, such as bread, cooked dishes, fruit, and other foods customarily given. And Allah knows best.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man who was unable to earn a living and possessed nothing, but had a wife and children. Was it permissible for his well-to-do son to support him, his wife, and his young children?

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Yes, the well-to-do son must support his father, his father’s wife, and his young siblings. If he does not, he is undutiful towards his father, severs his ties of kinship, and deserves the punishment of Allah Most High in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah knows best.”

عَنْ رَجُلٍ لَهُ وَلَدٌ وَطَلَبَ مِنْهُ مَا يَمُونُهُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا كَانَ مُوسِرًا وَأَبُوهُ مُحْتَاجًا فَعَلَيْهِ أَنْ يُعْطِيَهُ تَمَامَ كِفَايَتِهِ وَكَذَلِكَ إخْوَتُهُ إذَا كَانُوا عَاجِزِينَ عَنْ الْكَسْبِ:
 فَعَلَيْهِ أَنْ يُنْفِقَ عَلَيْهِمْ إذَا كَانَ قَادِرًا عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَلِأَبِيهِ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ مِنْ مَالِهِ مَا يَحْتَاجُهُ بِغَيْرِ إذْنِ الِابْنِ؛ وَلَيْسَ لِلِابْنِ مَنْعُهُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ لَهُ وَلَدٌ وَلَهُ مَالٌ وَالْوَالِدُ فَقِيرٌ وَلَهُ عَائِلَةٌ وَزَوْجُهُ غَيْرُ وَالِدَةِ الْوَلَدِ الْكَبِيرِ:
 فَهَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ نَفَقَةُ وَالِدِهِ وَنَفَقَةُ إخْوَتِهِ وَزَوْجَتِهِ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا كَانَ الْأَبُ عَاجِزًا عَنْ النَّفَقَةِ وَالِابْنُ قَادِرًا عَلَى الْإِنْفَاقِ عَلَيْهِمْ فَعَلَيْهِ الْإِنْفَاقُ عَلَيْهِمْ.
translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man who had a son and asked him for enough to support himself.

He replied:

“If the son is well-to-do and his father is in need, he must provide enough to meet all his father’s needs. Likewise, if his siblings are unable to earn a living, he must support them if he can afford to do so. His father may take whatever he needs from his son’s wealth without his permission, and the son has no right to prevent him.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a man whose son possessed wealth, while the father was poor and had a family to support. His wife was not the mother of his grown son. Was the son obliged to support his father, his siblings, and his father’s wife?

He replied:

“If the father is unable to provide for them and the son is able to support them, then he must do so.”

original_text:

 فَيَسْتَحِقُّ السَّفَرَ بِهَا وَتَكُونُ الْحَضَانَةُ لِأُمِّهَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا الْمُدَّةُ الَّتِي كَانَ عَاجِزًا عَنْ النَّفَقَةِ فِيهَا فَلَا نَفَقَةَ عَلَيْهِ وَلَا رُجُوعَ لِمَنْ أَنْفَقَ فِيهَا بِغَيْرِ إذْنِهِ بِغَيْرِ نِزَاعٍ بَيْنَ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَإِنَّمَا النِّزَاعُ فِيمَا إذَا أَنْفَقَ مُنْفِقٌ بِدُونِ إذْنِهِ مَعَ وُجُوبِ النَّفَقَةِ عَلَى الْأَبِ.
 فَقِيلَ:

translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a man who could not afford to support his daughter and was away. She was staying with her mother, and her grandmother was supporting her, although she was well-to-do and no maintenance payment had been assessed against him:

“May she recover the maintenance expenses for the period during which he could not afford to support his daughter? If he is not known to possess any wealth, is his word concerning his poverty to be accepted, or that of the claimant?

“If he resides in a town where his interests are best served and wishes to take his daughter with him when moving permanently, is he entitled to take her with him while her mother retains custody?”

He replied:

“For the period during which he could not afford to support her, no maintenance was due from him. Anyone who spent on her during that period without his permission has no right to reimbursement. There is no disagreement among the scholars concerning this. The disagreement concerns only cases in which someone spent without the father’s permission while the father was obliged to provide maintenance.

“One view is that the person may recover what he spent, provided he did not intend it as a gift. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī, and one position reported from Ahmad. The father may not be imprisoned over this maintenance or a claim for its reimbursement until his obligation has been established by proving that he had the means to pay.

“If they disagree over whether he had sufficient means, and he is not known to possess any wealth, his word is to be accepted upon his oath. If he resides in a town other than the mother’s, custody belongs to him, not to her, even though the mother has the stronger right to custody when they reside in the same town. This, too, is the position of the four imams. And Allah knows best.”

The boy had reached seven years of age, and they wished to have maintenance assessed for him. His mother had remarried, and his grandmother had taken him into her care and sent his guardian. He replied:

“If a judge has ruled in his favor, the mother has no right to keep the child away from him. If she keeps him away under these circumstances, she has no right to demand either the assessed maintenance or reimbursement for what they spent on him during that time. And Allah knows best.”

He replied:

Yes, he must provide reasonable maintenance for his son if the son is poor and unable to earn a living, while the father has sufficient means. If providing for the son is possible only by renting out idle portions of his property and renovating whatever can be renovated, or by allowing the son to rent out and renovate property from which he can support himself, then the father must do so. Indeed, anyone who owns property but neither maintains it nor rents it out is foolishly squandering his wealth. The judge should therefore restrict his control over his property for his own good, lest his wealth be lost. If he has a child, this becomes obligatory for both his own welfare and that of his child. And Allah knows best.

He also said—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

Section

Allah Most High says:

“The one for whom the child is born is responsible for their provision and clothing in a reasonable manner.”

The expression “the one for whom the child is born” is more apt than “the father” for several reasons. It encompasses both the father and a slave’s master, and it makes clear that the child belongs to his father, not his mother. This establishes that the child belongs to his father, as we maintain when we say that the father may lawfully benefit from his child’s wealth and services. It also explains the basis of his obligation: the child belongs to him, not to the mother. Furthermore, it is the mother who actually gives birth to the child, not the father. These are four reasons.

Hence one says, “A child was born to so-and-so,” and, “A child was born to me.”

translated_text:
This verse obliges the father to provide for his nursing child, for Allah says:

“And if they are pregnant, spend on them until they give birth. Then if they breastfeed for you, give them their payment.”

He thus made maintenance obligatory for the child both in the womb and while nursing, through providing for the woman who carries and nurses him, since he cannot be provided for without providing for her.

I was then asked: “Where, then, is the father’s obligation to maintain his child after weaning established?”

I replied: “The text indicates this by implication. If, while the child is hidden in the womb and while nursing, Allah requires maintenance for the woman who carries and nurses him—since he cannot otherwise be maintained—then providing for him after weaning, if he takes nourishment directly himself, is all the more incumbent.”

This is sound reasoning from the text. The passage indicates that the ruling applies with greater force to the unmentioned case than to the case expressly stated. It also explains the rationale for the ruling: maintenance is obligatory upon the father because the child belongs to him, not to the mother; and whatever belongs to someone must be maintained by him. Hence the child is described as one’s earnings in His words, “and what he has earned,” and in the saying:

“The best food a man eats is from his own earnings, and his child is part of his earnings.”

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him:

“Concerning a man who has a slave woman who has repented, prays and fasts: what is her master required to do if he does not have intercourse with her?”

He replied:

“If she needs marriage, he must safeguard her chastity, either by having intercourse with her himself or by marrying her to someone who will have intercourse with her. No one may have intercourse with her except her husband or her master.”

“If a person’s wealth is insufficient to provide for both relatives and others, maintaining his relatives is obligatory upon him, so he must not give to others in a way that harms his relatives. As for zakat and expiatory payments, these may be given to a relative whom he does not maintain. When circumstances are equal, relatives have priority.”

Chapter on Child Custody

He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

“A man had a son who died, leaving an eight-year-old child. The wife is asking the grandfather for maintenance. She subsequently remarried and was divorced, without the grandfather knowing about this. She has taken the child and travelled away, and the grandfather does not know her whereabouts. Is the grandfather obliged to pay maintenance or not?”

He replied:

“If the mother marries, she has no right to custody. If she travels to settle elsewhere, custody belongs to the grandfather rather than to her. If a woman has a child in her custody without being entitled to custody and demands maintenance, she has no right to it, for she is wrongfully retaining custody. She is therefore not entitled to demand maintenance.

“If the grandfather is unable to maintain his son’s son, he is not obliged to maintain him.”

He also said—may Allah sanctify his soul:

Section

Among human beings, an “orphan” is someone who has lost his father, for it is his father who shapes his character, provides for him, and protects him by virtue of his innate disposition. Hence, the child follows his father in religion, and his maintenance and custody are his father’s responsibility. Maintenance means provision, while “custody” means protection, since it consists of providing shelter and warding off harm.

When his father is gone, people are tempted to exploit him, for man is unjust and ignorant, while the victim is helpless and weak. The potential for wrongdoing thus increases: the incentive is strong, and the deterrent is weak. This produces two evils: harm to the orphan, who has no one to defend him and is shown no kindness; and wickedness on the part of the person who has nothing to restrain him.

For this reason, Allah has emphasized the importance of caring for orphans in many verses of His Book, such as His words:

“And when We took a covenant from the Children of Israel: ‘Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy.’”

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man has a seven-year-old daughter whose mother is married. He has taken custody of his daughter under the noble Sharia, and she has no caregiver other than him. Her mother now wishes to take her from him and undertake her care for a specified period. However, he fears that she may subsequently claim reimbursement from him for clothing and maintenance according to some schools of jurisprudence. How should the agreement between them be worded?

The answer:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

As long as the child remains with her and she supports her, having taken her on the condition that she will provide for her from her own resources without seeking reimbursement from the father, she has no claim to maintenance from him, by agreement of the imams. That is, she cannot recover from him what she has spent during this period. However, if she wishes to demand maintenance in the future, the father may take the child back from her. In these circumstances, and given what we have mentioned, she cannot both retain custody and demand maintenance from the father; there is no disagreement on this.

However, if they agree to this arrangement, is their agreement binding? There is disagreement on this, and the well-known position in Mālik’s school is that it is binding. That being so, undertaking this obligation entails no harm to the father. Allah knows best.

Section:

The position of Imam Ahmad and other scholars regarding “custody of a child who has reached the age of discernment”: Does custody belong to the father or the mother, or is the child given a choice between them?

Many books by scholars of Ahmad’s school state only that, when a boy reaches seven years of age, he is given a choice between his parents, whereas the father has the greater right to custody of a girl. Those who mentioned this, such as al-Khiraqī and others, had received some of Ahmad’s statements on this question, but not the rest. Ahmad’s statements are numerous and very widely dispersed. Few have a comprehensive grasp of all his statements on many questions, given their abundance and wide dispersal, and the great number of people who studied under him.

3. At 34/115: “But al-Hasan ibn Sālih ibn Hayy reported that she is given a choice when she becomes a kā'ib (a girl whose breasts have begun to develop). Giving a boy a choice. And the position of al-Shāfi'ī, Ahmad—according to the well-known report from him—and Ishāq …”
The correct wording, as in the Egyptian Fatwas version, p. 617, is: “But it is reported from al-Hasan ibn Hayy that she is given a choice when she becomes a kā'ib. Giving a boy a choice is the position of al-Shāfi'ī, Ahmad—according to the well-known report from him—and Ishāq …”

4. At 34/120:
“Regarding the expiation for someone who has intercourse during Ramadan: may he choose among its alternatives, or must he follow their prescribed order? There are two positions, both reported from Ahmad. Most scholars maintain that the prescribed order must be followed. However, that order is established through the account of the man who had intercourse, not through wording of general application. For this reason, some scholars ventured to require certain kings specifically to fast, holding that this order is not a universally applicable prescription, but rather a matter of tanqīh al-manāt (determining the operative rationale of the ruling). Emancipation was given precedence for someone who finds it harder than fasting, such as the Bedouins. As for someone who finds emancipation easier, he is not required to give it precedence.”
I say—the speaker is Shaykh Nāsir al-Fahd: These lines appear to have been omitted from the manuscript underlying the Egyptian Fatwas version; see p. 621. Perhaps Shaykh al-Islām himself—may Allah have mercy on him—omitted them in another copy. Allah Most High knows best.

5. At 34/128: “Giving the boy a choice, as established by the sunnah, is preferable to assigning him whichever parent he loves more. Thus, assigning the father, as held by Abū Hanīfa and Ahmad … the mother, as held by Mālik and, in one report, Ahmad; and the choice is one based on desire.”
I say—the speaker is Shaykh Nāsir al-Fahd: This wording is confused. The corresponding passage in the Egyptian Fatwas version, p. 627, reads:
“Giving the boy a choice, as established by the sunnah, is preferable to assigning him one of his parents. Thus, assigning the father, as held by Mālik and Ahmad in his report, and the choice is one based on desire.”
This wording is also confused.

As for the well-known position reported from Ahmad—that the boy is given a choice between his parents—this is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh. Ahmad agreed with al-Shāfiʿī and Ishāq more often than with others, and his principles more closely resembled theirs than those of others. He praised them, held them in high esteem, and preferred the principles underlying their legal schools to those of scholars whose principles differed from theirs. He held that the principles of the hadith jurists were sounder than those of others, and he regarded al-Shāfiʿī and Ishāq as among the foremost hadith jurists of their time.

The two were brought together at al-Khayf Mosque, where they debated the question of renting out houses in Mecca. The account is well known. Ahmad mentioned that al-Shāfiʿī prevailed over Ishāq in argument on one point, while Ishāq prevailed over him on another. Al-Shāfiʿī permitted both their sale and their rental, whereas Ishāq prohibited both. The evidence supported al-Shāfiʿī regarding the permissibility of selling them, and Ishāq regarding the prohibition of renting them out.

The third position reported from Ahmad is that the mother has the greater right to the boy without qualification, as in Mālik’s school. This is inferred from his statement in Hanbal’s report concerning a man who divorces his wife and has young children by her:

“The mother is more tender towards them up to the age when they can understand discipline. She therefore has the greater right to them so long as she does not remarry. If she remarries, the father has the greater right to his child, whether a boy or a girl.”

I say: Hanbal and Ahmad ibn al-Faraj used to ask Imam Ahmad about the legal opinions of Mālik and the scholars of Medina, just as Ishāq ibn Mansūr and others asked him about the opinions of Sufyān al-Thawrī and others, al-Maymūnī asked him about the opinions of al-Awzāʿī, and Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd al-Shālanjī asked him about the opinions of Abū Hanīfa and his companions. The latter had studied jurisprudence according to Abū Hanīfa’s school, then exercised independent legal judgment on many questions, favoring the position of the scholars of hadith. He asked Ahmad and others about those questions, and Ibrāhīm ibn Yaʿqūb al-Jawzajānī, the imam of the mosque of Damascus, expounded them.

As for custody of a girl once she reaches the age of discernment, we have found two positions explicitly reported from Ahmad. More than one scholar of his school, including Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Taymiyya and others, has transmitted both. The first is that the father has the greater right to her, as stated in the well-known books of his school. The second is that the mother has the greater right to her. In the report of Ishāq ibn Mansūr, he said: “Custody of the girl is awarded to the mother and the maternal aunt. Once she needs to be married, however, the father has the greater right to her.”

 إنَّ الْأُمَّ وَالْجَدَّةَ أَحَقُّ بِالْجَارِيَةِ حَتَّى تَتَزَوَّجَ. قَالَ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ فِي 
" تَرْغِيبِ الْقَاصِدِ "
 وَإِنْ كَانَتْ جَارِيَةً فَالْأَبُ أَحَقُّ بِهَا بِغَيْرِ تَخْيِيرٍ.
 وَعَنْهُ:
 الْأُمُّ أَحَقُّ بِهَا حَتَّى تَحِيضَ. وَهَذِهِ الرِّوَايَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ هِيَ نَحْوَ مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ. فَفِي 
" الْمُدَوَّنَةِ "

And in the report of Muhannā ibn Yahyā, he said: “The mother and grandmother have the greater right to the girl until she marries.” Abū ʿAbd Allāh said in Targhīb al-Qāsid: “If the child is a girl, the father has the greater right to her, without her being given a choice. Another report from him states that the mother has the greater right to her until she menstruates.”

This second report is similar to the positions of Mālik and Abū Hanīfa. In al-Mudawwana, Mālik’s position is that the mother has the greater right to the child until puberty, whether the child is male or female. If the child reaches puberty and is female, the circumstances are examined: if the mother lives in a secure household, with protection and safeguards, she retains the greater right to her for as long as she remains unmarried, even if she reaches forty years of age. If the mother lacks such protection, security, and safeguards, or her own conduct is unsatisfactory, the father or testamentary guardian may take the girl from her. The same applies to the other guardians. In this respect, the testamentary guardian is like the father, provided that he takes her into trustworthy and protected care.

The position of al-Layth ibn Saʿd is similar. He said: “The mother has the greater right to the girl until she reaches puberty, unless the mother is unsatisfactory in her own conduct and her upbringing of her child; in that case, the girl is taken from her when she reaches puberty—unless she is still young and there is no fear for her.”

Abū Hanīfa said: “The mother and grandmother have the greater right to the girl until she menstruates. Those other than the mother and grandmother have the greater right to her until she reaches an age at which she may be sexually desired.” Al-Tahāwī’s wording is: “Until she no longer needs such care, just as with a boy, without qualification.”

As for giving a girl the choice, this is al-Shāfiʿī’s position. I have not found it transmitted from either Ahmad or Ishāq, as giving a boy the choice has been transmitted from both of them. It has, however, been transmitted from al-Hasan ibn Sālih ibn Hayy that she is given the choice once her breasts have begun to develop. Giving a boy the choice is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad according to the well-known report from him, and Ishāq, on the basis of the hadith reported

on this matter, in which “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave a boy a choice between his parents.” This was a particular case; no general statement has been transmitted from him giving children a choice without qualification. The hadith concerning giving a girl a choice is weak and contradicts their consensus.

The distinction between giving a boy and a girl a choice is that such choice involves personal inclination as well as judgment and considerations of welfare, like the choice exercised by someone acting on behalf of others, such as a ruler or guardian. When the ruler is given a choice concerning captives between execution, enslavement, release without compensation, and ransom, he must choose what best serves the Muslims’ interests. He thereby reaches the correct conclusion through his independent judgment, rules in accordance with Allah’s judgment, and receives two rewards. He may, however, fail to identify the best course; he is then rewarded for exerting his utmost and incurs no sin for being unable to discern what best serves their interests.

This is like someone who accepts the surrender of the people of a fortress on the understanding that they submit to his judgment:

“Banū Qurayza surrendered to the judgment of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal appealed to him on their behalf, he said, ‘Would you not be content for me to entrust the matter to your chief, Saʿd ibn Muʿādh?’ They agreed. Those who wished them to be spared hoped that Saʿd would show them favour because of the alliance between him and them in the pre-Islamic period. When Saʿd arrived, he ruled that their fighting men should be killed, their dependants taken captive, and their property divided. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘You have indeed judged concerning them according to Allah’s judgment from above seven heavens.’”

This implies that, had he ruled otherwise, his ruling would not, in reality, have been Allah’s judgment, even though it would still have had to be implemented.

A similar example is found in the well-known hadith of Burayda, recorded in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, in which he said:

translated_text:

For this reason, the jurists said that if the ruler besieges a fortress and its inhabitants surrender to an adjudicator’s judgment, this is permissible, provided that he is a free, upright Muslim man qualified to exercise independent judgment in matters of jihad. He may rule only in a way that serves the interests of Islam, whether by execution, enslavement, or ransom. They differed, however, over whether his ruling is binding if he orders their release without compensation and the ruler refuses: is it binding, not binding, or should a distinction be drawn between the fighting men and their dependants? There are three opinions. This disagreement arose only because those who disputed such a ruling believed that release without compensation brought no benefit to the Muslims.

The “main point” is that the choice granted to the ruler and to the adjudicator to whose judgment they surrendered is a choice governed by judgment and considerations of welfare. He seeks to determine which of the two courses is more pleasing to Allah and His Messenger, and then follows it, just as a scholar exercising independent judgment examines the evidence concerning an issue and follows whichever of the two proofs carries greater weight. What we mean by “choice,” however, is that no single course among these is invariably required at all times. Rather, one may be required on one occasion and another on a different occasion.

His words in the Quran,

“Then either release them without compensation or for ransom,”

require one of the two courses to be taken. This does not preclude varying between one course in one situation and the other in another. Similarly, He says:

“Are you awaiting anything for us except one of the two best outcomes? But we await for you that Allah should afflict you with punishment from Himself or at our hands.”

Thus, anticipating one of the two outcomes does not preclude a particular one of them from occurring. When jihad is obligatory upon us at certain times, Allah then afflicts them with punishment at our hands, as He says:

“Fight them: Allah will punish them at your hands, disgrace them, grant you victory over them, and heal the hearts of a believing people,”

“and remove the rage from their hearts.”

And for this reason, all scholars hold that Allah’s words concerning those who wage war against Him and His Messenger:

“The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is only that they be killed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land,”

do not give the ruler an unrestricted choice based on personal preference. In all four of these matters, they agree that one course is required in one situation and another in another.

Most of them maintain that these circumstances are defined by the revealed text: if they kill, they must be executed; if they take property without killing, their hands and feet must be cut off on opposite sides. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad. A hadith traced back to the Prophet has also been related to this effect.

Others maintain that the particular penalty is determined by the ruler’s independent judgment, as Mālik held. Thus, if he considers execution to serve the public interest, he executes the offender, even if the offender has not killed anyone.

The same principle applies to “the ruler’s choice concerning land conquered by force”: whether to make it fay’ (property held for the Muslim community) or spoils of war. This is the position of most scholars, including Abū Hanīfa, al-Thawrī, Abū ‘Ubayd, and Ahmad, according to the well-known position reported from him.

They said that if he considers it beneficial to treat the land as spoils of war, he distributes it among the combatants who acquired it, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, distributed Khaybar. If he considers it best not to distribute it, that is permissible, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not distribute Mecca, although he conquered it by force. This is attested by authentic hadiths and widely transmitted accounts of his life, and is the position of the majority of scholars.

Moreover, his successors—Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān—conquered the lands they conquered from the Arabs, Byzantines, and Persians, including Iraq, Syria, Egypt, and Khurāsān. Yet none of the caliphs distributed any of the conquered real estate among the combatants who acquired it, whether in the Sawād or elsewhere. Rather, they made the real estate fay’ for the Muslims, bringing it within the scope of His words:

They did not seek the consent of the combatants who had acquired the spoils. Indeed, many combatants requested that the land be divided, but their requests were not granted. Bilāl, for example, asked ‘Umar to divide the land of Syria, and al-Zubayr asked him to divide the land of Egypt, but these requests were not granted. None of the caliphs sought any combatant’s consent in this matter.

This is among the arguments advanced by those who hold that land becomes fay’ by the very act of conquest. This is also explicitly stated as his school’s position, as by Ismā‘īl ibn Ishāq. They argued that land is not included in spoils of war, for Allah forbade the Children of Israel to take spoils, yet granted them ownership of land. It follows that land is not included in spoils of war. This view is mentioned as one position reported from Ahmad.

A third position is also reported from him, agreeing with al-Shāfi‘ī: both immovable and movable property must be divided, since both constitute spoils of war. Al-Shāfi‘ī said: “Mecca was not conquered by force, but through a peace agreement, so its case cannot be used as evidence against me.” Those who report that he said it was conquered by force—such as the author of al-Wasīt and others—have misrepresented his position.

He also said: “For, concerning the Sawād, I do not know what to say except to form a supposition informed by knowledge and the supposition that ‘Umar obtained the combatants’ consent, as Qays ibn Hāritha related.” A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The majority’s position is the most balanced of these views and the closest to the Quran, the Sunnah, and established principles. They say: “We give the ruler a choice between the two courses based on judgment and public interest, not on personal desire and preference.”

The same applies to every matter in which those in authority are given a choice, and to anyone empowered to act on another’s behalf, such as the administrator of an endowment, an orphan’s guardian, or an agent with unrestricted authority. Their choice is not governed by personal preference and desire, but by considered judgment, careful examination, and the pursuit of the most beneficial permissible course—as in the case of a man beset

“Whoever appoints a man over a group when he can find among them someone more pleasing to Allah than him has betrayed Allah, betrayed His Messenger, and betrayed the believers.”

This differs from someone given a choice between two things who may do whichever he wishes. For example, someone making expiation may choose between feeding the needy, clothing them, and freeing a slave. Even if one of these options is better, he may choose the less meritorious one. Likewise, someone wearing leather socks may choose between wiping over them and washing his feet, even if one is better. Someone offering prayer may similarly choose between praying at the beginning of its prescribed time and at its end, even if one is better.

The same applies to choosing among different kinds of permissible food and drink, even though eating and drinking themselves become obligatory in cases of necessity. Indeed, if a particular food is the only option, eating it becomes obligatory, even if it is carrion. Thus, someone compelled by necessity to eat carrion must eat it, according to the well-known position reported from the four imams and other scholars.

Regarding “the expiation for intercourse during Ramadan,” may one choose among its forms, or must one follow a prescribed order? There are two views, both reported from Ahmad. The majority hold that a prescribed order must be followed. However, this order is established through the account of the man who had intercourse, not through wording of general scope. For this reason, some scholars went so far as to require certain kings specifically to fast, holding that the prescribed order is not a universally applicable rule. Rather, it is a matter of isolating the operative basis of the ruling: freeing a slave was given precedence for those who find it harder than fasting, such as the Bedouins. As for someone who finds freeing a slave easier, he is not obliged to give it precedence.

translated_text:
The same applies to “the pilgrim’s choice” between performing ‘umrah followed by Hajj with a release from ihrām between them, performing Hajj alone, and combining Hajj and ‘umrah in one state of ihrām, according to the majority, who allow a choice among these three forms. Likewise, according to the majority, travellers may choose between fasting and not fasting.

As for those who maintain that Hajj may only be performed after ‘umrah with a release from ihrām between them, or that not fasting while travelling is obligatory—as some among the earlier and later generations of Ahl al-Sunnah and the Shia hold—this example does not apply according to their principles. Likewise, regarding “shortening prayers,” the majority maintain that a traveller may pray only two units, not four. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, only ever prayed two units while travelling, as did all his Companions during his lifetime. The report from ‘Ā’ishah stating that she prayed four units while travelling during his lifetime has been judged false by expert hadith scholars, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The point here is that “choice in Islamic law is of two kinds.” Someone given a choice concerning what he does on another’s behalf, by virtue of his authority over that person or an unrestricted mandate to act for them, is not permitted to do whatever he wishes. Rather, he must choose what best serves their interests. As for someone acting on his own behalf, the Lawgiver sometimes commands him to choose what is best according to his own considered judgment, just as He commands a jurist exercising independent judgment to seek the strongest opinions and the rulings that are in fact best. At other times, He permits him to select whichever he wishes from the alternatives offered to him, as explained above.

This applies to someone who is legally accountable. As for “a child who has reached the age of discernment,” he is allowed to choose according to his own preference whenever both parents are equally suitable. No general rule giving precedence to the father or the mother has been established for him. Thus, one cannot say:

translated_text:
that every father is better suited than the mother to care for a child who has reached the age of discernment, or that every mother is better suited than the father. Rather, some fathers may be better suited, and some mothers may be better suited. The father may be better suited in some circumstances and the mother in others. Neither can therefore be designated categorically in this case. This differs from the case of a young child, for whom the mother is better suited than the father, because women are gentler with young children, more knowledgeable about feeding and carrying them, more patient with these tasks, and more compassionate towards them. In this respect, she is more capable, knowledgeable, compassionate, and patient. Islamic law therefore assigns the mother custody of a child who has not yet reached the age of discernment.

Yet there remains the question of “isolating the operative basis of the ruling”: did the Lawgiver designate women because maternal relatives take precedence over paternal relatives in custody, or simply because women fulfil the purpose of custody better than men? Scholars hold two views on this. Their implications become apparent when considering whether female relatives on the agnatic side take precedence over maternal relatives—for example, the maternal grandmother and the paternal grandmother, the maternal half-sister and the paternal half-sister, the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt, and similar cases.

There are two views on this, both transmitted from Ahmad. The view better supported by the evidence gives precedence to female relatives on the agnatic side. This is the view al-Khiraqī mentions in his “Compendium” concerning the paternal and maternal aunts. Accordingly, the paternal grandmother takes precedence over the maternal grandmother, the paternal half-sister over the maternal half-sister, and the paternal aunt over the maternal aunt, as previously explained. Male relatives on the father’s side likewise take precedence over maternal relatives: the paternal half-brother has a stronger claim than the maternal half-brother, and the paternal uncle than the maternal uncle. Indeed, it has even been held that male relatives on the mother’s side have no right to custody under any circumstances, and that custody

is granted only to a male agnate, a woman who is an heir, or a woman related through an agnate or an heir; if none of these is available, it falls to the judge. According to the second view, male relatives on the mother’s side have no right to custody. Both views are found in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

If one side of the family enjoyed precedence by virtue of that relationship, both its men and its women would take precedence. Since its men do not take precedence, by agreement, neither should its women. The principles of Islamic law, taken together, give precedence to paternal relatives in inheritance, contracting, maintenance, authority in matters of death and property, and other matters. The Lawgiver has not given maternal kinship precedence in any ruling. Whoever gives its women precedence in custody therefore departs from the principles of Islamic law. Rather, the mother is given precedence because she is a woman, and women as a class take precedence over men in custody.

This entails giving the paternal grandmother precedence over the grandfather, just as the mother is given precedence over the father; likewise, the child’s sisters take precedence over his brothers, his paternal aunts over his paternal uncles, and his maternal aunts over his maternal uncles. This is sound analogy and reasoning. Giving the women on the mother’s side precedence as a class over those on the father’s side, however, conflicts with both legal principles and reason. Thus, those who adopt this position fall into inconsistency and fail to apply their principle uniformly. Accordingly, those who have not properly grasped the principle and purpose of Islamic law in this matter hold contradictory views. Indeed, more contradictory views of this kind are found concerning custody than concerning other matters.

Some give the maternal grandmother precedence over the paternal grandmother, as in one of the two views in Ahmad’s school, which is also the position of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Abū Hanīfah. Yet some of these scholars give the paternal half-sister precedence over the sister

on the mother’s side, while giving the maternal aunt precedence over the paternal aunt, as in al-Shāfiʿī’s later position and the view of a group of Ahmad’s followers. They based their position on maternal aunts taking precedence over paternal aunts because they are related through the mother.

Yet, concerning paternal aunts, maternal aunts, and sisters, they said: “Those related through both parents take precedence, followed by those related through the father, then those related through the mother.” What they say here accords with the principles of Islamic law. But when it is considered alongside their position that maternal relatives take precedence, the contradiction becomes apparent. They also gave the mothers of the father and grandfather precedence over maternal aunts and maternal half-sisters. This accords with the principles of Islamic law, but contradicts their own principle. Accordingly, it is incompatible with the other view—that the maternal aunt and maternal half-sister take precedence over the paternal grandmother—as in al-Shāfiʿī’s earlier position. This latter view applies their principle more consistently, but is utterly at odds with the principles of Islamic law.

“Another group” applied its principle consistently, giving maternal half-sisters precedence over paternal half-sisters, in accordance with the position of Abū Hanīfah, al-Muzanī, and Ibn Surayj. Some of them pursued their analogy so far as to give the maternal aunt precedence over the paternal half-sister, as held by Zufar and reported in one narration from Abū Hanīfah; Ibn Surayj also agreed with it?

Abū Yūsuf, however, found this objectionable and gave the paternal half-sister precedence, reporting this position from Abū Hanīfah. It is also reported that Zufar pursued his analogy still further, saying: “The maternal aunt takes precedence over the paternal grandmother.”

They relate that Abū Hanīfah said: “Do not follow Zufar’s analogies, for if you follow his analogies, you will declare lawful things unlawful and unlawful things lawful.”

Zufar was known for rigorously extending his analogies—to the established basis of the case he used as a precedent, and from the effective cause of the ruling in that original case—“which answers the demand for proof of the effective cause.” Whoever firmly establishes this foundation will have sound analogical reasoning.

For example, Zufar held that when a marriage is contracted for a specified term, the time limit is void but the marriage remains valid and binding. Some scholars derived this as a position within Ahmad’s school. This position effectively means that a temporary marriage becomes valid and binding without a time limit, contrary to Ahmad’s explicit ruling and the consensus of the early generations. When the Muslim community has differed over an issue, holding two positions, later scholars may not introduce a position that contradicts both and implies that the early generations unanimously erred and departed from what was correct. The early generations held only that temporary marriage was invalid or that it was valid for the specified term. To hold that it becomes binding indefinitely therefore contradicts their consensus.

This position arose from their belief that every invalid condition in a marriage contract is void while the marriage itself remains binding. This includes annulling the stipulation that the marriage is intended to make the woman lawful again for her former husband, and similar conditions.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections, on the authority of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The conditions most deserving of fulfilment are those by which you have made marital intimacy lawful.”

This text indicates that fulfilling conditions in marriage is more deserving of observance than fulfilling conditions in a sale. If, when invalid conditions are stipulated in a sale, the contract does not remain binding without them—rather, either the contract is invalid or the party whose stipulated purpose has been frustrated gains the option to rescind when the condition is annulled—then what of conditions stipulated in marriage?

Their principal argument rests on the fact that marriage is valid without specifying the bridal gift, as established by the Quran, the Sunnah, and consensus. They therefore drew an analogy between a marriage in which the absence of a bridal gift is stipulated

translated_text:
and a marriage in which provision for the bridal gift remains in place, as did the followers of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī and most later followers of Ahmad. Abū Hanīfah then consistently extended his analogy, holding shighār (exchange marriage) to be valid on the grounds that it does not necessarily leave the marriage devoid of a bridal gift.

Al-Shāfiʿī and those followers of Ahmad who agreed with him, however, strained to distinguish shighār from other marriages, arguing that it involves sharing in the right to marital intimacy, making the contract conditional, or other considerations discussed at length elsewhere. It was also explained there that none of these distinctions affects the ruling. The correct position is that of the scholars of Medina, Mālik and others. It is also Ahmad’s explicit position in most of his answers, and that of the great majority of his early followers: what invalidates it is the stipulation that the marriage be devoid of a bridal gift. A marriage is not binding when it stipulates either the absence of a bridal gift or an invalid bridal gift, for Allah has made the bridal gift obligatory in marriage. Marriage without a bridal gift is therefore not lawful for anyone other than the Messenger.

Whoever marries on condition that no bridal gift is due has failed to observe what Allah has permitted. Allah has permitted the marriage contract only for someone who seeks marriage through his wealth, seeking chastity rather than fornication, as the Most High says:

“Lawful to you are all beyond these, provided that you seek them with your wealth in marriage, not in fornication.”

Thus, whoever seeks marriage without a bridal gift has not done what Allah has made lawful. This differs from someone who acknowledges that a bridal gift is indispensable but has not fixed its amount, as the Most High says:

“There is no blame upon you if you divorce women before you have touched them or fixed a bridal gift for them.”

This is a marriage with the customary bridal gift: the bridal gift appropriate to a woman of comparable standing.

This is the distinction between marriage and sale: a sale at the customary price—that is, the prevailing market price—or a hire at the customary rate is not valid. Al-Shāfiʿī and many of Ahmad’s followers conceded to them, with regard to sales, this premise upon which they based their analogy.

As for hire, the followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, Ahmad and others hold that the customary fee is due wherever established practice dictates it. Examples include entering a bathhouse whose proprietor ordinarily charges admission; staying in an inn or room customarily let for payment; entrusting one’s food or bread to someone who cooks or bakes for payment, or building work to someone who works for payment; riding an animal belonging to someone who hires out mounts; or boarding a boat whose boatman carries passengers for payment. According to the majority of scholars, these constitute contracts of hire, and the customary fee is due even if payment was not stipulated.

These, then, are contracts of hire at the customary rate. Likewise, if someone buys food at the price at which the market settles, at the price charged to other customers, at its purchase price in its place of origin, or at its marked price, this is permissible according to one of the two positions within the school of Ahmad and others. Ahmad explicitly addressed these and similar cases elsewhere, although the books of many of his later followers contain only the view that these contracts are invalid, following the position of al-Shāfiʿī and others. A detailed discussion of these questions belongs elsewhere.

Our purpose here was to discuss “questions of child custody.” Those who believed that the mother was given precedence because maternal kinship takes precedence built upon a weak premise, and the conclusions following from that weak premise were therefore weak as well. The invalidity of a necessary consequence entails the invalidity of the premise from which it follows. Rather, the correct view, beyond any doubt, is that she

was given precedence because she is a woman; thus, a woman has a greater right to custody of a young child than a man. The mother therefore takes precedence over the father, the grandmother over the grandfather, the sister over the brother, the maternal aunt over the maternal uncle, and the paternal aunt over the paternal uncle. As for a case involving a more distantly related woman and a more closely related man, its detailed discussion belongs elsewhere.

Our purpose here is to discuss the child who has reached the age of discernment and the distinction between boys and girls. Giving the boy a choice, as established in the Sunnah, is preferable to assigning him to either parent. Thus, assigning him to the father, as maintained by Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad … (1) the mother, as maintained by Mālik and, according to one report, Ahmad. The choice is based on personal preference. Hence they said that if he chooses the father for a time and then chooses the mother, he may do so. They even said that whenever he chooses one parent and subsequently chooses the other, he is transferred to the latter; this remains the case even if he continues changing his choice indefinitely. This is the position of those who uphold giving him a choice: al-Hasan ibn Sālih, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

They said that if he chooses the mother, he stays with her at night, but spends the daytime with his father so that he may teach him and discipline him. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. Mālik likewise said this, although he holds that the child stays with his mother without being given a choice: the father attends to him while he is with her, disciplines him and sends him to school, but he spends the night only with his mother.

The followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad said that if he chooses the father, he stays with him both night and day. He is not prevented from visiting his mother, nor is she prevented from nursing him if he falls ill.

As for the “girl,” if she is given a choice and stays sometimes with her mother and sometimes with her father, this leads to her frequently going out, displaying herself and moving from place to place

translated_text:
and neither the father nor the mother remains entrusted with safeguarding her. Experience has shown that whatever people take turns guarding is lost. As the common proverb says, “A pot shared by two cooks will not turn out well.”

Moreover, choosing either parent weakens the other’s desire to care for and protect her, so neither the father nor the mother remains fully committed to safeguarding her. The male is not like the female, as the wife of ‘Imrān said:

“My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb.”

“I have given birth to a female.”

“The male is not like the female. I have named her Mary, and I seek Your protection for her and her offspring from Satan, the accursed.”

“Her Lord graciously accepted her, caused her to grow up in goodness, and entrusted her to the care of Zechariah. Whenever Zechariah entered the sanctuary to visit her”—up to His words—“You were not with them when they cast their pens to determine which of them would care for Mary.”

Even Mary needed someone to take responsibility for her and bring her up, and they hastened to undertake her care. How much more, then, do other women need this! Experience establishes that a woman needs a degree of safeguarding and protection that a boy does not need. Whatever affords her greater concealment and protection is better for her. Hence, the clothing prescribed for her covers her, and women who wear men’s clothing are cursed. He said to Umm Salamah concerning her headwrap:

“Wrap it once, not twice.”

This was narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others. He also said in an authentic hadith:

“There are two groups among the people of Hell from my community whom I have not yet seen: women who are clothed yet naked, who stray and lead others astray, with heads like the humps of Bactrian camels—they will neither enter Paradise nor smell its fragrance; and men carrying whips like cattle’s tails, with which they beat the servants of Allah.”

They also instruct a woman, when praying, to keep her limbs close together rather than spread them apart, and to sit cross-legged rather than on a foot laid flat beneath her. During pilgrimage consecration, she should raise her voice only enough for her female companion to hear, and should not climb to the top of al-Safā and al-Marwah. All this is intended to ensure her concealment and protection. She is also forbidden to travel without a husband or an unmarriageable male relative, because she needs men to safeguard her even when she is mature and knowledgeable. How much more so when she is a young girl of discernment who has reached the age when sexual desire awakens, yet remains susceptible to deception! A report states:

“Women are like meat laid on a board, unless it is guarded.”

This analogy indicates that a girl of discernment in such circumstances is among those most in need of safeguarding and protection. Moving back and forth between her parents undermines this: she herself cannot feel settled in any particular place, nor can either parent remain fully committed to safeguarding her.

Furthermore, allowing her to choose one parent at one time and the other at another compromises her full protection and opens the way for her to appear and venture out in public. It is therefore better for her to remain with one parent without being given a choice, as the majority of Muslim scholars have held, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad, and others. There is neither a scriptural text nor a sound analogy supporting giving her this choice. The distinction between giving her a choice and giving a son a choice is clear, especially since a son is cherished and sought after, whereas a daughter is little valued. One parent may have little interest in her despite her attachment to that parent; how much more so if she has little attachment to that parent! It is therefore better for her to remain with one of them rather than move back and forth between them.

Scholarly judgment is then exercised to determine which parent this should be. Those who designate the mother—such as Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, and Ahmad according to one of the two reported positions—must also take into account whether the mother protects her. For this reason, they stated what Mālik, al-Layth, and others mentioned: if the mother is not in a secure place

translated_text:
and well protected, or if she is unsuitable, the father may take the girl from her. This is the consideration Ahmad took into account in the well-known position transmitted by his followers. Since safeguarding and protecting her must be taken into account, and the father undoubtedly has the right to remove her from her mother if the mother does not safeguard her, the father is better able to safeguard and protect her. She has reached the age of discernment and no longer needs anyone to attend to her bodily needs, while the father commands an authority and respect that the mother does not.

Ahmad and his followers give the father precedence only when she has no secure protection in those circumstances. If, however, the father is unable to safeguard and protect her, or neglects to do so, Ahmad gives the mother precedence in that situation. Whichever parent we give precedence to, we do so only if this serves her welfare or averts harm from her. If her circumstances deteriorate with either parent, the other undoubtedly has a stronger claim to her. Even when a young boy chooses one of his parents and we give that parent precedence, we do so only on condition that his welfare is secured and harm to him is removed.

Suppose, then, that the father is indifferent to sexual misconduct and does not safeguard the boy, whereas the mother does. We would disregard the boy’s choice, for his judgment is immature. He may choose one parent because that parent indulges his corrupt desires. The boy may wish to engage in immoral conduct, associate with immoral people, and abandon the beneficial pursuit of knowledge, religion, good manners, and a trade. He therefore chooses the parent with whom he can satisfy his desires, whereas the other might restrain and reform him. In such circumstances, there is no doubt that the parent with whom his condition deteriorates must not be allowed to take charge of him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Instruct them to pray at seven, discipline them by striking them for neglecting it at ten, and separate them in their beds.”

translated_text:

For the parent who instructs him is obeying Allah and His Messenger in raising him, whereas the other is disobeying Allah and His Messenger. We therefore do not give precedence to someone who disobeys Allah concerning him over someone who obeys Allah concerning him.

Rather, if one parent treats him as Allah and His Messenger have commanded and refrains from what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, while the other neglects the obligations owed to him or treats him in a forbidden manner, precedence must be given to the parent who fulfils those obligations, even if the boy chooses the other. Indeed, the disobedient parent has no authority over him whatsoever. Anyone who fails to fulfil the obligations of guardianship has no authority over the child. Either that person must be removed from guardianship and replaced by someone who fulfils those obligations, or someone must be appointed alongside that person to help fulfil them.

Thus, if keeping him with one parent does not secure obedience to Allah and His Messenger concerning him, whereas keeping him with the other does, the former must unquestionably be given precedence. This right is not like inheritance, which arises through kinship, marriage, and guardianship, whether the heir is hājiz (one who restrains) or incapable. Rather, it belongs to the category of “guardianship”—guardianship concerning marriage and property—which requires the ability to fulfil the relevant obligations and their actual fulfilment to the extent possible.

Suppose that the father has married another wife and the girl is left with her mother’s co-wife, who does not attend to her welfare but instead harms her or neglects her interests, whereas her mother attends to her welfare and does not harm her. In this case, custody belongs to the mother, even supposing that giving the girl a choice is prescribed and that she has chosen her mother. How much more so when that is not the case.

It should be understood that the Lawgiver has laid down no general text giving either parent precedence in all circumstances, nor one allowing a choice between the parents in all circumstances. The scholars agree that neither parent is invariably entitled to custody. Rather, where there is abuse or neglect, the parent responsible must not be given precedence over one who is righteous, just, caring, and fulfils the required duties. And Allah knows best.

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ لَهُ وَلَدٌ كَبِيرٌ فَسَافَرَ مَعَ كَرَائِمِ أَمْوَالِهِ فِي الْبَحْرِ الْمَالِحِ وَلَهُ آخَرُ مُرَاهِقٌ مِنْ أُمٍّ أُخْرَى مُطَلَّقَةٍ مِنْهُ وَلَهَا أَبٌ وَأُمٌّ؛
 وَالْوَلَدُ عِنْدَهُمْ مُقِيمٌ فَأَرَادَ وَالِدُهُ أَخْذَهُ وَتَسْفِيرَهُ صُحْبَةَ أَخِيهِ بِغَيْرِ رِضَا الْوَالِدَةِ وَغَيْرِ رِضَا الْوَلَدِ:
 فَهَلْ لَهُ ذَلِكَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
يُخَيَّرُ الْوَلَدُ بَيْنَ أَبَوَيْهِ؛ فَإِنْ اخْتَارَ الْمُقَامَ عِنْدَ أُمِّهِ وَهِيَ غَيْرُ مُزَوَّجَةٍ كَانَ عِنْدَهَا وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لِلْأَبِ تَسْفِيرُهُ؛ لَكِنْ يَكُونُ عِنْدَ أَبِيهِ نَهَارًا لِيُعَلِّمَهُ وَيُؤَدِّبَهُ وَعِنْدَ أُمِّهِ لَيْلًا. وَإِنْ اخْتَارَ أَنْ يَكُونَ عِنْدَ الْأَبِ كَانَ عِنْدَهُ. وَإِذَا كَانَ عِنْدَ الْأَبِ وَرَأَى مِنْ الْمَصْلَحَةِ لَهُ تَسْفِيرَهُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ فِي ذَلِكَ ضَرَرٌ عَلَى الْوَلَدِ فَلَهُ ذَلِكَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ تَزَوَّجَ بِامْرَأَةِ وَمَعَهَا بِنْتٌ وَتُوُفِّيَتْ الزَّوْجَةُ وَبَقِيَتْ الْبِنْتُ عِنْدَهُ رَبَّاهَا؛
 وَقَدْ تَعَرَّضَ بَعْضُ الْجُنْدِ لِأَخْذِهَا:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ.
الْجَوَابُ:
لَيْسَ لِلْجُنْدِ عَلَيْهَا وِلَايَةٌ بِمُجَرَّدِ ذَلِكَ. فَإِذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهَا مَنْ يَسْتَحِقُّ الْحَضَانَةَ بِالنَّسَبِ فَمَنْ كَانَ أَصْلَحَ لَهَا حَضَنَهَا وَزَوْجُ أُمِّهَا مَحْرَمٌ لَهَا.
 وَأَمَّا الْجُنْدُ فَلَيْسَ مَحْرَمًا لَهَا:
 فَإِذَا كَانَ يَحْضُنُهَا حَضَانَةً تُصْلِحُهَا لَمْ تُنْقَلْ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ لِأَجْنَبِيٍّ لَا يَحِلُّ لَهُ النَّظَرُ إلَيْهَا وَالْخَلْوَةُ بِهَا.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man has a grown son who has travelled by sea with his most valuable possessions. He also has another son, approaching puberty, by another woman whom he has divorced. She has a father and mother, and the boy lives with them. His father wishes to take him away and send him travelling with his brother, without either his mother’s consent or the boy’s own consent. Is he entitled to do so?

He replied:

The boy should be given a choice between his parents. If he chooses to remain with his mother and she has not remarried, he should stay with her, and the father has no right to send him away on a journey. However, he should spend the daytime with his father, so that he may teach him and train him in proper conduct, and the night with his mother. If he chooses to stay with his father, he should stay with him. If he is staying with his father, and the father considers it in the boy’s best interests to send him travelling, he may do so provided that this causes the boy no harm. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man married a woman who had a daughter. His wife died, and the girl remained with him, and he raised her. Some soldiers have sought to take her away. Is that permissible?

The answer:

The soldiers have no guardianship over her merely on that account. If she has no relative entitled to her custody, whoever is best suited to care for her should have custody of her. Her mother’s husband is her mahram (a man permanently prohibited from marrying her), whereas the soldier is not.

If her mother’s husband is caring for her in a manner that serves her welfare, she must not be removed from his care and placed with a man who is not her mahram and who is not permitted to look at her or be alone with her.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

If a son is in his mother’s custody and she spends on his maintenance intending to seek reimbursement from his father, she may seek reimbursement from him according to the stronger of the two scholarly views. This is Mālik’s position and the apparent position of Ahmad’s school, followed by his early adherents. A principle shared by both is that whoever discharges an obligation on another’s behalf may seek reimbursement from him, even if he acted without permission—for example, paying his debt or providing for his slave, or fearing that the enemy might kill him.

Allah Most High says:

“If they breastfeed for you, then give them their payment.”

He thus commands payment simply on account of breastfeeding, without stipulating a contract or permission. If, however, she provided the maintenance gratuitously, she has no right to seek reimbursement.

If he stipulates that she will have no claim to maintenance if she travels with the daughter, and she accepts this condition and then travels with her, she has no claim to maintenance, even if she intended to seek reimbursement. This is because, by travelling with her, she is acting wrongfully and exceeding her rights: she may not take the child travelling without her father’s permission, and he only permitted her to travel on condition that she bear the maintenance expenses gratuitously. Thus, if she travels and seeks reimbursement for those expenses, she has no right to it. And Allah knows best.
