translated_text:
Chapter on Criminal Offences

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about retaliation in kind.

He replied:

Retaliation in kind is established among Muslims by the consensus of the Muslim community. A Hāshimite Muslim may exact retaliation from an Abyssinian Muslim, and an Abyssinian Muslim from a Hāshimite Muslim, in matters of bloodshed, property, honour, and other matters. Where retaliation for an affront to honour is permissible, a man may exact it.

Thus, if the Hāshimite says to him, “You dog!” he may reply, “You dog!” And if he says, “May Allah curse you!” he may reply, “May Allah curse you!” This is permissible and falls within the meaning of Allah Most High’s words:

“As for those who defend themselves after being wronged, there is no blame on them. Blame is only on those who wrong people and transgress in the land without right. They will have a painful punishment. But whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is a matter requiring firm resolve.”

However, if someone lies about him, he may not lie about that person in return. Likewise, if someone insults a man’s father, the latter may not insult his father in return, whether he is a Hāshimite or not, for the father of the one who uttered the insult

“No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.”

However, if a Muslim insults another Muslim’s father, he is subject to discretionary punishment for that. Thus, if a Hāshimite insults a Muslim’s father, the Hāshimite is subject to discretionary punishment. Likewise, anyone who insults a Hāshimite’s father is subject to discretionary punishment, but this is not deemed an insult to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Even if someone insults his father and grandfather, this is not construed as referring to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, since the wording does not evidently mean that. The unqualified word “grandfather” means one’s paternal grandfather. If a man is called an ancestor, his ancestors are numerous, so no particular one is specified.

Insulting the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is disbelief warranting execution. Established faith is not nullified by doubt, nor may an inviolable life be taken on the basis of doubt—especially since a Muslim would ordinarily not intend to refer to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Neither his wording nor his circumstances imply that. An unsupported claim that he intended the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is not accepted against him. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām was asked:

What is the ruling on intentional killing, and what constitutes it? Is it when someone kills another over money, or out of resentment? Or for what reason does a killing count as intentional?

Someone said, “If it is over money, that is not it; nor, if it is out of resentment or over a debt, is he an intentional killer.”

The questioner said, “Then who is the intentional killer?”

He replied, “If he kills someone because of his Islamic faith, he is not a Muslim.”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

If he kills him because of his Islamic faith—as a Christian fights Muslims because of their religion—then he is an unbeliever worse than an unbeliever bound by a treaty. He is an unbeliever at war with the Muslims, like the unbelievers who fight the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions. Such people will remain in Hell forever, as will other unbelievers.

But if he kills him unlawfully out of enmity, over money, because of a dispute, or for a similar reason, this is a major sin. According to Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, he is not deemed an unbeliever merely for that; it is the Kharijites who declare people unbelievers for such acts. According to Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, no one who upholds Allah’s oneness will remain in the Fire forever, contrary to the Muʿtazilites, who maintain that sinful Muslims will remain there eternally.

They may cite as evidence the words of the Most High:

“Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, to remain there forever. Allah is angry with him, has cursed him, and has prepared for him a tremendous punishment.”

One response to them is that this refers to someone who deliberately kills a believer because of his faith. Most, however, have not interpreted the verse in this way. Rather, they have said: This is an unqualified threat of punishment, clarified by the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.”

In this connection, an account is related from a follower of the Sunnah who was at a gathering attended by ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, the leader of the Muʿtazilites. ʿAmr said, “I will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection and asked, ‘ʿAmr, on what basis did you say that I would not forgive a killer?’ I will reply, ‘You, my Lord, said: “Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, to remain there forever.”’”

The narrator said: “I said to him, ‘What if He says to you: “But I also said: ‘Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.’ On what basis did you know that I would not will to forgive this person?”’”

ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd fell silent.

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Must someone who kills deliberately or accidentally perform the expiation mentioned in the Quran—“fasting for two consecutive months”—or is he required to pay blood money?

He replied:

“Accidental killing” entails only blood money and expiation; no sin attaches to it. Someone who kills deliberately, however, incurs sin. If the victim’s heirs pardon him or accept blood money, this does not extinguish the victim’s claim in the Hereafter. If they put him to death, there is disagreement within Ahmad’s school as to whether that claim is extinguished. The stronger view is that it is not. However, if the killer has many good deeds, enough of them will be taken from him to satisfy the victim; or Allah will compensate the victim from His own bounty if the killer sincerely repents.

Blood money is obligatory for someone who kills accidentally, according to the explicit text of the Quran and the consensus of the Muslim community. Blood money is due for both a Muslim and a person protected by a treaty, as the Quran indicates. This is the position of the early generations and the imams, and no disagreement among the earlier scholars is known on this matter. Some later Zāhirīs, however, claimed that no blood money is due for the latter.

As for the “deliberate killer,” he is liable to execution in retaliation. If they agree to accept blood money, this is permissible according to the scriptural texts and scholarly consensus. The blood money is then paid from the killer’s own wealth, unlike accidental killing, for which the blood money is borne by his ‘āqila (blood-money guarantors).

As for “expiation,” the majority of scholars hold that deliberate killing is too grave to be expiated in this way. They say the same of a deliberately false oath. This is the position of Mālik, Abū Hanīfa, and Ahmad according to the well-known report from him. Likewise, they all agree that unlawful sexual intercourse is too grave to be expiated in this way; expiation is prescribed only for intercourse by a man who has pronounced zihār (a declaration likening his wife to a female relative forbidden to him in marriage), and for intercourse during Ramadan.

Al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad according to the other report from him, hold instead that expiation is obligatory for deliberate killing and a deliberately false oath. They agree that expiation alone does not remove the sin.

He replied:

If they jointly killed him, all of them are liable to execution in retaliation, by agreement of the four imams. The heirs may have them executed, or they may pardon them. If the adult heirs agree to

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

If someone kills a believer deliberately or accidentally, and the victim’s heirs and the ruler exact retaliation from him in this world, will he also be subject to retaliation in the Hereafter? Allah Most High has said:

“A life for a life.”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. No retaliation is exacted from an accidental killer, either in this world or in the Hereafter. Rather, what is obligatory in such a case is expiation and blood money paid to the victim’s family, unless they waive it as an act of charity.

As for the “deliberate killer,” if retaliation is exacted from him in this world, may the victim still claim his due in the Hereafter? There are two views on this in Ahmad’s school and, I believe, in other schools as well. Some say that the victim has no further claim against him, because what he owed has already been exacted from him in this world.

Others say that the victim still has a claim against him, for his right is not extinguished by the heirs’ execution of the killer, just as Allah’s right is not extinguished by that. Likewise, the right of a wronged person whose property was seized is not extinguished when it is returned to his heirs. Rather, he may demand recompense from the wrongdoer for depriving him of its use during his lifetime. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man deliberately killed another man. The victim left a five-year-old daughter, a wife pregnant with his child, and sons of his paternal uncles. May retaliation be exacted from the killer before the daughter reaches maturity and the wife gives birth, or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The other heirs may not exact retaliation from him before the child is born, except according to Mālik, who allows the agnatic heirs to exact retaliation before then.

If she gives birth to a daughter or twin daughters, so that the sons of the victim’s paternal uncles have a share in the estate, the agnatic heirs may exact retaliation before the daughters reach maturity according to Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, and one report from Ahmad. According to the best-known report from him, however, retaliation may not be exacted for the daughters; this is also al-Shāfiʿī’s view.

May the daughters’ guardian, such as the judge, act on their behalf in exacting retaliation or accepting a financial settlement? There are two reports from Ahmad. “The first,” which is also the view of the majority of scholars, permits this. “The second” does not permit retaliation, in agreement with al-Shāfiʿī’s view. However, if the daughters are in need, may their guardian negotiate a financial settlement for them? There is a well-known disagreement on this within al-Shāfiʿī’s school.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a man killed by a group. Two men were present at his killing, the group had agreed to kill him, and the district judge and the provincial authorities’ deputies witnessed him being struck.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If evidence establishes who struck him until he died, whether one person or more, the victim’s heirs may have all of them executed in retaliation, or only some of them. If the killer’s identity is unknown, the victim’s heirs may swear that a particular individual killed him, and judgment granting them the right to retaliation shall be given in their favour. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A group gathered and swore an oath together to kill a Muslim man. They took along another group who had not been present when they swore their oath. They approached the man, struck him with swords and maces, and threw him into the sea. Are they all subject to retaliation, or not?

He replied:

If he has no guardian, the ruler is his guardian, and the judge acts as the ruler’s deputy. According to the second view, this right cannot be exercised until the heir reaches puberty. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to the other report from him.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning a man whom his children, his neighbours and an unrelated man had agreed to kill: what is Allah’s ruling regarding them?

He replied:

If they jointly killed him, all of them may be executed. The decision does not rest with those who participated in killing him, but with his other heirs. If he has brothers, they are entitled to seek retaliation for his death, and they also inherit his property, for a killer does not inherit from his victim. The ruler has no right either concerning retaliation for his death or to his property. Rather, his brothers have the choice: they may have all the adults who participated in killing him executed, or they may have only some of them executed. This is agreed upon by the four imams. As for those who directly carried out his killing, the imams agree that they may be executed.

translated_text:
As for those who assisted by bringing the man into the house, guarding the doors, or similar acts, scholars hold two views concerning their execution. Their execution is permissible according to Mālik and others. The person who restrained him may be executed according to Mālik, Ahmad in one of the two reports from him, and others. Neither of the two is entitled to inherit.

If his minor children also helped to kill him, the right to seek retaliation for his death belongs neither to them nor to their guardian, but to his brothers. Whether they inherit from his property, however, is disputed. The well-known position in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad is that they do not inherit from his property. The minors are subject to disciplinary punishment, but are not executed. The position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik is that the minors inherit from his property. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning two men who exchanged blows and tried to strangle one another, whereupon one of them fell down and died: what is the other liable for?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

If he strangled him in a manner that ordinarily causes death, he is liable to execution in retaliation according to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad and the two leading disciples of Abū Hanīfa. Even if he claims that this does not ordinarily cause death, his claim is not accepted without evidence.

If, however, one of them lost consciousness after being strangled, and the other kicked him with his foot until something came out of his mouth and he died, then the latter is undoubtedly liable to execution in retaliation. He has deliberately killed a person and must therefore face execution in retaliation, provided the victim is his equal in legal status, being a free Muslim. He is then handed over to the victim’s heirs: they may choose to have him executed, pardon him, or accept blood money.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning two men who quarrelled and grappled with one another: one headbutted the other in the nose, causing it to bleed. The man whose nose was bleeding then strangled the other and kicked him in the testicles, whereupon he fell down dead. What is the ruling?

He replied:

The man who strangled the other and kicked him in the testicles is liable to execution in retaliation, for an act of this kind ordinarily causes death. His death from this act is evidence that what was done to him was ordinarily fatal.

An act that ordinarily causes death entails execution in retaliation according to the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and the two leading disciples of Abū Hanīfa. Thus, if someone strikes another in the testicles until he dies, execution in retaliation is required. Likewise, if he strangles him until he dies, execution in retaliation is required. How much more so when both acts are combined!

The victim’s heir has the choice: he may have the killer executed, accept blood money, or pardon him. The ruler has no right to take anything from the killer for himself or for the public treasury. This right belongs solely to the victim’s heirs.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning someone who struck a man a single blow, after which the man lived for some time before dying, remaining weakened by the blow throughout that period: what is the assailant liable for?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. If he struck him unlawfully, this constitutes quasi-intentional homicide, for which aggravated blood money is due, but not execution in retaliation. This applies if his death was not caused by the blow. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning a Jewish man killed by a Muslim: is the Muslim to be executed in retaliation for him, or what is he liable for?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. According to the leading Muslim scholars, he is not liable to execution in retaliation. However, it is not permissible to kill a non-Muslim under Muslim protection without right. It is established in al-Sahīh that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“A Muslim is not to be executed in retaliation for a disbeliever.”

However, he must pay blood money. One view holds that the amount due is half the blood money for a Muslim; another holds that it is one-third. A further view distinguishes between intentional and accidental killing: for intentional killing, the same blood money as for a Muslim is due. This is reported from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān: when a Muslim killed a non-Muslim under Muslim protection, he imposed the heavier liability upon him, requiring payment of the full blood money. For accidental killing, half the blood money is due. The Sunan collections report that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—set the blood money for a non-Muslim under Muslim protection at half that for a Muslim.

In all cases, expiation for killing is also obligatory: freeing a believing slave or, if he cannot find one, fasting for two consecutive months.

translated_text:
Mālik, have him given a hundred lashes and imprisoned for a year. Such discretionary punishment achieves the intended aim. Accordingly, if the victim’s heirs have accepted the killing of their kinsman, may Allah humiliate none but them.

If it is said that, in certain cases, blood money is imposed on the local inhabitants in conjunction with the qasāma oaths, then that blood money belongs to the victim’s heirs, not to the public treasury. None of the leading scholars has said that the blood money for a slain person belongs to the public treasury. Likewise, the leading scholars agree that blood money is not imposed without qasāma.

As for those known for fomenting strife and spreading corruption, the ruler may apprehend and imprison any of them known to engage in such conduct. He may also transfer him to another land to curb his aggression. He may likewise impose discretionary punishment on anyone whose wrongdoing has become manifest, to restrain his evil and aggression. Punishments administered in accordance with justice and Islamic law suffice to safeguard lives and property, sparing rulers the need to impose levies that corrupt the people and the land. If someone accused of killing is known for wickedness, then, according to a group of scholars, the ruler may punish him for his wickedness and subject him to disciplinary correction. Through this and similar measures, the purpose of just governance is achieved. And Allah knows best.

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about someone who said, “I struck him, and Allah killed him.”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. This person is held to his confession and is subject to the legal consequences applicable to a killer.

As for his statement, “And Allah killed him,” if he means that Allah took his soul, or that Allah is the One who causes everyone to die and is the Creator of His servants’ actions, or something similar, this does not absolve him of the legal consequences of killing. Rather, he remains subject to the legal consequences applicable to a killer.

translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a man riding a horse. A bear-handler passed him with a bear, causing the horse to bolt and throw its rider. It then ran away and knocked a man down, killing him.

He replied:

The owner of the horse bears no liability in these circumstances, but the bear-handler is subject to punishment. And Allah knows best.

He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a man whose property had been stolen and who suspected someone known for being implicated in wrongdoing. The accusation was mentioned in his presence, and he beat the suspect to extract a confession. The suspect confessed, then denied it, so he beat him until he died. What is he liable for, given that he beat him only because of what he had been told concerning the accusation?

He replied:

He must free a believing slave as expiation, and blood money is due for the slain man, unless he reaches a settlement with his heirs for a lesser amount. Had he subjected him, without any right or semblance of justification, to treatment that ordinarily causes death, retaliatory execution would have been obligatory. Had he acted rightfully, nothing would have been due. And Allah knows best.

 إنَّهُ لَا يَعْرِفُ مَكَانَهُ فَالْقَوْلُ قَوْلُهُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ عَثَرَ عَلَى سَبْعَةِ أَنْفُسٍ فَحَصَلَ بَيْنَهُمْ خُصُومَةٌ؛ فَقَامُوا بِأَجْمَعِهِمْ ضَرَبُوهُ بِحَضْرَةِ رَجُلَيْنِ لَا يَقْرَبَا لِهَؤُلَاءِ وَلَا لِهَؤُلَاءِ؛ وَعَايَنَاهُ إلَى أَنْ مَاتَ مِنْ ضَرْبِهِمْ؛ فَمَا يَلْزَمُ السَّبْعَةَ الَّذِينَ يُسَاعِدُونَ عَلَى قَتْلِهِ؟
translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah sanctify his soul—about a soldier who held a grant of revenue from a locality. He reported that a man had been killed there, and the people said that the killer was a Christian peasant from the area covered by the grant. He sought to bring the killer before the authorities, but the man could not be found. They arrested the accused Christian’s brother, who is in prison. Despite this, they are demanding that the soldier produce the Christian, although he had not stood surety for him.

He replied:

If the soldier knows nothing of the accused man’s situation and has not stood surety for him, he may not be required to produce him. However, if the accused is rightfully wanted and the soldier knows his whereabouts, he must disclose them. If he says that he does not know his whereabouts, his word is to be accepted.

He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about a man who came upon seven people, and a dispute arose between them. All seven proceeded to beat him in the presence of two men who were related to neither side. These two witnessed the beating until he died from it. What liability falls upon the seven who took part in killing him?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
 إذَا شَهِدَ لِأَوْلِيَاءِ الْمَقْتُولِ شَاهِدَانِ وَلَمْ يَثْبُتْ عَدَالَتُهُمَا: فَهَذَا لَوْثٌ إذَا حَلَفَ مَعَهُ الْمُدَّعُونَ خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا - أَيْمَانَ الْقَسَامَةِ - عَلَى وَاحِدٍ بِعَيْنِهِ حُكِمَ لَهُمْ بِالدَّمِ؛ وَإِنْ أَقْسَمُوا عَلَى أَكْثَرِ مِنْ وَاحِدٍ فَفِي الْقَوَدِ نِزَاعٌ.
 وَأَمَّا إنْ ادَّعَوْا أَنَّ الْقَتْلَ كَانَ خَطَأً أَوْ شِبْهَ عَمْدٍ مِثْلَ أَنْ يَضْرِبُوهُ بِعَصَا ضَرْبًا لَا يَقْتُلُ مِثْلَهُ غَالِبًا:
 فَهُنَا إذَا ادَّعَوْا عَلَى الْجَمَاعَةِ أَنَّهُمْ اشْتَرَكُوا فِي ذَلِكَ فَدَعْوَاهُمْ مَقْبُولَةٌ وَيَسْتَحِقُّونَ الدِّيَةَ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَمَّا إذَا قَالَ الْمَضْرُوبُ:
 مَا قَاتِلِي إلَّا فُلَانٌ: فَهَلْ يُقْبَلُ قَوْلُهُ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، لَا يُؤْخَذُ بِمُجَرَّدِ قَوْلِهِ بِلَا نِزَاعٍ؛ وَلَكِنْ هَلْ يَكُونُ قَوْلُهُ لَوْثًا يَحْلِفُ مَعَهُ أَوْلِيَاءُ الْمَقْتُولِ خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا وَيَسْتَحِقُّونَ دَمَ الْمَحْلُوفِ عَلَيْهِ؟
 عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ مَذْكُورَيْنِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ:
 
" أَحَدُهُمَا "
 أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ بِلَوْثِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ. و 
" الثَّانِي "
 أَنَّهُ لَوْثٌ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ مَالِكٍ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلَيْنِ شَرِبَا؛ وَكَانَ مَعَهُمَا رَجُلٌ آخَرُ فَلَمَّا أَرَادُوا أَنْ يَرْجِعُوا إلَى بُيُوتِهِمْ تَكَلَّمَا فَضَرَبَ وَاحِدٌ صَاحِبَهُ ضَرْبَةً بِالدَّبُّوسِ فَوَقَعَ عَنْ فَرَسِهِ فَوَقَفَ
translated_text:
He replied:

If two witnesses testify on behalf of the slain person’s heirs, but their uprightness has not been established, this constitutes grounds for suspicion. If, on that basis, the claimants swear fifty oaths—the qasāma (homicide) oaths—against one particular person, they are awarded the right to retaliatory execution. If they swear against more than one person, there is disagreement over whether retaliatory execution applies.

If, however, they claim that the killing was accidental or quasi-intentional—for example, that the assailants struck him with a stick in a manner that would not ordinarily be fatal—then their claim that the group participated jointly in this is admissible, and they are entitled to blood money.

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him:

If a person who has been beaten says, “My killer is none other than so-and-so,” is his statement accepted?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. There is no disagreement that his statement alone is insufficient grounds for action. But does his statement constitute grounds for suspicion on the basis of which the slain person’s heirs may swear fifty oaths and become entitled to the retaliatory execution of the person against whom they swear?

The scholars have two stated opinions on this:

The first is that it does not constitute grounds for suspicion. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad and Abū Hanīfa.

The second is that it does constitute grounds for suspicion. This is Mālik’s position.

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about two men who had been drinking, with another man accompanying them. When they wished to return to their homes, the two exchanged words, and one struck the other a blow with a mace. He fell from his horse, and he stopped

original_text:
عِنْدَهُ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي مَعَهُمَا حَتَّى رَكِبَ فَرَسَهُ وَجَاءَ مَعَهُ إلَى مَنْزِلِهِ؛ وَلَمْ يَقِفْ عِنْدَهُ فَوَقَعَ عَنْ فَرَسِهِ ثَانِيَةً ثُمَّ إنَّهُ أَصْبَحَ مَيِّتًا؛ فَسَأَلَ رَجُلٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الْمَيِّتِ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلَ خِفْيَةً؛ وَلَمْ يُعْلِمْهُ بِمَوْتِهِ؛ فَذَكَرَ لَهُ قَضِيَّتَهُمَا فَشَهِدَ عَلَيْهِ الشُّهُودُ بِأَنَّ فُلَانًا ضَرَبَهُ وَلَمْ يَسْمَعْ الشُّهُودُ مِنْ الْمَيِّتِ؛ وَأَنَّ الْمُتَّهَمَ لَمْ يُظْهِرْ نَفْسَهُ خَوْفَ الْعُقُوبَةِ؛ لِكَيْ لَا يُقِرَّ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ وَلِلْمَيِّتِ بِنْتٌ تَرْضَعُ وَإِخْوَةٌ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ كَانَ الَّذِي شَرِبَ الْخَمْرَ يَعْلَمُ مَا يَقُولُ فَهَذَا إذَا قَتَلَ فَهُوَ قَاتِلٌ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ الْقَوَدُ وَعُقُوبَةُ قَاتِلِ النَّفْسِ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ. وَأَمَّا إنْ كَانَ قَدْ سَكِرَ بِحَيْثُ لَا يَعْلَمُ مَا يَقُولُ أَوْ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ؛
 وَقَتَلَ:
 فَهَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ الْقَوَدُ وَيُسَلَّمُ إلَى أَوْلِيَاءِ الْمَقْتُولِ لِيَقْتُلُوهُ إنْ شَاءُوا؟ هَذَا فِيهِ قَوْلَانِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ وَفِيهِ رِوَايَتَانِ عَنْ أَحْمَد؛ لَكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ الْفُقَهَاءِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَكَثِيرٍ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد يُوجِبُونَ عَلَيْهِ الْقَوَدَ؛ كَمَا يُوجِبُونَهُ عَلَى الصَّاحِي فَإِنْ لَمْ يَشْهَدْ بِالْقَتْلِ إلَّا وَاحِدٌ لَمْ يُحْكَمْ بِهِ إلَّا أَنْ يَحْلِفَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ أَوْلِيَاءُ الْمَقْتُولِ خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا؛
 وَهَذَا إذَا مَاتَ بِضَرْبِهِ وَكَانَ ضَرْبُهُ عُدْوَانًا مَحْضًا فَأَمَّا إنْ مَاتَ مَعَ ضَرْبِ الْآخَرِ:
 فَفِي الْقَوَدِ نِزَاعٌ وَكَذَلِكَ إنْ ضَرَبَهُ دَفْعًا لِعُدْوَانِهِ عَلَيْهِ أَوْ ضَرْبِهِ مِثْلَ مَا ضَرَبَهُ سَوَاءٌ مَاتَ بِسَبَبِ آخَرَ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ وَاعَدَ آخَرَ عَلَى قَتْلِ مُسْلِمٍ بِمَالِ مُعَيَّنٍ ثُمَّ قَتَلَهُ؛ فَمَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ فِي الشَّرْعِ؟
translated_text:
beside him. This was the man who had been accompanying them; he waited until the injured man remounted his horse, then accompanied him home but did not stay with him. The injured man fell from his horse a second time and was found dead the next morning. One of the deceased’s companions privately questioned the man who had accompanied them, without telling him of the death, and he related what had happened between the two men. Witnesses then testified against the accused that so-and-so had struck the deceased, although they had heard nothing from the deceased himself. The accused had not come forward, fearing punishment and wishing to avoid incriminating himself. The deceased left an infant daughter who was still nursing, as well as siblings.

He replied:

If the man who drank wine knew what he was saying, then, if he killed someone, he is a killer liable to retaliatory execution and the punishment for taking a life, by scholarly consensus. But if he was so intoxicated that he did not know what he was saying, or was even more intoxicated than that, and killed someone, is he liable to retaliatory execution and to be handed over to the slain person’s heirs for them to execute him if they wish?

The scholars hold two opinions on this, and two positions are reported from Ahmad. However, most jurists among the followers of Abū Hanīfa, Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, and many of Ahmad’s followers, hold him liable to retaliatory execution, just as they would a sober person. If only one witness testifies to the killing, no judgment may be based on that testimony unless the slain person’s heirs also swear fifty oaths.

This applies if he died from the accused’s blow and that blow was an entirely unjustified assault. If, however, another person’s blow also contributed to his death, there is disagreement over retaliatory execution. Likewise, there is disagreement if he struck him to repel his aggression or struck him just as he himself had been struck, whether he died from another cause or otherwise. Allah knows best.

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him:

About a man who promised another a specified sum of money to kill a Muslim, and the latter then killed him: what is he liable to under Islamic law?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ،
 إذَا قَتَلَهُ الْمَوْعُودُ وَالْحَالَةُ هَذِهِ وَجَبَ الْقَوَدُ وَأَوْلِيَاءُ الْمَقْتُولِ بِالْخِيَارِ:
 إنْ أَحَبُّوا قَتَلُوا وَإِنْ أَحَبُّوا أَخَذُوا الدِّيَةَ وَإِنْ أَحَبُّوا عَفَوْا. وَأَمَّا الْوَاعِدُ فَيَجِبُ أَنْ يُعَاقَبَ عُقُوبَةً تَرْدَعُهُ وَأَمْثَالَهُ عَنْ مِثْلِ هَذَا. وَعِنْدَ بَعْضِهِمْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ الْقَوَدُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ الْقَاتِلِ وَلَدَهُ عَمْدًا لِمَنْ دِيَتُهُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
وَأَمَّا الْوَارِثُ كَالْأَبِ وَغَيْرِهِ إذَا قَتَلَ مُورِثَهُ عَمْدًا فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَرِثُ شَيْئًا مِنْ مَالِهِ؛ وَلَا دِيَتِهِ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ؛ بَلْ تَكُونُ دِيَتُهُ كَسَائِرِ مَالِهِ يَحْرِمُهَا الْقَاتِلُ أَبًا كَانَ أَوْ غَيْرَهُ وَيَرِثُهَا سَائِرُ الْوَرَثَةِ غَيْرِ الْقَاتِلِ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ تَخَاصَمَ مَعَ شَخْصٍ فَرَاحَ إلَى بَيْتِهِ فَحَصَلَ لَهُ ضَعْفٌ فَلَمَّا قَارَبَ الْوَفَاةَ أَشْهَدَ كُلَّ نَفْسِهِ أَنَّ قَاتِلَهُ فُلَانٌ فَقِيلَ لَهُ. كَيْفَ قَتَلَك؟ فَلَمْ يَذْكُرْ شَيْئًا. فَهَلْ يَلْزَمُهُ شَيْءٌ أَمْ لَا؟ وَلَيْسَ بِهَذَا الْمَرِيضِ أَثَرُ قَتْلٍ وَلَا ضَرْبٍ أَصْلًا وَقَدْ شَهِدَ خَلْقٌ مِنْ الْعُدُولِ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَضْرِبْهُ وَلَا فَعَلَ بِهِ شَيْئًا؟
translated_text:
He replied:

Yes. If the man who was promised payment killed him under these circumstances, he is liable to retaliatory execution. The slain person’s heirs have the choice: they may have him executed, accept blood money, or pardon him. As for the man who promised payment, he must receive a punishment that deters him and others like him from such conduct. Some scholars hold that he too is liable to retaliatory execution.

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him:

If a man deliberately kills his own child, who receives the child’s blood money?

He replied:

If an heir, whether the father or someone else, deliberately kills the person from whom he would inherit, he inherits neither any of that person’s property nor any of his blood money, by agreement of the imams. Rather, the blood money is treated like the rest of the deceased’s property: the killer, whether the father or someone else, is barred from inheriting it, and the remaining heirs inherit it instead.

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him:

About a man who quarreled with someone, then returned home and became weak. As death approached, he called witnesses to his declaration that so-and-so was his killer. He was asked, “How did he kill you?” but gave no explanation. Is the accused liable to anything or not, given that the sick man bore no sign whatsoever of fatal injury or beating, and many upright witnesses testified that the accused had neither struck him nor done anything to him?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا بِمُجَرَّدِ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ فَلَا يَلْزَمُهُ شَيْءٌ بِإِجْمَاعِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛
 بَلْ إنَّمَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْمُدَّعَى عَلَيْهِ الْيَمِينُ بِنَفْيِ مَا ادَّعَى عَلَيْهِ إمَّا يَمِينٌ وَاحِدَةٌ عِنْدَ أَكْثَرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ:
 كَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَأَحْمَد.
 وَإِمَّا خَمْسُونَ يَمِينًا:
 كَقَوْلِ الشَّافِعِيِّ. وَالْعُلَمَاءُ قَدْ تَنَازَعُوا فِي الرَّجُلِ إذَا كَانَ بِهِ أَثَرُ الْقَتْلِ - كَجُرْحِ أَوْ أَثَرِ ضَرْبٍ -
 فَقَالَ فُلَانٌ:
 ضَرَبَنِي عَمْدًا: هَلْ يَكُونُ ذَلِكَ لَوْثًا؟
 فَقَالَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ كَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد:
 لَيْسَ بِلَوْثِ؛
 وَقَالَ مَالِكٌ:
 هُوَ لَوْثٌ فَإِذَا حَلَفَ أَوْلِيَاءُ الدَّمِ خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا حُكِمَ بِهِ. وَلَوْ كَانَ الْقَتْلُ خَطَأً فَلَا قَسَامَةَ فِيهِ فِي أَصَحِّ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْ مَالِكٍ.
 وَهَذِهِ الصُّورَةُ قِيلَ:
 لَمْ تَكُنْ خَطَأً فَكَيْفَ وَلَيْسَ بِهِ أَثَرُ قَتْلٍ؛
 وَقَدْ شَهِدَ النَّاسُ بِمَا شَهِدُوا بِهِ:
 فَهَذِهِ الصُّورَةُ لَيْسَ فِيهَا قَسَامَةٌ بِلَا رَيْبٍ عَلَى مَذْهَبِ الْأَئِمَّةِ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ اُتُّهِمَ بِقَتِيلِ، فَهَلْ يُضْرَبُ لِيُقِرَّ؟ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ كَانَ هُنَاكَ لَوْثٌ وَهُوَ مَا يَغْلِبُ عَلَى الظَّنِّ أَنَّهُ قَتَلَهُ جَازَ لِأَوْلِيَاءِ الْمَقْتُولِ أَنْ يَحْلِفُوا خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا وَيَسْتَحِقُّونَ دَمَهُ وَأَمَّا ضَرْبُهُ لِيُقِرَّ فَلَا يَجُوزُ إلَّا مَعَ الْقَرَائِنِ الَّتِي تَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّهُ قَتَلَهُ فَإِنَّ بَعْضَ الْعُلَمَاءِ جَوَّزَ تَقْرِيرَهُ بِالضَّرْبِ فِي هَذِهِ الْحَالِ وَبَعْضُهُمْ مَنَعَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ مُطْلَقًا.
translated_text:
He replied:

On the strength of this statement alone, he incurs no liability, by the consensus of the Muslims. The defendant is required only to swear an oath denying the allegation against him: either a single oath, according to most scholars, including Abū Hanīfa and Ahmad, or fifty oaths, according to al-Shāfiʿī.

The scholars have differed concerning a man who bears signs of a fatal assault—such as a wound or marks of a beating—and says, “So-and-so struck me deliberately.” Does this constitute presumptive evidence of guilt (lawth)? Most scholars, including Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, hold that it does not. Mālik holds that it does, and that if the slain person’s heirs swear fifty oaths, judgment is rendered on that basis. If the killing was accidental, however, the fifty-oath procedure (qasāma) does not apply, according to the sounder of the two reports from Mālik.

In the case at hand, it was said that the killing was not accidental. What, then, when he bears no sign of fatal injury and the witnesses have testified as they did? Undoubtedly, the fifty-oath procedure does not apply to this case according to the doctrines of the imams.

He was asked:

May someone suspected of killing a person be beaten to make him confess, or not?

He replied:

If there is presumptive evidence of guilt—that is, evidence making it highly probable that he killed the victim—the slain person’s heirs may swear fifty oaths, thereby becoming entitled to have him executed in retaliation. As for beating him to obtain a confession, this is not permissible unless there is circumstantial evidence indicating that he killed the victim. Some scholars permitted extracting a confession through beating in these circumstances, while others prohibited it altogether.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ أَهْلِ قَرْيَتَيْنِ بَيْنَهُمَا عَدَاوَةٌ فِي الِاعْتِقَادِ وَخَاصَمَ رَجُلٌ آخَرَ فِي غَنَمٍ ضَاعَتْ لَهُ وَقَالَ:
 مَا يَكُونُ عِوَضُ هَذَا إلَّا رَقَبَتَك. ثُمَّ وُجِدَ هَذَا مَقْتُولًا وَأَثَرُ الدَّمِ أَقْرَبُ إلَى الْقَرْيَةِ الَّتِي مِنْهَا الْمُتَّهَمُ وَذَكَرَ رَجُلٌ لَهُ قَتَلَهُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا حَلَفَ أَوْلِيَاءُ الْمَقْتُولِ خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الْمُخَاصِمَ هُوَ الَّذِي قَتَلَهُ حُكِمَ لَهُمْ بِدَمِهِ؛ وَبَرَاءَةِ مَنْ سِوَاهُ فَإِنَّمَا بَيْنَهُمَا مِنْ الْعَدَاوَةِ وَالْخُصُومَةِ وَالْوَعِيدِ بِالْقَتْلِ وَأَثَرِ الدَّمِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ لَوْثٌ وَقَرِينَةٌ وَأَمَارَةٌ عَلَى أَنَّ هَذَا الْمُتَّهَمَ هُوَ الَّذِي قَتَلَهُ فَإِذَا حَلَفُوا مَعَ ذَلِكَ أَيْمَانَ الْقَسَامَةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ اسْتَحَقُّوا دَمَ الْمُتَّهَمِ وَسُلِّمَ إلَيْهِمْ بِرُمَّتِهِ كَمَا قَضَى بِذَلِكَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي قَضِيَّةِ الَّذِي قُتِلَ بِخَيْبَرِ وَلَمْ يَجِبْ عَلَى أَهْلِ الْبُقْعَةِ جِنَايَةٌ؛ لَا فِي الْعَادَةِ السُّلْطَانِيَّةِ وَلَا فِي حُكْمِ الشَّرِيعَةِ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ شَخْصَيْنِ اُتُّهِمَا بِقَتِيلِ فَأُمْسِكَا وَعُوقِبَا الْعُقُوبَةَ الْمُؤْلِمَةَ فَأَقَرَّ أَحَدُهُمَا عَلَى نَفْسِهِ وَعَلَى رَفِيقِهِ وَلَمْ يُقِرَّ الْآخَرُ وَلَا اعْتَرَفَ بِشَيْءِ:
 فَهَلْ يُقْبَلُ قَوْلُهُ أَمْ لَا؟
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

The inhabitants of two villages are hostile to one another over matters of belief. A man disputed with another over some sheep he had lost and said, “Nothing but your life will compensate for this.” The latter was then found murdered, and the traces of blood were nearer the village from which the accused came. A man also mentioned his killing to him?

He replied:

If the slain person’s heirs swear fifty oaths that the man who disputed with him was his killer, judgment is rendered granting them the right to have him executed in retaliation and absolving everyone else. The hostility and dispute between the two, the threat to kill him, the traces of blood and other such circumstances constitute presumptive evidence of guilt and indications that this accused man was the killer. If, alongside this evidence, they swear the legally prescribed oaths of the fifty-oath procedure, they become entitled to have the accused executed in retaliation, and he is placed entirely in their custody. This accords with the judgment of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning the man killed at Khaybar. No liability for the killing falls upon the inhabitants of the locality, whether under the customary practice of the governing authorities or under Islamic law.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Two men were suspected of a killing, detained and subjected to painful punishment. One confessed, implicating both himself and his companion, while the other neither confessed nor admitted anything. Is the former’s statement to be accepted or not?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ شَهِدَ شَاهِدٌ مَقْبُولٌ عَلَى شَخْصٍ أَنَّهُ قَتَلَهُ كَانَ لِأَوْلِيَاءِ الْمَقْتُولِ أَنْ يَحْلِفُوا خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا وَيَسْتَحِقُّوا الدَّمَ. وَكَذَلِكَ إنْ كَانَ هُنَاكَ لَوْثٌ يَغْلِبُ عَلَى الظَّنِّ الصِّدْقُ؛ وَإِلَّا حَلَفَ الْمُدَّعَى عَلَيْهِ وَلَا يُؤَاخَذُ بِلَا حُجَّةٍ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
مَنْ اُتُّهِمُوا بِقَتِيلِ فَضَرَبُوهُمْ وَاعْتَرَفَ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمْ بِالْعُقُوبَةِ:
 فَهَلْ يَسْرِي عَلَى الْبَاقِي؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، إنْ أَقَرَّ وَاحِدٌ عَدْلٌ أَنَّهُ قَتَلَهُ كَانَ لَوْثًا فَلِأَوْلِيَاءِ الْمَقْتُولِ أَنْ يَحْلِفُوا خَمْسِينَ يَمِينًا وَيَسْتَحِقُّوا بِهِ الدَّمَ.
 وَأَمَّا إذَا أَقَرَّ مُكْرَهًا وَلَمْ يَتَبَيَّنْ صِدْقَ إقْرَارِهِ:
 فَهُنَا لَا يَتَرَتَّبُ عَلَيْهِ حُكْمٌ وَلَا يُؤْخَذُ هُوَ بِهِ وَلَا غَيْرُهُ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ سُفَّارٍ جَاءَتْهُمْ حَرَامِيَّةٌ فَقَاتَلُوهُمْ فَقَتَلَ الْحَرَامِيَّةُ مِنْ السُّفَّارِ رَجُلًا ثُمَّ إنَّ ابْنَ عَمِّ الْمَقْتُولِ اتَّبَعَ الْحَرَامِيَّةَ هُوَ وَنَاسٌ مِنْ قَوْمِهِ فَلَحِقَهُمْ وَقَبَضَهُمْ وَسَأَلَ عَنْ الْقَاتِلِ فَعَيَّنَ الْحَرَامِيَّةُ شَخْصًا مِنْهُمْ وَقَالُوا:
 هَذَا قَتَلَ ابْنَ عَمِّك: فَقَتَلَهُ؛ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ طَلَعَ الْقَاتِلُ أَخَا ذَلِكَ الشَّخْصِ الَّذِي عَيَّنَهُ الْحَرَامِيَّةُ؟
translated_text:
He replied:

If a witness whose testimony is admissible testifies that a particular person killed him, the slain person’s heirs may swear fifty oaths and thereby become entitled to have the accused executed in retaliation. The same applies if there is presumptive evidence of guilt that makes the allegation likely to be true. Otherwise, the defendant must swear an oath and cannot be held liable without proof.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Some people were accused of a killing and were beaten, and one of them confessed under punishment. Does his confession implicate the others?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If one upright man confesses that he killed him, this constitutes presumptive evidence of guilt. The slain person’s heirs may therefore swear fifty oaths and thereby become entitled to have the accused executed in retaliation.

But if he confesses under coercion and the truth of his confession has not been established, no legal ruling follows from it, and neither he nor anyone else may be held liable on its basis. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A group of travelers encountered bandits, and they fought one another. The bandits killed one of the travelers. The slain man’s cousin then pursued the bandits with some of his own people, caught up with them and captured them. He asked who the killer was, and the bandits singled out one of their number, saying, “This man killed your cousin.” So he killed him. It subsequently emerged, however, that the actual killer was the brother of the man whom the bandits had identified?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا الْمُسَافِرُ الْمَقْتُولُ ظُلْمًا فَيَجِبُ عَلَى مَنْ قَتَلَهُ مِنْ الْحَرَامِيَّةِ الْقَوَدُ بِشُرُوطِهِ وَأَمَّا الشَّخْصُ الثَّانِي الْمَقْتُولُ ظُلْمًا إذَا كَانَ مَعْصُومًا فَإِنْ كَانَ الدَّالُّ عَلَيْهِ مُتَعَمِّدًا الْكَذِبَ فَعَلَيْهِ الْقَوَدُ وَإِنْ كَانَ مُخْطِئًا وَجَبَتْ الدِّيَةُ عَلَى عَاقِلَتِهِ إنْ كَانَ لَهُ عَاقِلَةٌ؛ وَإِلَّا فَعَلَيْهِ. وَأَمَّا قَاتِلُهُ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَتَعَمَّدْ قَتْلَهُ؛ بَلْ أَخْطَأَ فِيهِ؛ فَلِلْوَرَثَةِ أَنْ يُطَالِبُوا بِالدِّيَةِ لَهُ أَوْ لِعَاقِلَتِهِ؛ لَكِنْ إذَا ضَمِنَ الدِّيَةَ رَجَعَ بِهَا عَلَى الدَّالِّ أَوْ عَاقِلَتِهِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ هُوَ الَّذِي يُضَافُ إلَيْهِ الْقَتْلُ فِي مِثْلِ هَذَا؛ وَلِهَذَا يَجِبُ قَتْلُهُ إذَا تَعَمَّدَ الْكَذِبَ؛ كَمَا يَجِبُ الْقَتْلُ عَلَى الشُّهُودِ إذَا رَجَعُوا عَنْ الشَّهَادَةِ وَقَالُوا تَعَمَّدْنَا الْكَذِبَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَتَلَ قَتِيلًا؛
 وَلَهُ أَبٌ وَأُمٌّ وَقَدْ وَهَبَا لِلْقَاتِلِ دَمَ وَلَدِهِمَا وَكَتَبَا عَلَيْهِ حُجَّةً أَنَّهُ لَا يَنْزِلُ بِلَادَهُمْ وَلَا يَسْكُنُ فِيهَا وَمَتَى سَكَنَ فِي الْبِلَادِ كَانَ دَمُ وَلَدِهِمَا عَلَى الْقَاتِلِ فَإِذَا سَكَنَ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهُمْ الْمُطَالَبَةُ بِالدَّمِ؛ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، إذَا عَفَوْا عَنْهُ بِهَذَا الشَّرْطِ وَلَمْ يَفِ بِهَذَا الشَّرْطِ لَمْ يَكُنْ الْعَفْوُ لَازِمًا؛ بَلْ لَهُمْ أَنْ يُطَالِبُوهُ بِالدِّيَةِ فِي قَوْلِ بَعْضِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَبِالدَّمِ فِي قَوْلٍ آخَرَ.
 وَسَوَاءٌ قِيلَ:
 هَذَا الشَّرْطُ صَحِيحٌ؛ أَمْ فَاسِدٌ.
 وَسَوَاءٌ قِيلَ:
 يَفْسُدُ الْعَقْدُ بِفَسَادِهِ أَوْ لَا يَفْسُدُ؛ فَإِنَّ ذَيْنِك الْقَوْلَيْنِ مَبْنِيَّانِ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْأُصُولِ
translated_text:
He replied:

As for the traveler who was wrongfully killed, the bandit who killed him must be executed in retaliation, provided the requisite conditions are met. As for the second man who was wrongfully killed, if his life was legally protected, then the person who identified him must be executed in retaliation if he deliberately lied. If he was mistaken, blood money must be paid by his kin group responsible for such payments, if he has one; otherwise, he himself must pay it.

As for the man who killed him, if he did not kill him deliberately but did so in error, the heirs may claim blood money from him or his kin group. However, if he is held liable for the blood money, he has recourse against the person who identified the victim or that person’s kin group, since, in cases such as this, the killing is attributed to the person who identified him. For this reason, he must be executed if he deliberately lied, just as witnesses must be executed if they retract their testimony and say, “We deliberately lied.” Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man killed someone whose father and mother were still alive. They waived their right to retaliation against the killer and drew up a written undertaking stipulating that he must neither enter their territory nor reside there, and that, should he reside there, he would again be answerable for their son’s blood. If he does reside there, may they demand retaliation for the killing, or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If they pardoned him on this condition and he failed to fulfill it, the pardon is not binding. Rather, according to some scholars, they may demand blood money from him; according to another opinion, they may demand his execution in retaliation.

This applies whether the condition is considered valid or invalid, and whether its invalidity is considered to invalidate the agreement or not, for those two opinions rest on these principles.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ صَبِيٍّ دُونَ الْبُلُوغِ جَنَى جِنَايَةً يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ فِيهَا دِيَةٌ:
 مِثْلَ أَنْ يَكْسِرَ سِنًّا أَوْ يَفْقَأَ عَيْنًا وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ؛
 خَطَأً:
 فَهَلْ لِأَوْلِيَاءِ ذَلِكَ أَنْ يَأْخُذُوا دِيَةَ الْجِنَايَةِ مِنْ أَبِي الصَّبِيِّ وَحْدَهُ إنْ كَانَ مُوسِرًا؟ أَمْ يَطْلُبُوهَا مِنْ عَمِّ الصَّبِيِّ أَوْ ابْنِ عَمِّهِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، أَمَّا إذَا فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ خَطَأً فَدِيَتُهُ عَلَى عَاقِلَتِهِ بِلَا رَيْبٍ؛ كَالْبَالِغِ وَأَوْلَى.
 وَإِنْ فَعَلَ عَمْدًا فَعَمْدُهُ خَطَأٌ عِنْدَ الْجُمْهُورِ:
 كَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد فِي الْمَشْهُورِ عَنْهُ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ فِي أَحَدِ قَوْلَيْهِ. وَفِي الْقَوْلِ الْآخَرِ عَنْهُ وَعَنْ أَحْمَد أَنَّ عَمْدَهُ إذَا كَانَ غَيْرَ بَاغٍ فِي مَالِهِ. وَأَمَّا 
" الْعَاقِلَةُ "
 الَّتِي تَحْمِلُ: فَهُمْ عَصَبَتُهُ: كَالْعَمِّ وَبَنِيهِ وَالْإِخْوَةِ وَبَنِيهِمْ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ.
 وَأَمَّا أَبُو الرَّجُلِ وَابْنُهُ فَهُوَ مِنْ عَاقِلَتِهِ أَيْضًا عِنْدَ الْجُمْهُورِ:
 كَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد فِي أَظْهَرِ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْهُ.
 وَفِي الرِّوَايَةِ الْأُخْرَى وَهُوَ قَوْلُ الشَّافِعِيِّ:
 أَبُوهُ وَابْنُهُ لَيْسَا مِنْ الْعَاقِلَةِ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A boy who has not reached puberty accidentally causes an injury requiring compensation, such as breaking a tooth, putting out an eye, or the like. May those entitled to compensation collect it from the boy’s father alone if he is wealthy, or should they seek it from the boy’s paternal uncle or paternal cousin?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If he did this accidentally, the compensation is undoubtedly payable by his kin group responsible for such payments, just as in the case of an adult—indeed, all the more so.

If he did it deliberately, his deliberate act is treated as accidental according to the majority of scholars, including Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, Ahmad—according to the well-known position reported from him—and al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two opinions. According to the other opinion reported from al-Shāfiʿī, and also reported from Ahmad, compensation for his deliberate act, if he is not an aggressor, is payable from his own property.

As for the “kin group responsible for payment,” these are his agnatic relatives, such as his paternal uncle and that uncle’s sons, and his brothers and their sons, by scholarly consensus.

A man’s father and son are also included in this kin group according to the majority, including Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and Ahmad, according to the stronger of the two positions reported from him. According to the other position, which is also al-Shāfiʿī’s view, his father and son are not included in this kin group.

What is “borne by the kin group responsible for payment,” by scholarly agreement, is compensation exceeding one-third of the full blood money. For example, putting out an eye requires payment of half the full blood money.

As for compensation below one-third—such as that for a tooth, which is half of one-tenth of the full blood money, or a finger, which is one-tenth—the kin group does not bear it according to the schools of Mālik and Ahmad. Rather, according to al-Shāfiʿī, it is payable from the offender’s own property. According to Abū Hanīfah, the kin group does not bear compensation below the prescribed amount for a tooth or a wound exposing the bone, such as compensation for a head wound less severe than one exposing the bone.

If a boy becomes liable for a payment but has no property, his father bears it on his behalf according to one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. This was also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. According to the other position, which is the view of most scholars, it remains a debt owed by the boy, and his father bears no liability. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man said to his wife, “Abort what is in your womb, and I shall bear the sin.” If she does so, obeying him, what expiation must they offer?

He replied:

If she does that, they must offer the expiation of freeing a believing slave. If they cannot find one, they must fast for two consecutive months. They must also give a male or female slave as compensation to the unborn child’s heir who took no part in killing it—not to the father, for the father ordered its killing and is therefore entitled to nothing.

Praise be to Allah.

This is the burying alive of children concerning which Allah Most High said:

“And when the girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Do not kill your children for fear of poverty.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Mas‘ūd reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked, “Which sin is the gravest?” He replied, “To set up a rival to Allah when He created you.” He was asked, “Then which?” He replied, “To kill your child for fear that he will share your food.”

If Allah has forbidden killing one’s child even in circumstances of need and fear of poverty, then its prohibition in the absence of such circumstances is all the more certain. According to the majority of scholars, this woman must pay blood money to the child’s heirs. By agreement of the imams, she is entitled to none of it. There are two opinions as to whether she must offer expiation. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

If a man slaps, wounds, or insults another man, may the latter do to him what he did?

He replied:

As for “retaliation for a slap or a blow” and similar acts, the position of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and other Companions, as well as the Successors, is that retaliation is prescribed in all such cases. This is also Ahmad’s expressly stated position, as transmitted by Ismā‘īl ibn Sa‘īd al-Shālanjī. Many jurists, however, held that retaliation is not prescribed in such cases, because exact equivalence is generally unattainable. This is the position of many followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad.

{وَجَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُهَا}
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{فَمَنِ اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ فَاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ مَا اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ}
 وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ.
 وَأَمَّا قَوْلُ الْقَائِلِ:
 إنَّ الْمُمَاثَلَةَ فِي هَذِهِ الْجِنَايَةِ مُتَعَذِّرَةٌ.
 فَيُقَالُ:
 لَا بُدَّ لِهَذِهِ الْجِنَايَةِ مِنْ عُقُوبَةٍ: إمَّا قِصَاصٌ وَإِمَّا تَعْزِيرٌ. فَإِذَا جُوِّزَ أَنْ يُعَزَّزَ تَعْزِيرًا غَيْرَ مَضْبُوطِ الْجِنْسِ وَالْقَدْرِ فَلَأَنْ يُعَاقِبَ إلَى مَا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ إلَى الضَّبْطِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَوْلَى وَأَحْرَى. وَالْعَدْلُ فِي الْقِصَاصِ مُعْتَبَرٌ بِحَسَبِ الْإِمْكَانِ وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّ الضَّارِبَ إذَا ضُرِبَ ضَرْبَةً مِثْلَ ضَرْبَتِهِ أَوْ قَرِيبًا مِنْهَا كَانَ هَذَا أَقْرَبَ إلَى الْعَدْلِ مِنْ أَنْ يُعَزَّرَ بِالضَّرْبِ بِالسَّوْطِ؛ فَاَلَّذِي يَمْنَعُ الْقِصَاصَ فِي ذَلِكَ خَوْفًا مِنْ الظُّلْمِ يُبِيحُ مَا هُوَ أَعْظَمُ ظُلْمًا مِمَّا فَرَّ مِنْهُ. فَعُلِمَ أَنَّمَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ أَعْدَلُ وَأَمْثَلُ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ لَهُ أَنْ يَسُبَّهُ كَمَا يَسُبُّهُ:
 مِثْلَ أَنْ يَلْعَنَهُ كَمَا يَلْعَنُهُ.
 أَوْ يَقُولُ:
 قَبَّحَك اللَّهُ.
 فَيَقُولُ:
 قَبَّحَك اللَّهُ.
 أَوْ:
 أَخْزَاك اللَّهُ.
 فَيَقُولُ لَهُ:
 أَخْزَاك اللَّهُ.
 أَوْ يَقُولُ:
 يَا كَلْبُ يَا خِنْزِيرُ فَيَقُولُ: يَا كَلْبُ يَا خِنْزِيرُ فَأَمَّا إذَا كَانَ مُحَرَّمَ الْجِنْسِ مِثْلَ تَكْفِيرِهِ أَوْ الْكَذِبِ عَلَيْهِ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ أَنْ يُكَفِّرَهُ وَلَا يَكْذِبَ عَلَيْهِ. وَإِذَا لَعَنَ أَبَاهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ أَنْ يَلْعَنَ أَبَاهُ لِأَنَّ أَبَاهُ لَمْ يَظْلِمْهُ.
translated_text:
The former view is more correct, for the Sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, established retaliation in such cases, as did the practice of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Allah Most High said:

“The recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it.”

Allah Most High also said:

“If anyone commits aggression against you, retaliate against him in the same measure as his aggression against you.”

There are other passages to the same effect.

As for the assertion that exact equivalence is unattainable in this kind of injury, the answer is that such an injury must incur a punishment: either retaliation or discretionary punishment. If discretionary punishment is permitted even though its kind and extent are not precisely defined, then imposing a punishment that can be more precisely measured is all the more fitting and appropriate. Justice in retaliation is required to the extent possible. It is well known that striking an assailant with a blow equal or close to his own is nearer to justice than subjecting him to discretionary punishment by flogging. Thus, whoever prohibits retaliation in such cases for fear of injustice permits something more unjust than what he sought to avoid. This shows that what the Sunnah prescribes is more just and more appropriate.

Likewise, a person may answer an insult with the same insult, such as cursing someone just as that person cursed him. If someone says, “May Allah disgrace you,” he may reply, “May Allah disgrace you.” If someone says, “May Allah humiliate you,” he may reply, “May Allah humiliate you.” If someone says, “You dog! You pig!” he may reply, “You dog! You pig!”

But if the speech is of a kind that is inherently forbidden, such as declaring him a disbeliever or lying about him, he may not declare the other person a disbeliever or lie about him in return. If the other person curses his father, he may not curse that person’s father in return, for that father has done him no wrong.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَمَّنْ ضَرَبَ غَيْرَهُ فَعَطَّلَ مَنْفَعَةَ أُصْبُعِهِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا تَعَطَّلَتْ مَنْفَعَةُ أُصْبُعِهِ بِالْجِنَايَةِ الَّتِي اعْتَدَى فِيهَا وَجَبَتْ دِيَةُ الْأُصْبُعِ وَهِيَ عُشْرُ الدِّيَةِ الْكَامِلَةِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - قَدَّسَ اللَّه رُوحَهُ -:
عَنْ اثْنَيْنِ:
 أَحَدُهُمَا حُرٌّ وَالْآخَرُ عَبْدٌ: حَمَلُوا خَشَبَةً فَتَهَوَّرَتْ مِنْهُمْ الْخَشَبَةُ مِنْ غَيْرِ عَمْدٍ؛ فَأَصَابَتْ رَجُلًا؛
 فَأَقَامَ يَوْمَيْنِ وَتُوُفِّيَ:
 فَمَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْحُرِّ وَالْعَبْدِ؟ وَمَاذَا يَجِبُ عَلَى مَالِكِ الْعَبْدِ إذَا تَغَيَّبَ الْعَبْدُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا حَصَلَ مِنْهُمَا تَفْرِيطٌ أَوْ عُدْوَانٌ وَجَبَ الضَّمَانُ عَلَيْهِمَا. وَإِنْ كَانَ هُوَ الْمُفَرِّطَ بِوُقُوفِهِ حَيْثُ لَا يَصْلُحُ فَلَا ضَمَانَ. وَإِنْ لَمْ يَحْصُلْ تَفْرِيطٌ مِنْهُمَا فَلَا ضَمَانَ عَلَيْهِمَا. وَإِنْ كَانَ بِطَرِيقِ السَّبَبِ فَلَا ضَمَانَ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about someone who struck another person, causing him to lose the use of a finger.

He replied:

If his finger loses its function because of the wrongful injury inflicted upon him, the prescribed compensation for that finger is due, namely one tenth of the full blood money. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked about two men, one free and the other a slave, who were carrying a piece of timber. It accidentally fell from them and struck a man, who survived for two days and then died. What is due from the free man and the slave? And what is due from the slave’s owner if the slave is absent?

He replied:

If there was negligence or wrongful conduct on their part, both are liable for compensation. If, however, the victim himself was negligent by standing where he ought not to have stood, there is no liability. If there was no negligence on their part, neither is liable. If the harm occurred through indirect causation, there is no liability.

original_text:
وَإِذَا وَجَبَ الضَّمَانُ عَلَيْهِمَا نِصْفَيْنِ فَنَصِيبُ الْعَبْدِ يَتَعَلَّقُ بِرَقَبَتِهِ فَإِنْ شَاءَ سَيِّدُهُ أَنْ يُسَلِّمَهُ فِي الْجِنَايَةِ وَإِنْ شَاءَ أَنْ يَفْتَدِيَهُ. وَإِذَا افْتَدَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَفْتَدِيهِ بِأَقَلِّ الْأَمْرَيْنِ مِنْ قِيمَتِهِ وَقَدْرِ جِنَايَتِهِ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْهُ وَفِي الْأُخْرَى وَفِي مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ يَفْدِيهِ بِأَرْشِ الْجِنَايَةِ بَالِغًا مَا بَلَغَ. فَأَمَّا إنْ جَنَى الْعَبْدُ وَهَرَبَ بِحَيْثُ لَا يُمْكِنُ سَيِّدَهُ تَسْلِيمُهُ فَلَيْسَ عَلَى السَّيِّدِ شَيْءٌ إلَّا أَنْ يَخْتَارَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ ثَلَاثَةٍ حَمَلُوا عَمُودَ رُخَامٍ ثُمَّ أَنَّ مِنْهُمْ اثْنَيْنِ رَمَوْا الْعَمُودَ عَلَى الْآخَرِ كَسَرُوا رِجْلَهُ. فَمَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِمْ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، نَعَمْ إذَا أَلْقَوْا عَلَيْهِ عَمُودَ الرُّخَامِ حَتَّى كَسَرُوا سَاقَهُ وَجَبَ ضَمَانُ ذَلِكَ؛
 لَكِنْ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ مَنْ يُوجِبُ بَعِيرَيْنِ مِنْ الْإِبِلِ كَمَا هُوَ الْمَشْهُورُ عَنْ أَحْمَد:
 وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُوجِبُ فِيهِ حُكُومَةً وَهُوَ أَنْ يُقَوَّمَ الْمَجْنِيُّ عَلَيْهِ كَأَنَّهُ لَا كَسْرَ بِهِ ثُمَّ يُقَوَّمَ مَكْسُورًا؛
 فَيُنْظَرُ مَا نَقَصَ مِنْ قِيمَتِهِ:
 فَيَجِبُ بِقِسْطِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
And if they are liable for compensation in equal shares, the slave’s share attaches to his person: his master may either surrender him in settlement of the injury claim or redeem him. If he redeems him, he pays whichever is less: the slave’s value or the compensation due for the injury. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and one of the two reported positions of Ahmad. According to the other reported position, and the school of Mālik, he redeems him by paying the full compensation for the injury, however much it may be. If, however, the slave causes an injury and flees, so that his master cannot surrender him, the master is under no obligation unless he voluntarily chooses to assume it. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Three men were carrying a marble column. Two of them then threw the column onto the third, breaking his leg. What is due from them?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Yes, if they dropped the marble column onto him and thereby broke his lower leg, they must pay compensation for that injury. Some scholars require two camels, as is the well-known position reported from Ahmad. Others require assessed compensation: the injured person’s value is assessed as though he had no fracture, then assessed with the fracture. The reduction in his value is determined, and compensation is due in proportion to that reduction. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلَيْنِ تَخَاصَمَا وَتَمَاسَكَا بِالْأَيْدِي وَلَمْ يَضْرِبْ أَحَدُهُمَا الْآخَرَ وَكَانَ أَحَدُهُمَا مَرِيضًا ثُمَّ تَفَارَقَا فِي عَافِيَةٍ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ أُسْبُوعٍ تُوُفِّيَ أَحَدُهُمَا وَهَرَبَ الْآخَرُ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِ بِثَلَاثَةِ أَيَّامٍ فَمُسِكَ أَبُو الْهَارِبِ وَأَلْزَمُوهُ بِإِحْضَارِ وَلَدِهِ فَاعْتَقَدَ أَنَّ الْخَصْمَ لَمْ يَمُتْ؛ وَالْتَزَمَ لِأَهْلِهِ أَنَّهُ مَهْمَا تَمَّ عَلَيْهِ كَانَ هُوَ الْقَائِمَ بِهِ؛
 فَلَمَّا مَاتَ اعْتَقَلُوا أَبَاهُ تِسْعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ فَرَاضَى أَبُوهُ أَهْلَ الْمَيِّتِ بِمَالِ وَأُبْرِئَ المتهوم وَكُلُّ أَهْلِهِ:
 فَهَلْ لِهَذَا الْمُلْتَزِمِ بِالْمَبْلَغِ أَنْ يَرْجِعَ كُلُّ أَحَدٍ مِنْ بَنِي عَمِّهِ بِشَيْءِ مِنْ الْمَبْلَغِ وَهَلْ يَبْرَأُ الْهَارِبُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ ثَبَتَ أَنَّ الْهَارِبَ قَتَلَهُ خَطَأً بِأَنْ يَكُونَ أَحَدُهُمَا مَرِيضًا وَقَدْ ضَرَبَهُ الْآخَرُ ضَرْبًا شَدِيدًا يَزِيدُ فِي مَرَضِهِ وَكَانَ سَبَبًا فِي مَوْتِهِ:
 فَالدِّيَةُ عَلَى الْعَاقِلَةِ. فَعَلَى عَصَبَةِ بَنِي الْعَمِّ وَغَيْرِهَا أَنْ يَتَحَمَّلُوا هَذَا الْقَدْرَ الَّذِي رَضِيَ بِهِ أَهْلُ الْقَتِيلِ فَإِنَّهُ أَخَفُّ مِنْ الدِّيَةِ وَأَمَّا إنْ لَمْ يَثْبُتْ شَيْءٌ مِنْ ذَلِكَ؛
 لَكِنْ أَخَذَ الْأَبُ بِمُجَرَّدِ إقْرَارِهِ:
 لَمْ يَلْزَمْهُمْ بِإِقْرَارِ الْأَبِ شَيْءٌ؛ وَلَيْسَ لِأَهْلِ الدِّيَةِ الَّذِينَ صَالَحُوا عَلَى هَذَا الْقَدْرِ أَنْ يُطَالِبُوا بِأَكْثَرَ مِنْهُ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Two men quarrelled and grappled with one another, but neither struck the other. One of them was ill. They then parted without injury. A week later, one of them died; the other had fled three days before his death. The fugitive’s father was detained and required to produce his son. Believing that his son’s adversary had not died, he undertook before the man’s family to discharge whatever liability might be established against his son.

When the man died, they imprisoned the father for nine months. The father then reached a financial settlement with the deceased’s family, and the accused and all his family were released from liability. May the father, who undertook to pay this sum, recover a contribution from each of his paternal cousins? And is the fugitive absolved of liability?

He replied:

If it is established that the fugitive killed him unintentionally—that one of them was ill and the other beat him severely, aggravating his illness and causing his death—then the blood money is payable by his liable kin. His agnatic relatives, whether paternal cousins or others, must therefore bear the sum accepted by the slain man’s family, since it is less than the blood money.

If, however, none of this is established, and the father was held liable solely on the basis of his own admission, his admission imposes no liability upon them. Those entitled to the blood money who agreed to settle for this sum have no right to demand more than it. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - قَدَّسَ اللَّهُ رُوحَهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ رَأَى رَجُلًا قَتَلَ ثَلَاثَةً مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ فِي شَهْرِ رَمَضَانَ وَلَحِسَ السَّيْفَ بِفَمِهِ.
 وَأَنَّ وَلِيَّ الْأَمْرِ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَيْهِ لِيُقِيمَ عَلَيْهِ الْحَدَّ وَأَنَّ الَّذِي رَآهُ قَدْ وَجَدَهُ فِي مَكَانٍ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَى مَسْكِهِ:
 فَهَلْ لَهُ أَنْ يَقْتُلَ الْقَاتِلَ الْمَذْكُورَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ؟ وَإِذَا قَتَلَهُ هَلْ يُؤْجَرُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ أَوْ يُطَالَبُ بِدَمِهِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إنْ كَانَ قَاطِعَ طَرِيقٍ قَتَلَهُمْ لِأَخْذِ أَمْوَالِهِمْ وَجَبَ قَتْلُهُ وَلَا يَجُوزُ الْعَفْوُ عَنْهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ قَتَلَهُمْ لِغَرَضِ خَاصٍّ مِثْلِ خُصُومَةٍ بَيْنَهُمْ أَوْ عَدَاوَةٍ:
 فَأَمْرُهُ إلَى وَرَثَةِ الْقَتِيلِ: إنْ أَحَبُّوا قَتْلَهُ قَتَلُوهُ وَإِنْ أَحَبُّوا عَفَوْا عَنْهُ وَإِنْ أَحَبُّوا أَخَذُوا الدِّيَةَ. فَلَا يَجُوزُ قَتْلُهُ إلَّا بِإِذْنِ الْوَرَثَةِ الْآخَرِينَ.
 وَأَمَّا إنْ كَانَ قَاطِعَ طَرِيقٍ:
 فَقِيلَ: بِإِذْنِ الْإِمَامِ؛
 فَمَنْ عَلِمَ أَنَّ الْإِمَامَ أَذِنَ فِي قَتْلِهِ بِدَلَائِلِ الْحَالِ جَازَ أَنْ يَقْتُلَهُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَذَلِكَ مِثْلُ أَنْ يَعْرِفَ أَنَّ وُلَاةَ الْأُمُورِ يَطْلُبُونَهُ لِيَقْتُلُوهُ وَأَنَّ قَتْلَهُ وَاجِبٌ فِي الشَّرْعِ:
 فَهَذَا يَعْرِفُ أَنَّهُمْ آذِنُونَ فِي قَتْلِهِ؛ وَإِذَا وَجَبَ قَتْلُهُ كَانَ قَاتِلُهُ مَأْجُورًا فِي ذَلِكَ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلَيْنِ قَبَضَ أَحَدُهُمَا عَلَى وَاحِدٍ وَالْآخَرُ ضَرَبَهُ فَشُلَّتْ يَدُهُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، هَذَا فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ. وَالْأَظْهَرُ أَنَّهُ يَجِبُ عَلَى الِاثْنَيْنِ الْقَوَدُ إنْ وَجَبَ وَإِلَّا فَالدِّيَةُ عَلَيْهِمَا. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

A man saw another man kill three Muslims during Ramadan and lick the sword. The ruler had been unable to apprehend him to carry out the prescribed punishment. The witness later encountered him somewhere but was unable to seize him. May he kill the aforementioned man, who committed these unlawful killings? If he kills him, will he be rewarded or held liable for his death?

He replied:

If he was a highway robber who killed them to take their property, he must be put to death and may not be pardoned. If, however, he killed them for a personal reason, such as a dispute or enmity between them, then his fate rests with the victim’s heirs: if they wish, they may put him to death; if they wish, they may pardon him; and if they wish, they may accept blood money. He may therefore only be killed with the permission of the other heirs.

As for a highway robber, one view requires the ruler’s permission. Whoever knows from the circumstances that the ruler has authorized his killing may kill him on that basis. For example, someone may know that the authorities are seeking him to put him to death and that his execution is obligatory under Islamic law. Such a person knows that they authorize his killing. When putting him to death is obligatory, whoever kills him is rewarded for doing so.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Two men were involved: one held a man while the other struck him, leaving his hand paralyzed. What is the ruling?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. There is disagreement on this matter. The stronger view is that both are subject to retaliation in kind if it is applicable; otherwise, both are liable for the blood money. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man found another man with his wife and killed her, then repented after her death. He had young children. When one of the two grew up, he wished to offer the expiation for killing. Unable to afford to free a slave, he wished to fast for two consecutive months.

Is expiation obligatory for the killer? Is it valid for his child to perform it on his behalf? If the child is female and menstruates during those two months, does that interrupt the required continuity? If she considers it most likely that her menstruation will end at a particular time, must she abstain from the things that invalidate fasting, or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If he found them committing the indecent act and killed her, he bears no liability before Allah according to the stronger of the two scholarly opinions. This is also the stronger of the two opinions in Ahmad’s school, even if he could have stopped the man from having intercourse with her by speaking to him. For it is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If a man were to peer into your house and you put out his eye, you would bear no liability.”

And:

“A man once peered into his house, and he began aiming a pointed comb at the man’s eye; had it struck him, it would have put out his eye.”

He also said:

“Seeking permission to enter was prescribed only to prevent people from looking in.”

Yet he could have stopped him by speaking to him. A man came to Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him

with a bloodstained sword in his hand. He had killed his wife, and her family came to complain against him. The man said:

“I found a scoundrel lying between her thighs, so I struck there with the sword.”

Umar took the sword, shook it, then handed it back to him and said, “If he does it again, do the same again.”

Some scholars hold that the killer is not subject to legal retaliation if the adulterer had consummated a valid marriage, whether the killer was the woman’s husband or someone else. This is the view of a group of scholars in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

The basis of the first view, however, is that the man violated the husband’s honour. It is therefore comparable to putting out the eye of someone peering into one’s home, or to the case of the man who pulled his hand from a biter’s mouth, causing the biter’s front teeth to fall out. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled that no compensation was due for the injury, saying:

“Should he leave his hand in your mouth for you to gnaw at it like a male camel?”

Acting upon the first hadith is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. Some scholars did not act upon it, arguing that an aggressor must be repelled by the least force necessary. But the explicit text takes precedence over this opinion.

This opinion has been disputed among both earlier and later scholars. A thief entered upon Abdullah ibn Umar, and he drew his sword against him. They said:

“Had we not stopped him, he would have struck him.”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal cited this action of Ibn Umar as evidence, together with the two hadiths mentioned earlier, and adopted that position.

If, however, the man had not yet committed an indecent act but had come for that purpose, the matter is disputed. The more cautious course for the killer in such circumstances is to repent of the killing. As for

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man struck another man with a sword, paralyzing his hand. He later came to him and gave him exactly four feddans of farmland as a settlement. The injured man enjoyed its yield for twelve years, but they never put anything in writing, and the injured man is in poor circumstances. Is the assailant liable for compensation?”

Answer

He replied:

“If he reached a settlement with him for the paralysis of his hand in return for something, then the agreed settlement is binding. The injured man may not demand more, nor may the assailant reduce it. If, however, he gave him something without reaching a settlement, the injured man may claim the remainder of his entitlement. Paralysis of a hand entails the compensation prescribed for the loss of a hand. Allah knows best.”

قَاتِلُ النَّفْسِ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ عَلَيْهِ 
" حَقَّانِ "
: حَقٌّ لِلَّهِ بِكَوْنِهِ تَعَدَّى حُدُودَ اللَّهِ وَانْتَهَكَ حُرُمَاتِهِ. فَهَذَا الذَّنْبُ يَغْفِرُهُ اللَّهُ بِالتَّوْبَةِ الصَّحِيحَةِ كَمَا قَالَ
translated_text:
He—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

“A man struck another man, displacing his jaw and knocking out his canine teeth. His jaw was then stitched with needles. What compensation is due?”

He replied:

“For each tooth, one-twentieth of the full blood money is due: fifty dinars, five camels, or six hundred dirhams. Assessed compensation is due for the displacement of the jaw. The injured person is valued as though he were an uninjured slave, then valued as though he were a slave with that injury. The difference between the two valuations is then determined, and the corresponding proportion of the full blood money is payable. If the blow was of a kind that ordinarily knocks out teeth, the injured person is entitled to retaliation, meaning that he may have the corresponding teeth removed from his assailant.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Concerning a Muslim who deliberately killed another Muslim without right, then subsequently repented: may it be hoped that his repentance will be accepted and that he will escape the Fire, or not? Must he pay blood money, or not?”

He replied:

“One who kills a person without right has ‘two claims’ against him: a claim belonging to Allah, because he has transgressed Allah’s limits and violated what He has made inviolable. Allah forgives this sin through sincere repentance, as He says,

the Most High:

“O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.”

That is, for those who repent. He also says:

“And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah, nor kill a soul whom Allah has forbidden to be killed except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse. Whoever does these things will face punishment. His punishment will be doubled on the Day of Resurrection, and he will remain in it forever, humiliated—except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds. For them, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.”

In the two Sahīh collections and elsewhere, Abū Sa‘īd reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“A man killed ninety-nine men, then asked who was the most learned person on earth and was directed to him. He asked him, ‘Is there any repentance for me?’ He replied, ‘Can there be repentance for you after ninety-nine killings?’ So he killed him, bringing the total to one hundred. He then remained as he was for as long as Allah willed, before asking who was the most learned person on earth. He was directed to him and asked, ‘Is there any repentance for me?’ He replied, ‘Who could stand between you and repentance? But go to such-and-such a village, for there are righteous people there, and worship Allah with them.’ Death overtook him on the way, and the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment disputed over him. Allah sent an angel to judge between them. He ordered that the distances be measured and that the man be assigned to whichever of the two villages he was nearer. They found him nearer to the righteous village, so Allah forgave him.”

“The second claim” belongs to other people. The killer must give the victim’s heirs their due by allowing them to exact retaliation, reaching a financial settlement with them, or asking them to pardon him. If he does so, he has discharged his obligation towards them. This is part of making his repentance complete.

original_text:
وَهَلْ يَبْقَى لِلْمَقْتُولِ عَلَيْهِ حَقٌّ يُطَالِبُهُ بِهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ؛ وَمَنْ قَالَ يَبْقَى لَهُ؛ فَإِنَّهُ يَسْتَكْثِرُ الْقَاتِلُ مِنْ الْحَسَنَاتِ حَتَّى يُعْطِيَ الْمَقْتُولَ مِنْ حَسَنَاتِهِ بِقَدْرِ حَقِّهِ وَيَبْقَى لَهُ مَا يَبْقَى فَإِذَا اسْتَكْثَرَ الْقَاتِلُ التَّائِبُ مِنْ الْحَسَنَاتِ رُجِيَتْ لَهُ رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ؛ وَأَنْجَاهُ مِنْ النَّارِ وَلَا يَقْنَطُ مِنْ رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ إلَّا الْقَوْمُ الْفَاسِقُونَ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلَيْنِ اخْتَلَفَا فِي قَتْلِ النَّفْسِ عَمْدًا.
 فَقَالَ أَحَدُهُمَا:
 إنَّ هَذَا ذَنْبٌ لَا يُغْفَرُ وَقَالَ الْآخَرُ: إذَا تَابَ تَابَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا حَقُّ الْمَظْلُومِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَسْقُطُ بِاسْتِغْفَارِ الظَّالِمِ الْقَاتِلِ؛ لَا فِي قَتْلِ النَّفْسِ؛ وَلَا فِي سَائِرِ مَظَالِمِ الْعِبَادِ؛ فَإِنَّ حَقَّ الْمَظْلُومِ لَا يَسْقُطُ بِمُجَرَّدِ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ؛ لَكِنْ تُقْبَلُ تَوْبَةُ الْقَاتِلِ وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الظُّلْمَةِ؛ فَيَغْفِرُ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِالتَّوْبَةِ الْحَقَّ الَّذِي لَهُ.
 وَأَمَّا حُقُوقُ الْمَظْلُومِينَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ يُوَفِّيهِمْ إيَّاهَا:
 إمَّا مِنْ حَسَنَاتِ الظَّالِمِ وَإِمَّا مِنْ عِنْدِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
Does the victim retain a claim against the killer that he may pursue on the Day of Resurrection? Scholars within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere hold two views on this. According to those who hold that he does, the killer should accumulate good deeds so that the victim may receive enough of them to satisfy his claim, leaving the killer whatever remains. If the repentant killer accumulates good deeds, there is hope that Allah will have mercy on him and save him from the Fire. None despair of Allah’s mercy except the defiantly disobedient.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about two men who disagreed concerning intentional killing. One said, “This is a sin that cannot be forgiven,” while the other said, “If he repents, Allah will accept his repentance.”

He replied:

The victim’s claim is not extinguished by the killer’s plea for forgiveness. This applies both to killing and to all other wrongs committed against people: the victim’s claim is not extinguished merely by asking Allah’s forgiveness. Nevertheless, the repentance of a killer, like that of other wrongdoers, is accepted, and through repentance Allah forgives the violation of His own right.

As for the rights of those who have been wronged, Allah will grant them their full due, either from the wrongdoer’s good deeds or from His own bounty. And Allah knows best.

 قَضَى نَحْوَ ذَلِكَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

Christians accused a man of killing some Christians, but nothing was proved against him. They brought him before the deputy governor in al-Karak and compelled him to punish the man. He was punished until he died, without confessing to anything. What liability, then, do the Christians who undertook responsibility for his death bear?

He replied:

They must pay compensation for the man for whose death they undertook responsibility, if he died under punishment. Indeed, they too are to be punished as he was, as Abū Dāwūd relates in al-Sunan from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, who issued a similar ruling. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Book of Prescribed Punishments

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

Allah addressed the believers in unrestricted terms concerning prescribed punishments and rights, as in His words:

“As for the male and female thief, cut off [their hands].”

And His words:

“Flog the woman and the man who commit unlawful sexual intercourse.”

And His words:

“Those who accuse chaste women and then fail to produce four witnesses—flog them.”

Likewise, His words:

“And never accept their testimony.”

However, it is known that anyone commanded to perform an action must be capable of it; those unable to perform it are not obliged to do so. It is also known that this is a collective obligation, like jihad; indeed, it is a form of jihad.

Thus, His words:

“Fighting has been prescribed for you.”

And His words:

“Fight in the cause of Allah.”

And His words:

“If you do not go forth, He will punish you.”

These and similar commands impose a collective obligation upon those capable of fulfilling it. Here, “capability” means authority. Hence, implementing the prescribed punishments is obligatory upon the ruler and his deputies.

The Sunnah is for the Muslims to have a single imam, with the others serving as his deputies. If, however, we suppose that the community has departed from this arrangement because of disobedience on the part of some and inability on the part of the rest, or for some other reason,
