translated_text:
so that it came to have several imams, each imam would be obliged to implement the prescribed punishments and secure the fulfillment of rights. Hence, the scholars have said that the judicial rulings of rebels are to be upheld to the same extent as those of just authorities. Likewise, if they shared authority and formed factions, each faction would be obliged to carry out these duties among those who obeyed it.

This applies when the rulers are divided and multiple. The same applies if they are not divided, but their obedience to the supreme ruler is incomplete. In that case too, even if he is relieved of the duty to compel them to fulfill these obligations, they are not relieved of fulfilling them; rather, they must carry them out. Likewise, if some rulers were unable to implement the prescribed punishments and uphold rights, or neglected to do so, that obligation would fall upon whoever was capable of fulfilling it.

The statement, “Only the ruler and his deputies may implement the prescribed punishments,” applies when they are capable and act justly. Similarly, when the jurists say, “The matter rests with the judge,” they mean a just and capable judge. If he neglects the property of orphans or is incapable of managing it, it is not obligatory to hand it over to him when it can be safeguarded without him. Likewise, if the ruler neglects the prescribed punishments or is incapable of implementing them, it is not obligatory to entrust them to him when they can be implemented without him.

The governing principle is that these obligations should be fulfilled in the best possible manner. Whenever one ruler can fulfill them, there is no need for two. Whenever they can only be fulfilled by several people and without a ruler, they are to be fulfilled, provided that doing so does not cause greater harm than neglecting them. For they fall under “enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.” If, however, doing so entails harm involving the rulers or their subjects that exceeds the harm of neglecting these duties, one harm must not be averted by a greater harm. And Allah knows best.

 . وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ مُزَوَّجَةٍ بِزَوْجِ كَامِلٍ وَلَهَا أَوْلَادٌ فَتَعَلَّقَتْ بِشَخْصِ مِنْ الْأَطْرَافِ أَقَامَتْ مَعَهُ عَلَى الْفُجُورِ؛
 فَلَمَّا ظَهَرَ أَمْرُهَا سَعَتْ فِي مُفَارَقَةِ الزَّوْجِ:
 فَهَلْ بَقِيَ لَهَا حَقٌّ عَلَى أَوْلَادِهَا بَعْدَ هَذَا الْفِعْلِ؟ وَهَلْ عَلَيْهِمْ إثْمٌ فِي قَطْعِهَا؟ وَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لِمَنْ تَحَقَّقَ ذَلِكَ مِنْهَا قَتْلُهَا سِرًّا؟ وَإِنْ فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ غَيْرُهُ يَأْثَمُ؟
translated_text:
Chapter on the Prescribed Punishment for Unlawful Sexual Intercourse

Shaykh al-Islam—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

What punishment is due for someone who has unlawful intercourse with his sister?

He replied:

As for someone who has unlawful intercourse with his sister, knowing that it is forbidden, he must be put to death. The evidence for this is the report narrated by al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib:

“My maternal uncle, Abū Burdah, passed by me carrying a banner. I asked, ‘Where are you going, Uncle?’ He replied, ‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has sent me to a man who married his father’s wife. He ordered me to strike off his head and take a fifth of his property.’”

And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A woman with a worthy husband and children became attached to a man from the outlying districts and lived with him in adultery. When her conduct became known, she sought to separate from her husband. Does she still have any rights over her children after this deed? Do they incur sin by severing ties with her? Is it permissible for someone who has ascertained that she did this to kill her in secret? If someone else does so, does he incur sin?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، الْوَاجِبُ عَلَى أَوْلَادِهَا وَعُصْبَتِهَا أَنْ يَمْنَعُوهَا مِنْ الْمُحَرَّمَاتِ فَإِنْ لَمْ تَمْتَنِعْ إلَّا بِالْحَبْسِ حَبَسُوهَا؛ وَإِنْ احْتَاجَتْ إلَى الْقَيْدِ قَيَّدُوهَا. وَمَا يَنْبَغِي لِلْوَلَدِ أَنْ يَضْرِبَ أُمَّهُ. وَأَمَّا بِرُّهَا فَلَيْسَ لَهُمْ أَنْ يَمْنَعُوهَا بِرَّهَا وَلَا يَجُوزَ لَهُمْ مُقَاطَعَتُهَا بِحَيْثُ تَتَمَكَّنُ بِذَلِكَ مِنْ السُّوءِ؛ بَلْ يَمْنَعُوهَا بِحَسَبِ قُدْرَتِهِمْ. وَإِنْ احْتَاجَتْ إلَى رِزْقٍ وَكِسْوَةٍ رَزَقُوهَا وَكَسَوْهَا وَلَا يَجُوزُ لَهُمْ إقَامَةُ الْحَدِّ عَلَيْهَا بِقَتْلِ وَلَا غَيْرِهِ وَعَلَيْهِمْ الْإِثْمُ فِي ذَلِكَ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ بَلَدٍ فِيهَا جَوَارٍ سَائِبَاتٍ يَزْنُونَ مَعَ النَّصَارَى وَالْمُسْلِمِينَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
عَلَى سَيِّدِ الْأَمَةِ إذَا زَنَتْ أَنْ يُقِيمَ عَلَيْهَا الْحَدَّ كَمَا فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{إذَا زَنَتْ أَمَةُ أَحَدِكُمْ فَلْيَجْلِدْهَا؛ ثُمَّ إنْ زَنَتْ فَلْيَجْلِدْهَا؛ ثُمَّ إنْ زَنَتْ فَلْيَجْلِدْهَا؛ ثُمَّ إنْ زَنَتْ فِي الرَّابِعَةِ فَلْيَبِعْهَا وَلَوْ بظفير}
 والظفير الْحَبْلُ. فَإِنْ لَمْ يَفْعَلْ مَا أَمَرَهُ بِهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ عَاصِيًا لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ. وَكَانَ إصْرَارُهُ عَلَى الْمَعْصِيَةِ قَادِحًا فِي عَدَالَتِهِ.
 فَأَمَّا إذَا كَانَ هُوَ يُرْسِلُهَا لِتَبْغِيَ وَتُنْفِقَ عَلَى نَفْسِهَا مِنْ مَهْرِ الْبِغَاءِ أَوْ يَأْخُذَ هُوَ شَيْئًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ:
 فَهَذَا مِمَّنْ لَعَنَهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ؛ وَهُوَ فَاسِقٌ خَبِيثٌ؛ أَذِنَ فِي الْكَبِيرَةِ وَأَخَذَ مَهْرَ الْبَغِيِّ؛ وَلَمْ يَنْهَهَا عَنْ الْفَاحِشَةِ. وَمِثْلُ هَذَا لَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَعْدِلًا؛ بَلْ لَا يَجُوزُ إقْرَارُهُ بَيْنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛ بَلْ يَسْتَحِقُّ الْعُقُوبَةَ
translated_text:
He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Her children and her male agnatic relatives must prevent her from committing forbidden acts. If she will desist only through confinement, they should confine her; if restraints are necessary, they should restrain her. A child should not strike his mother. They must not, however, withhold the dutiful kindness they owe her. Nor may they sever ties with her in a way that enables her to commit wrongdoing; rather, they must prevent her wrongdoing as far as they are able. If she needs food and clothing, they must provide them for her. They may not carry out the prescribed punishment against her, whether by killing her or otherwise; doing so would be sinful on their part.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

What about a town where slave women are left unrestrained and engage in unlawful intercourse with Christians and Muslims?

He replied:

If a slave woman commits unlawful intercourse, her master must carry out the prescribed punishment against her, as related in the two Sahīh collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If the slave woman of any one of you commits unlawful intercourse, let him flog her. If she does so again, let him flog her. If she does so again, let him flog her. Then, if she does so a fourth time, let him sell her, even for a rope.”

The word zafīr means a rope. If he does not do what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded him to do, he is disobedient to Allah and His Messenger. His persistence in that disobedience impairs his uprightness.

If, however, he sends her out to engage in prostitution and support herself from its proceeds, or takes any of those proceeds himself, then he is among those whom Allah and His Messenger have cursed. He is a vile evildoer: he has permitted a major sin, taken the earnings of a prostitute, and failed to forbid her indecency. Such a person may not serve as an assessor of others’ uprightness. Rather, he must not be allowed to remain among the Muslims; indeed, he deserves punishment

فَأَجَابَ:

عَمَّنْ وَجَبَ عَلَيْهِ حَدُّ الزِّنَا فَتَابَ قَبْلَ أَنْ يُحَدَّ:

translated_text:
of a severe kind until he safeguards his slave women. The least punishment is that he be shunned: he should not be greeted, prayer should not be offered behind him when another prayer leader is available, he should not be called upon as a witness, and he should not be entrusted with any position of authority whatsoever. Whoever regards this as lawful is an unbeliever and an apostate. He must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he is to be executed as an apostate, and his Muslim heirs do not inherit from him. If he is unaware that it is forbidden, he must be informed until the proof has been established against him, for this is among the matters unanimously agreed to be forbidden.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man swore to his son that, if the son committed a wrongful act, he would carry out the prescribed punishment against him. The son confessed to his father, who gave him one hundred lashes, leaving a year’s banishment outstanding. May an expiation be offered in place of the year’s banishment?

He replied:

If he carries out the banishment by confining him, even in the father’s house, he has fulfilled his oath, even if the son is left free and unshackled within a designated place. Neither shackling him nor placing him somewhere dark is required. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

If someone becomes liable to the prescribed punishment for unlawful intercourse but repents before it is carried out, does his repentance absolve him of that punishment?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:

الْجَوَابُ
فَأَجَابَ:
 إذَا تَابَ تَوْبَةً صَحِيحَةً تَابَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ حَاجَةٍ إلَى أَنْ يُقِرَّ بِذَنْبِهِ حَتَّى يُقَامَ عَلَيْهِ الْحَدُّ وَفِي الْحَدِيثِ:

 وَفِي الْأَثَرِ أَيْضًا: 
{مَنْ أَذْنَبَ سِرًّا فَلْيَتُبْ سِرًّا وَمَنْ أَذْنَبَ عَلَانِيَةً فَلْيَتُبْ عَلَانِيَةً}

{وَالَّذِينَ إذَا فَعَلُوا فَاحِشَةً أَوْ ظَلَمُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ ذَكَرُوا اللَّهَ فَاسْتَغْفَرُوا لِذُنُوبِهِمْ}
 الْآيَةُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ إثْمِ الْمَعْصِيَةِ وَحَدِّ الزِّنَا:
 هَلْ تُزَادُ فِي الْأَيَّامِ الْمُبَارَكَةِ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ، الْمَعَاصِي فِي الْأَيَّامِ الْمُفَضَّلَةِ وَالْأَمْكِنَةِ الْمُفَضَّلَةِ تُغَلَّظُ وَعِقَابُهَا بِقَدْرِ فَضِيلَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَالْمَكَانِ.
translated_text:
He replied:

If he repents of unlawful intercourse, theft, or drinking wine before his case is brought before the ruler, the correct view is that the prescribed punishment is waived, just as it is waived, by unanimous agreement, for brigands who repent before they are apprehended.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man committed a sin carrying a prescribed punishment, such as flogging or stoning, then repented of that sin, ceased committing it, sought forgiveness, and resolved never to return to it. Is that sufficient, or must he go to the ruler and disclose his sin so that the prescribed punishment may be carried out against him? Is it better for him to conceal his sin and repent?

The Answer

He replied:

If he sincerely repents, Allah will accept his repentance without any need for him to confess his sin so that the prescribed punishment may be carried out against him. It is stated in the hadith:

“Whoever falls into any of these filthy deeds should keep it concealed as Allah has concealed it. For whoever discloses his offence to us, we shall enforce against him the punishment prescribed in Allah’s Book.”

It is also stated in a report:

“Whoever sins in secret should repent in secret, and whoever sins openly should repent openly.”

Allah Most High says:

“And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins”—to the end of the verse.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Are the guilt incurred by sin and the prescribed punishment for unlawful intercourse increased on blessed days?

He replied:

Yes. Sins committed at specially favoured times and in specially favoured places are graver, and their punishment is more severe in proportion to the distinction of the time and place.

نَعَمْ،
 لِوَلِيِّ الْأَمْرِ كَصَاحِبِ الشُّرْطَةِ أَنْ يَصْرِفَ ضَرَرَهَا بِمَا يَرَاهُ مَصْلَحَةً:
 إمَّا بِحَبْسِهَا وَإِمَّا بِنَقْلِهَا عَنْ الْحَرَائِرِ؛ وَإِمَّا بِغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يَرَى فِيهِ الْمَصْلَحَةَ وَقَدْ كَانَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ يَأْمُرُ الْعُزَّابَ أَنْ لَا تَسْكُنَ بَيْنَ الْمُتَأَهِّلِينَ وَأَنْ لَا يَسْكُنَ الْمُتَأَهِّلُ بَيْنَ الْعُزَّابِ؛ وَهَكَذَا فَعَلَ الْمُهَاجِرُونَ لَمَّا قَدِمُوا الْمَدِينَةَ عَلَى عَهْدِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَنَفَوْا شَابًّا خَافُوا الْفِتْنَةَ بِهِ مِنْ الْمَدِينَةِ إلَى الْبَصْرَةِ وَثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ. 
{أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ نَفَى الْمُخَنَّثِينَ وأَمَرَ بِنَفْيِهِمْ مِنْ الْبُيُوتِ خَشْيَةَ أَنْ يُفْسِدُوا النِّسَاءَ}
 . فَالْقَوَّادَةُ شَرٌّ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ وَاَللَّهُ يُعَذِّبُهَا مَعَ أَصْحَابِهَا.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ 
" الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ "
 بَعْدَ إدْرَاكِهِمَا مَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِمَا؟ وَمَا يُطَهِّرُهُمَا؟ وَمَا يَنْوِيَانِ عِنْدَ الطَّهَارَةِ؟
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A woman acts as a procuress, bringing men and women together. She has been beaten and imprisoned, but has resumed her activities, and her neighbours have suffered harm because of her. May the ruler remove her from their midst?

He replied:

Yes. A person in authority, such as the chief of police, may prevent the harm she causes by whatever means he considers conducive to the public interest: by imprisoning her, relocating her away from free women, or taking other measures he considers beneficial. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb used to order unmarried men not to live among married people, and married men not to live among unmarried men. The Emigrants likewise did this when they came to Medina during the lifetime of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. They also banished a young man from Medina to Basra, fearing that he would become a source of temptation. It is established in the two Sahīh collections:

“The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, banished effeminate men and ordered their expulsion from homes, lest they corrupt the women.”

A procuress is worse than these men, and Allah will punish her along with her associates.

He was asked:

Regarding “the active and passive partners” in sodomy, once both have reached maturity: What is required of them? What purifies them? And what intention should they form when purifying themselves?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا الْفَاعِلُ وَالْمَفْعُولُ بِهِ فَيَجِبُ قَتْلُهُمَا رَجْمًا بِالْحِجَارَةِ سَوَاءٌ كَانَا مُحْصَنَيْنِ أَوْ غَيْرَ مُحْصَنَيْنِ؛
 لِمَا فِي السُّنَنِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{مَنْ وَجَدْتُمُوهُ يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ قَوْمِ لُوطٍ فَاقْتُلُوا الْفَاعِلَ وَالْمَفْعُولَ بِهِ}
 وَلِأَنَّ أَصْحَابَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ اتَّفَقُوا عَلَى قَتْلِهِمَا. وَعَلَيْهِمَا الِاغْتِسَالُ مِنْ الْجَنَابَةِ وَتَرْتَفِعُ الْجَنَابَةُ مِنْ الِاغْتِسَالِ؛
 لَكِنْ لَا يَطْهُرَانِ مِنْ نَجَاسَةِ الذَّنْبِ إلَّا بِالتَّوْبَةِ وَهَذَا مَعْنَى مَا رُوِيَ:
 
{أَنَّهُمَا لَوْ اغْتَسَلَا بِالْمَاءِ يَنْوِيَانِ رَفْعَ الْجَنَابَةِ وَاسْتِبَاحَةِ الصَّلَاةِ. . .}
 .
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ قَوْلِهِ فِي 
" التَّهْذِيبِ "
: مَنْ أَتَى بَهِيمَةً فَاقْتُلُوا الْمَفْعُولَ وَاقْتُلُوا الْفَاعِلَ بِهَا: فَهَلْ يَجِبُ ذَلِكَ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، هَذَا فِيهِ حَدِيثٌ رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُد فِي السُّنَنِ؛
 وَهُوَ قَوْلُهُ:
 
{مَنْ أَتَى بَهِيمَةً فَاقْتُلُوهُ وَاقْتُلُوهَا}
 وَهُوَ أَحَدُ قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ؛ كَأَحَدِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَمَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ.
translated_text:
He replied:

Both the active and passive partners must be put to death by stoning, whether or not they have consummated a lawful marriage. This is because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, as reported in the Sunan collections:

“Whoever you find committing the act of the people of Lot, kill both the active and passive partners.”

The Companions of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also agreed that both should be put to death. Both must perform a ritual bath to remove major ritual impurity, which is removed by bathing. However, they are not cleansed of the defilement of sin except through repentance. This is the meaning of the report:

“If they were to bathe with water, intending to remove major ritual impurity and make prayer permissible for themselves…”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Regarding the statement in al-Tahdhīb, “Whoever has intercourse with an animal, kill the animal subjected to the act and kill the person who commits it”: Is this obligatory or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. There is a hadith concerning this, narrated by Abū Dāwūd in his Sunan, in which the Prophet said:

“Whoever has intercourse with an animal, kill him and kill the animal.”

This is one of the two scholarly opinions, including one of the two positions in the schools of Ahmad and al-Shāfi'ī.

original_text:
بَابُ حَدِّ الْقَذْفِ
وَسُئِلَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَمَّنْ قَذَفَ رَجُلًا لِأَنَّهُ يَنْظُرُ إلَى حَرِيمِ النَّاسِ وَهُوَ كَذِبٌ عَلَيْهِ:
 فَمَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْقَاذِفِ؟ .
الْجَوَابُ:
إذَا كَانَ الْأَمْرُ عَلَى مَا ذُكِرَ فَإِنَّهُ يُعَزَّرُ عَلَى افْتِرَائِهِ عَلَى هَذَا الشَّخْصِ بِمَا يَزْجُرُهُ وَأَمْثَالَهُ إذَا طَلَبَ الْمَقْذُوفُ ذَلِكَ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ تَزَوَّجَ امْرَأَةً مِنْ أَهْلِ الْخَيْرِ وَلَهُ مُطَلَّقَةٌ وَشَرَطَ إنْ رَدَّ مُطَلَّقَتَهُ كَانَ الصَّدَاقُ حَالًّا ثُمَّ إنَّهُ رَدَّ الْمُطَلَّقَةَ وَقَذَفَ هُوَ وَمُطَلَّقَتُهُ عِرْضَ الزَّوْجَةِ وَرَمَوْهَا بِالزِّنَا؟
 بِإِنَّهَا كَانَتْ حَامِلًا مِنْ الزِّنَا وَطَلَّقَهَا بَعْدَ دُخُولِهِ بِهَا:
 فَمَا الَّذِي يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِمَا؟ وَهَلْ يُقْبَلُ قَوْلُهَا؟ وَهَلْ يَسْقُطُ الصَّدَاقُ أَمْ لَا؟
translated_text:
Chapter on the Prescribed Punishment for Accusations of Unlawful Sexual Intercourse

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man slandered another by falsely claiming that he looks at the women of other households. What punishment is due to the slanderer?

He replied:

If the matter is as described, he is to receive a discretionary punishment for his false accusation against this person, sufficient to deter him and others like him, if the person slandered requests it.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was also asked:

A man married a virtuous woman, having previously divorced another wife. He stipulated that if he took his divorced wife back, the dowry would become payable immediately. He then took her back, and he and his formerly divorced wife slandered the other wife’s honour, accusing her of fornication and alleging that she had been pregnant as a result of it. He divorced her after consummating the marriage. What punishment is due to the two of them? Is her word to be accepted? Does the dowry cease to be owed or not?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، أَمَّا مُطَلَّقَتُهُ فَتُحَدُّ عَلَى قَذْفِهَا ثَمَانِينَ جَلْدَةً إذَا طَلَبَتْ ذَلِكَ الْمَرْأَةُ الْمَقْذُوفَةُ وَلَا تُقْبَلُ لَهَا شَهَادَةٌ أَبَدًا لِأَنَّهَا فَاسِقَةٌ. وَكَذَلِكَ الرَّجُلُ عَلَيْهِ ثَمَانُونَ جَلْدَةً إذَا طَلَبَتْ الْمَرْأَةُ ذَلِكَ وَلَا تُقْبَلُ لَهُ شَهَادَةٌ أَبَدًا وَهُوَ فَاسِقٌ إذَا لَمْ يَتُبْ. وَهَلْ لَهُ إسْقَاطُ الْحَدِّ بِاللِّعَانِ؟ فِيهِ لِلْفُقَهَاءِ 
" ثَلَاثَةُ أَقْوَالٍ "
 فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ.
 قِيلَ:
 يُلَاعِنُ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 لَا يُلَاعِنُ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 إنْ كَانَ ثَمَّ وَلَدٌ يُرِيدُ نَفْيَهُ لَاعَنَ؛ وَإِلَّا فَلَا. وَصَدَاقُهَا بَاقٍ عَلَيْهِ لَا يَسْقُطُ بِاللِّعَانِ كَمَا سَنَّ ذَلِكَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَهَذَا كُلُّهُ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ؛ إلَّا مَا ذَكَرْنَاهُ مِنْ جَوَازِ اللِّعَانِ فَفِيهِ الْأَقْوَالُ الثَّلَاثَةُ 
" أَحَدُهَا "
 لَا يُلَاعِنُ؛ بَلْ يُحَدُّ حَدَّ الْقَذْفِ وَتَسْقُطُ شَهَادَتُهُ وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ أَحْمَد فِي أَشْهَرِ الرِّوَايَاتِ عَنْهُ وَأَحَدُ الْوَجْهَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ. و 
" الثَّانِي "
 يُلَاعِنُ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَأَحْمَد فِي رِوَايَةٍ عَنْهُ. و 
" الثَّالِثُ "
 إنْ كَانَ هُنَاكَ حَمْلٌ لَاعَنَ؛ لِنَفْيِهِ؛ وَإِلَّا فَلَا. وَهُوَ أَحَدُ الْوَجْهَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَرِوَايَةٌ عَنْ أَحْمَد. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَالَ لِرَجُلِ:
 أَنْتَ فَاسِقٌ شَارِبُ الْخَمْرِ وَمَنَعَهُ مِنْ أُجْرَةِ مِلْكِهِ الَّذِي يَمْلِكُ انْتِفَاعَهُ شَرْعًا؟
translated_text:
He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. As for the wife he had divorced, she is to receive the prescribed punishment of eighty lashes for her accusation, if the woman she accused requests it. Her testimony is never to be accepted, because she is a sinner. Likewise, the man is to receive eighty lashes if the woman requests it. His testimony is never to be accepted, and he remains a sinner unless he repents.

Can he avert the prescribed punishment through liʿān (mutual oaths of imprecation)? Jurists hold three opinions on this within the school of Ahmad and other schools. One opinion permits him to undertake liʿān; another does not. A third permits it if there is a child whose paternity he wishes to deny; otherwise, it does not.

Her dowry remains owed by him and is not forfeited through liʿān, as established by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The imams agree on all of this, except for the permissibility of liʿān mentioned above, concerning which there are three opinions:

The first: He may not undertake liʿān. Rather, he receives the prescribed punishment for accusing someone of unlawful sexual intercourse, and his testimony is no longer accepted. This is Ahmad’s position according to the best-known reports from him, and one of the two positions within the school of al-Shāfiʿī.

The second: He may undertake liʿān. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and of Ahmad according to one report from him.

The third: If there is a pregnancy, he may undertake liʿān to deny paternity of the unborn child; otherwise, he may not. This is one of the two positions within the school of al-Shāfiʿī and one report from Ahmad. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

About a man who said to another, “You are a sinner and a wine-drinker,” and withheld from him the rental income from property whose use he lawfully owns?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا كَانَ الْمَقْذُوفُ مُحْصَنًا وَجَبَ عَلَى الْقَاذِفِ حَدُّ الْقَذْفِ إذَا طَلَبَهُ الْمَقْذُوفُ وَأَمَّا شَتْمُهُ بِغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ إذَا كَانَ كَاذِبًا فَعَلَيْهِ أَنْ يُعَزَّرَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ. وَأَمَّا ضَرْبُهُ وَحَبْسُهُ إذَا كَانَ ظَالِمًا؛ فَإِنَّهُ يُفْعَلُ بِهِ كَمَا فَعَلَ وَمَا عَطَّلَهُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ الْمَنْفَعَةِ ضَمِنَهُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَذَفَ رَجُلًا وَقَالَ لَهُ:
 أَنْتَ عِلْقٌ وَلَدُ زِنَا: فَمَا الَّذِي يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا قَذَفَهُ بِالزِّنَا أَوْ اللِّوَاطِ كَقَوْلِهِ:
 أَنْتَ عِلْقٌ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلُ حُرًّا مُسْلِمًا لَمْ يُشْتَهَرْ عَنْهُ ذَلِكَ فَعَلَيْهِ حَدُّ الْقَذْفِ إذَا طَلَبَهُ الْمَقْذُوفُ وَهُوَ ثَمَانُونَ جَلْدَةً إنْ كَانَ الْقَاذِفُ حُرًّا؛ وَأَرْبَعُونَ إنْ كَانَ رَقِيقًا. عِنْدَ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ.
translated_text:
He replied:

If the person accused is chaste, the accuser must receive the prescribed punishment for accusing someone of unlawful sexual intercourse, if the accused requests it. As for other insults, if they are false, the offender must receive a discretionary punishment. If he wrongfully beats or imprisons him, he is to be treated as he treated the other man, and must compensate him for any benefit of which he deprived him.

He was asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

About a man who accused another man, saying, “You are a sodomite, an illegitimate child”: what punishment must he receive?

He replied:

If he accuses him of unlawful sexual intercourse or sodomy—for example, by saying, “You are a sodomite”—and the man accused is a free Muslim who is not known for such conduct, the accuser must receive the prescribed punishment for such an accusation if the accused requests it. This is eighty lashes if the accuser is free, and forty if he is enslaved, according to the four imams.

original_text:
بَابُ حَدِّ الْمُسْكِرِ
قَالَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -:
أَمَّا 
" الْأَشْرِبَةُ الْمُسْكِرَةُ "

Chapter: The Prescribed Punishment for Consuming Intoxicants

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

As for “intoxicating drinks,” the position of the majority of Muslim scholars—the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the other scholars—is that every intoxicant is khamr (wine), all khamr is forbidden, and whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden even in small quantities.

This is the position of Mālik and his followers, al-Shāfi'ī and his followers, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal and his followers. It is also one of the two positions within the school of Abū Hanīfah, and the position preferred by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, Abū Hanīfah’s disciple, and a number of the school’s leading scholars, such as Abū al-Layth al-Samarqandī and others.

This is also the position of al-Awzā'ī and his followers, al-Layth ibn Sa'd and his followers, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh and his followers, Dāwūd ibn 'Alī and his followers, Abū Thawr and his followers, Ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī and his followers, and other Muslim scholars and imams of the religion.

A group of scholars from Kufa, such as al-Nakha'ī, al-Sha'bī, Abū Hanīfah, Sharīk, and others, held that, in the case of intoxicating drinks derived from sources other than the two trees—the date palm and the grapevine—such as drinks made from wheat, barley, sorghum, honey, mares’ milk, and the like, the prohibition applies only to

Those who hold the “second position” maintain that only what is made from grapes is called khamr. They also say that when drinks made from dates or raisins are uncooked and intoxicating, both small and large quantities are forbidden, though they are not called khamr. If cooked even slightly, however, they become permissible. As for grape juice, if it is cooked while intoxicating, it does not become permissible unless two-thirds of it evaporates and one-third remains. Once it has become khamr, however, it remains impermissible even if cooked, provided it is still intoxicating; there is no disagreement on this.

The “first position,” held by the majority of Muslim scholars, is the correct one, supported by the Quran, the Sunnah, and sound reasoning. Allah Most High says in His Book:

“Intoxicants, gambling, sacrificial altars, and divining arrows are nothing but defilement from Satan’s handiwork, so avoid them that you may succeed.”

“Satan only seeks to sow enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Will you not then desist?”

In the language of the Arabs addressed by the Quran, the term “khamr” encompassed intoxicating drinks made from dates and other ingredients; it was not restricted to intoxicating drinks made from grapes. Al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh that Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:

“The prohibition of khamr was revealed when there were five kinds of drink in Medina, none of which was made from grapes.”

In the two Sahīhs, Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“When khamr was prohibited, it was made from unripe and dried dates.”

In a wording recorded by Muslim:

“Allah revealed this verse prohibiting khamr when there was no drink in Medina except that made from dried and unripe dates.”

In a wording recorded by al-Bukhārī:

“When it was prohibited for us, we could find very little grape khamr; most of our khamr was made from unripe and dried dates.”

In the two Sahīhs, Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“I was serving Abū ʿUbaydah and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb a drink made from crushed ripening dates and dried dates. Someone came and told them, ‘Khamr has been prohibited.’ Abū Talhah said, ‘Anas, go to these jars and pour out their contents.’ So I poured them out.”

Ibn ʿUmar narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden even in small quantities.”

This was narrated by Ibn Mājah and al-Dāraqutnī, who graded it authentic. The compilers of the Sunan narrated similar reports from Jābir and from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather. There are many authentic hadiths on this subject.

However, the scholars who held a contrary view were excused because these hadiths had not reached them. They had heard that some Companions drank nabīdh (a fruit infusion), and reports to that effect had reached them. They therefore assumed that what those Companions drank was intoxicating. Yet what the Companions actually disagreed about was what had been steeped in rigid vessels. For:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade making nabīdh in gourds, in earthenware vessels made from clay, in hollowed-out wooden vessels, and in vessels coated with pitch. He instructed them to make nabīdh in vessels whose mouths were tied shut.”

This means soaking dates or raisins in water until it becomes sweet, then drinking it while it is still sweet, before it becomes strong. This is lawful by the agreement of the Muslims. He forbade them to prepare this lawful nabīdh in those vessels because the drink gradually becomes stronger, so a Muslim might drink it without realizing that it had become intoxicating and would thus have drunk something forbidden. He instructed them to prepare nabīdh in vessels whose mouths they tied shut, because if the drink became strong, the vessel would split, preventing them from drinking an intoxicant.

There are many widely transmitted hadiths prohibiting “nabīdh prepared in sturdy vessels.” Subsequently, however, he was reported to have permitted this, as recorded in Sahīh Muslim, where Buraydah ibn al-Husayb reported the words of

the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I had forbidden you to prepare drinks in anything other than leather vessels. Now drink from any vessel, but do not drink anything intoxicating.”

In another narration:

“I had forbidden you to use certain vessels, but a vessel neither makes anything lawful nor makes it unlawful. Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Some of the Companions and Successors did not consider the abrogation established, so they followed the earlier hadiths. Others considered the abrogation authentic and therefore permitted preparing nabīdh in any vessel. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī. Mālik held that certain vessels remained prohibited, while two positions are reported from Ahmad.

When a group of scholars in Kufa heard that some of the early generations had drunk nabīdh, they assumed that they had drunk something intoxicating. A group of them—including al-Shāfiʿī, al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Hanīfah, Sharīk, Ibn Abī Laylā, and others—therefore held that this was lawful, as explained above. In this, they exercised independent legal judgment, seeking the truth. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a judge exercises independent judgment and reaches the correct decision, he receives two rewards. When he exercises independent judgment and errs, he receives one reward.”

The remaining scholars, however, followed those authentic hadiths. This is the position reliably established from the Companions, and clear analogical reasoning also supports it. For Allah Most High said:

“Satan seeks only to stir up enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Will you not then desist?”

The harm for which Allah, glorified and exalted is He, prohibited wine is that it turns people away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, and causes enmity and hatred. This is common to all intoxicants; in this respect, there is no difference between one intoxicant and another.

translated_text:
And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, prohibited small quantities because they lead to larger quantities. This applies to all intoxicants.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked about “wine and gambling”: “Is there great sin in them, as well as benefits for people? What are those benefits?”

He replied:

This was the first verse revealed concerning wine. They asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about it, so Allah revealed this verse without prohibiting it. He informed them that it contained “sin,” namely, the neglect of what is commanded and the commission of what is forbidden that result from drinking it. It also contained “benefit,” namely, the pleasure and bodily benefit it provides, and trade in it. Some people therefore refrained from drinking it, while others drank it.

Later, some people drank wine and then stood to pray while intoxicated, making mistakes in their recitation. Allah Most High then revealed:

“O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying.”

He thus forbade them to drink it near the time of prayer, and some of them gave it up.

After that, Allah Most High revealed:

“Wine, gambling, sacrificial altars, and divining arrows are an abomination of Satan’s work, so shun them so that you may prosper.”

Thus Allah established its prohibition in this verse in several ways. They said, “We have desisted! We have desisted!” The command of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to pour it away was then carried out, and the jars and vessels were broken. He cursed those who pressed it, those who had it pressed, those who drank it, and those who consumed its proceeds.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was also asked:

“Is it permissible to drink a small quantity of something other than grape wine that intoxicates in large quantities, such as sarmā’, qumaz, and mizr? Or is only the final cup forbidden?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that Abū Mūsā said:

“I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling concerning two drinks we used to make in Yemen: bit‘, which is honey steeped until it becomes strong, and mizr, which is made from sorghum steeped until it becomes strong.’” He said, “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had been granted the ability to express comprehensive meanings in few words. He replied, ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

‘Ā’ishah said:

“I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about bit‘, a drink made by steeping honey, which the people of Yemen used to drink. He replied, ‘Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.’”

In Sahīh Muslim, Jābir reported:

“A man from Yemen asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and grant him peace, about a drink made from sorghum that they drank in their land, called mizr. He asked, ‘Does it intoxicate?’

“The man replied, ‘Yes.’

“He said, ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden. Allah has pledged that whoever drinks an intoxicant, He will give him tīnat al-khabāl to drink.’

“They asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what is tīnat al-khabāl?’

“He replied, ‘The sweat of the inhabitants of the Fire—or the fluid that oozes from the inhabitants of the Fire.’”

فَفِي هَذِهِ الْأَحَادِيثِ الصَّحِيحَةِ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ سُئِلَ عَنْ أَشْرِبَةٍ مِنْ غَيْرِ الْعِنَبِ كَالْمِزْرِ وَغَيْرِهِ فَأَجَابَهُمْ بِكَلِمَةِ جَامِعَةٍ وَقَاعِدَةٍ عَامَّةٍ:
 
{إنَّ كُلَّ مُسْكِرٍ حَرَامٌ}
 وَهَذَا يُبَيِّنُ أَنَّهُ أَرَادَ كُلَّ شَرَابٍ كَانَ جِنْسُهُ مُسْكِرًا حَرَامٌ سَوَاءٌ سَكِرَ مِنْهُ أَوْ لَمْ يَسْكَرْ كَمَا فِي خَمْرِ الْعِنَبِ. وَلَوْ أَرَادَ بِالْمُسْكِرِ الْقَدَحَ الْأَخِيرَ فَقَطْ لَمْ يَكُنْ الشَّرَابُ كُلُّهُ حَرَامًا؛ وَلَكَانَ بَيَّنَ لَهُمْ؛ فَيَقُولُ اشْرَبُوا مِنْهُ وَلَا تَسْكَرُوا. وَلِأَنَّهُ 
{سَأَلَهُمْ عَنْ الْمِزْرِ أَمُسْكِرٌ هُوَ؟
 فَقَالُوا:
 نَعَمْ. فَقَالَ. كُلُّ مُسْكِرٍ حَرَامٌ}
 . فَلَمَّا سَأَلَهُمْ 
" أَمُسْكِرٌ هُوَ؟ "
 إنَّمَا أَرَادَ يُسْكِرُ كَثِيرُهُ كَمَا يُقَالُ. الْخُبْزُ يُشْبِعُ؛ وَالْمَاءُ يَرْوِي وَإِنَّمَا يَحْصُلُ الرَّيُّ وَالشِّبَعُ بِالْكَثِيرِ مِنْهُ لَا بِالْقَلِيلِ.
 كَذَلِكَ الْمُسْكِرُ إنَّمَا يَحْصُلُ السُّكْرُ بِالْكَثِيرِ مِنْهُ فَلَمَّا قَالُوا لَهُ:
 هُوَ مُسْكِرٌ.
 قَالَ:
 
{كُلُّ مُسْكِرٍ حَرَامٌ}
 فَبَيَّنَ أَنَّهُ أَرَادَ بِالْمُسْكِرِ كَمَا يُرَادُ بِالْمُشْبِعِ وَالْمُرْوِي وَنَحْوِهِمَا وَلَمْ يُرِدْ آخِرَ قَدَحٍ؛
 وَفِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عُمَرَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:
 
{كُلُّ مُسْكِرٍ خَمْرٌ؛ وَكُلُّ خَمْرٍ حَرَامٌ}
 وَفِي لَفْظٍ: 
{كُلُّ مُسْكِرٍ حَرَامٌ}
 وَمَنْ تَأَوَّلَهُ عَلَى الْقَدَحِ الْأَخِيرِ لَا يَقُولُ: إنَّهُ خَمْرٌ وَالنَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ جَعَلَ كُلَّ مُسْكِرٍ حَرَامًا. وَفِي السُّنَنِ عَنْ النُّعْمَانِ بْنِ بَشِيرٍ. قَالَ قَالَ رَسُول اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إنَّ مِنْ الْحِنْطَةِ خَمْرًا وَمِنْ الشَّعِيرِ خَمْرًا وَمِنْ الزَّبِيبِ خَمْرًا وَمِنْ الْعَسَلِ خَمْرًا}
 وَفِي الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الْخَطَّابِ قَالَ عَلَى مِنْبَرِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ:
translated_text:
These authentic hadiths show that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about drinks made from things other than grapes, such as mizr, and answered with a comprehensive statement and a general rule:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

This makes clear that he meant that every drink of an intoxicating kind is forbidden, whether or not a person becomes intoxicated from drinking it, just as with grape wine. Had he meant by “intoxicant” only the final cup, the drink as a whole would not have been forbidden. He would have explained this to them, saying, “Drink it, but do not become intoxicated.” Moreover:

“He asked them about mizr, ‘Does it intoxicate?’ They replied, ‘Yes.’ He said, ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

When he asked them, “Does it intoxicate?”, he meant whether a large quantity of it causes intoxication. This is like saying, “Bread satisfies hunger” and “Water quenches thirst,” although satisfaction and the quenching of thirst are achieved by consuming a substantial quantity, not a small amount. Likewise, intoxication results from consuming a large quantity of an intoxicant. When they told him that it intoxicates, he said:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

He thus made clear that he used “intoxicating” in the same way that “satisfying” and “thirst-quenching” and similar descriptions are used; he did not mean the final cup.

In Sahīh Muslim, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is khamr (wine), and all khamr is forbidden.”

Another wording reads:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Those who interpret this as referring to the final cup do not call it khamr, whereas the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declared every intoxicant forbidden.

In the Sunan collections, al-Nu‘mān ibn Bashīr reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Khamr is made from wheat, khamr is made from barley, khamr is made from raisins, and khamr is made from honey.”

It is also reported in the Sahīh collection that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said from the pulpit of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

 فَظَنُّوا أَنَّهُ السُّكْرُ؛ وَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ؛ بَلْ النَّبِيذُ الَّذِي شَرِبَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَالصَّحَابَةُ هُوَ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَنْبِذُونَ التَّمْرَ أَوْ الزَّبِيبَ أَوْ نَحْوَ ذَلِكَ فِي الْمَاءِ حَتَّى يَحْلُوَ فَيَشْرَبُهُ أَوَّلَ يَوْمٍ وَثَانِيَ يَوْمٍ؛ وَثَالِثَ يَوْمٍ؛ وَلَا يَشْرَبُهُ بَعْدَ ثَلَاثٍ؛ لِئَلَّا تَكُونَ الشِّدَّةُ قَدْ بَدَتْ فِيهِ؛ وَإِذَا اشْتَدَّ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يُشْرَبْ. وَقَدْ
translated_text:
“To proceed, O people: the prohibition of khamr was revealed when it was made from five things: grapes, dates, honey, wheat and barley. Khamr is whatever clouds the mind.”

There are many hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on this subject. They make clear that the khamr he prohibited is a term encompassing every intoxicant, whether made from honey, dates, wheat, barley, mares’ milk or anything else.

In the Sunan collections, ‘Ā’ishah reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden. If a faraq-measure of something intoxicates, even a palmful of it is forbidden.”

Al-Tirmidhī graded this hadith sound. The compilers of the Sunan collections also reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden in small quantities.”

This was transmitted through reports from Jābir, Ibn ‘Umar, ‘Amr ibn Shu‘ayb—from his father, from his grandfather—and others. Al-Dāraqutnī and others graded it authentic.

This is the position of the overwhelming majority of leading Muslim scholars: the Companions, the Successors, and the leading authorities in the scholarly centres and in transmitted traditions. However, some Muslim scholars heard that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had permitted nabīdh (an infused drink), and that the Companions used to drink it, so they assumed that it was an intoxicating drink. That was not the case. Rather, the nabīdh drunk by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions was made by steeping dates, raisins or similar things in water until it became sweet. He would drink it on the first, second and third days, but would not drink it after three days, lest it have begun to develop intoxicating strength. If it developed that strength before then, it would not be drunk.

Moreover,

original_text:
رَوَى أَهْلُ السُّنَنِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:

" الْقِيَاسُ الشَّرْعِيُّ "
 وَهُوَ التَّسْوِيَةُ بَيْنَ الْمُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ؛ فَلَا يُفَرِّقُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ بَيْنَ شَرَابٍ مُسْكِرٍ وَشَرَابٍ مُسْكِرٍ فَيُبِيحُ قَلِيلَ هَذَا وَلَا يُبِيحُ قَلِيلَ هَذَا؛ بَلْ يُسَوِّي بَيْنَهُمَا وَإِذَا كَانَ قَدْ حَرَّمَ الْقَلِيلَ مِنْ أَحَدِهِمَا حَرَّمَ الْقَلِيلَ مِنْهُمَا؛ فَإِنَّ الْقَلِيلَ يَدْعُو إلَى الْكَثِيرِ وَأَنَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ أَمَرَ بِاجْتِنَابِ الْخَمْرِ وَلِهَذَا يُؤْمَرُ بِإِرَاقَتِهَا؛ وَيَحْرُمُ اقْتِنَاؤُهَا وَحَكَمَ بِنَجَاسَتِهَا؛ وَأَمَرَ بِجِلْدِ شَارِبِهَا؛ كُلُّ ذَلِكَ حَسْمًا لِمَادَّةِ الْفَسَادِ؛ فَكَيْفَ يُبِيحُ الْقَلِيلُ مِنْ الْأَشْرِبَةِ الْمُسْكِرَةِ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
the compilers of the Sunan collections narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Some people of my nation will surely drink khamr, calling it by another name.”

This has been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through four routes. It applies to those who drink these beverages which they call al-sarmā’ and other names. The matter is clear: Muslims unanimously agree that grape wine is forbidden in both small and large quantities. Neither sensory experience nor reason distinguishes between khamr made from grapes and that made from dates, raisins or honey. One keeps people from remembering Allah and from prayer, and so does the other; one causes enmity and hatred, and so does the other.

Allah, glorified is He, has commanded justice and reasoning by comparison. This is “legal analogy”: treating like cases alike. Allah and His Messenger do not distinguish between one intoxicating drink and another by permitting a small quantity of one but not of the other. Rather, He treats them alike: if He has forbidden a small quantity of one, He has forbidden a small quantity of both, for a little leads to much.

Furthermore, He, glorified is He, has commanded that khamr be shunned. This is why it is to be poured away and its possession is forbidden. He has ruled it impure and commanded that its drinker be flogged—all to cut off corruption at its source. How, then, could He permit small quantities of intoxicating drinks? Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was also asked:

About nabīdh (drinks prepared from dates or raisins), mizr, “al-sawīqa,” which is made from carrots, and the grape drink called “al-nasūh”: Are they lawful? Is it permissible to use any of these or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

Every intoxicating drink is khamr and is therefore forbidden, according to the widely transmitted Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the agreement of the Companions. Thus, it is authentically reported from him in the hadith of Abū Mūsā:

“He was asked about a drink made from sorghum called mizr and a drink made from honey called bitʿ. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had been granted the gift of expressing comprehensive meanings in few words, so he said: ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, ʿĀ’isha reported that he said:

“Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.”

In the Sahīh, Ibn ʿUmar reported that he said:

“Every intoxicant is khamr, and every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Another wording in the Sahīh reads:

“Every intoxicant is khamr, and all khamr is forbidden.”

In the Sunan collections, it is reported that he said:

“Whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden in small quantities.”

More than one hadith master has graded this report authentic. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden uncooked grape juice once it ferments, becomes potent, and produces froth, because of its exhilarating potency, which turns people away from remembering Allah and from prayer and breeds enmity and hatred.

Anything possessing this exhilarating potency is khamr, whatever it is made from—grains, fruits, or anything else—and whether it is uncooked or cooked;

but if it is cooked until two-thirds have evaporated and one-third remains, it no longer intoxicates—unless spices or some other ingredient are added to it. The governing principle is:

“Everything that intoxicates is forbidden.”

This is the position of the vast majority of leading scholars, as stated by al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others. Drinking such an intoxicant incurs the prescribed punishment, and it is ritually impure according to the imams. Likewise, consuming intoxicating hashish incurs the prescribed punishment, and it is ritually impure according to the soundest juristic view. Some have held that it is ritually pure; others have distinguished between its dry and liquid forms. The first view is correct, because it intoxicates through transformation, like uncooked khamr. This differs from substances that do not intoxicate but merely deprive a person of reason, such as henbane, or those that intoxicate after transformation, such as nutmeg: these are not ritually impure.

Anyone who supposes that hashish does not intoxicate, but merely deprives a person of reason without giving pleasure, has not understood its true nature. Were it not for the pleasure it provides, people would neither take it nor eat it, unlike henbane and similar substances that provide no pleasure. In prohibiting things, the Lawgiver has distinguished between what people crave and what they do not crave. For things people do not crave, such as blood and carrion, the religious deterrent is deemed sufficient, and their consumption is subject to discretionary punishment. For things people crave, however, He has added a natural deterrent to the religious deterrent: the prescribed punishment. Hashish belongs to this category.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Numerous reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the authentic hadith collections, the Sunan collections, and the Musnad collections establish that he prohibited every intoxicant and classified it as khamr. Thus, in Sahīh Muslim, Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is khamr, and all khamr is forbidden.”

Another wording states:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

In the two Sahīh collections, ʿĀʾishah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Mūsā reports:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a drink made from honey called bitʿ. He had been endowed with concise, comprehensive speech, and he replied: ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb is reported to have said from the pulpit—the pulpit of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has forbidden khamr, which is made from five things: wheat, barley, grapes, dates, and raisins. Khamr is whatever clouds the mind.”

This is also related in the Sunan collections with a chain of transmission through Ibn ʿUmar from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

It has also been reported from him through several chains that he said:

“Whatever intoxicates in large amounts is forbidden even in small amounts.”

A number of hadith masters have graded this report authentic. The hadiths on this subject are numerous. They regard it as khamr, whatever its ingredients—grains, fruits, or anything else—whether grapes, dates, wheat, barley, mares’ milk, or otherwise; whether uncooked or cooked; and whether two-thirds, one-third, one-half, or some other proportion has evaporated. Whenever a large amount intoxicates, a small amount is forbidden, without disagreement among them.

Nevertheless, they accept what is authentically reported from ‘Umar. When ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, came to Syria and wished to prepare a drink for the Muslims that would not intoxicate even in large amounts, he boiled the juice until two-thirds had evaporated and one-third remained, becoming like thick fruit syrup. He dipped his finger into it, found it thick, and said, “It looks like tilā’.” He meant the paste used to coat camels, so they called this drink “tilā’.”

What ‘Umar permitted, then, was not intoxicating. Abū Bakr Abd al-Azīz ibn Ja‘far, the associate of al-Khallāl, stated that it was permissible by the consensus of the Muslims. This rests on its being non-intoxicating. None of the aforementioned imams said that it was permissible despite being intoxicating.

However, “confusion” arose because this boiled drink may become intoxicating for various reasons. One is that it may not have been thoroughly boiled. In describing its preparation, they stated that it should first be boiled until its scum is removed, then boiled further until two-thirds has evaporated. If two-thirds evaporates while the scum is still in it, less than two-thirds of the drink itself has evaporated, because the scum then forms part of what has not evaporated. Another reason is that spices and other ingredients may be added to the boiled drink

It is widely reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “forbade combining two ingredients in a drink,” because each strengthens the other. Thus, he forbade combining dates with raisins, fresh dates with dried dates, and similar mixtures.

Conditions in some lands may cause a drink to become intoxicating even after two-thirds has evaporated. It is then forbidden if it intoxicates, for intoxication is the criterion for prohibition by agreement of the imams. Whoever claims that ‘Umar or any other Companion permitted an intoxicating drink has falsely attributed this to them.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. As for wine made from grape juice that has fermented, become potent, and thrown up froth, both small and large quantities are forbidden by the agreement of the Muslims. Whoever attributes to Abū Hanīfah the permissibility of a small amount of this has lied. Indeed, whoever considers it lawful must be called upon to repent; if he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is put to death. Even if someone considers drinking wine lawful because of a misconception like that which affected some of the early Muslims—believing that it is forbidden only to ordinary people, not to those who believe and do righteous deeds—the Companions, including ‘Umar, ‘Alī, and others, agreed that anyone who considers it lawful must be called upon to repent. If he acknowledges its prohibition, he is flogged; if he persists in considering it lawful, he is put to death.

Moreover, Abū Hanīfah forbids both small and large quantities of other drinks, even though he does not call them wine, such as unboiled infusions of dates and raisins. In his view, both small and large quantities of these are forbidden if they are intoxicating. Likewise, grape juice that has been boiled without two-thirds of it evaporating is forbidden in small quantities, according to him, if a large quantity intoxicates. Thus, he forbids both small and large quantities of these four types, even if the person drinking them does not become intoxicated.

The “misconception” arose only concerning other intoxicants, such as mazr made from wheat and similar grains. The position held by the great majority of Muslim imams is reflected in the report in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī that the people of Yemen said, “O Messenger of Allah, we have a drink made from honey called bit‘, and a drink made from sorghum called mazr.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had been endowed with concise, comprehensive speech, and he said:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

And in the two Sahīh collections

it is narrated from ‘Ā’ishah that he said:

“Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.”

Also in the Sahīh, Ibn ‘Umar narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden.”

In the Sunan collections, it is narrated from him through several chains that he said:

“Whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden even in small quantities.”

Numerous hadiths convey this meaning. When Allah prohibited wine, the people of the Prophet’s city, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had no alcoholic drink other than that made from dates; that was their wine.

It is reported of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that “he used to drink nabīdh.” What is meant here is sweet nabīdh: dates or raisins are placed in water until it becomes sweet, and then it is drunk.

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had forbidden them to prepare nabīdh in gourds, wooden or stone vessels, or pitch-coated containers,” because, when prepared in these vessels, it could gradually become intoxicating without their knowing, so that a man might drink an intoxicant.

“He also forbade them to combine dates and raisins,” because each strengthens the effect of the other. “He forbade them to drink nabīdh after three days,” because it might have become intoxicating without a person realizing it. All of this reflected the utmost caution on his part, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Thus, any scholar who believed that the nabīdh he permitted could be intoxicating—meaning drinks made from honey, wheat, and the like—and consequently said that one may drink an amount that does not cause intoxication, was mistaken. The vast majority of scholars, however, understood that what he permitted was that which does not intoxicate. This view is correct according to both the revealed texts and analogical reasoning.

As for “the revealed texts,” there are numerous hadiths on the matter. As for “analogical reasoning,” all intoxicating drinks are alike in that they cause intoxication

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn ‘Abd al-Halīm ibn Taymiyyah said:

As for the accursed, intoxicating “hashish,” it has the same status as other intoxicants, and whatever of it is intoxicating is forbidden by scholarly consensus. Indeed, anything that deprives a person of reason is forbidden to consume, even if it is not an intoxicant, such as henbane. Consuming an intoxicant incurs the prescribed punishment, whereas consuming a non-intoxicating substance of this kind incurs discretionary punishment.

Even a small quantity of “intoxicating hashish” is forbidden according to the vast majority of scholars, just as small quantities of other intoxicants are forbidden. The Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

applies to everything that intoxicates. It makes no difference whether the intoxicant is eaten or drunk, solid or liquid. Thus, using it as a condiment, as with wine, would be forbidden; and if someone were to liquefy

Whenever he made a comprehensive statement, it applied generally to everything encompassed by its wording and meaning, whether or not those particular things existed in his time or place.

Thus, when he said:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden,”

this included the wine made from dates and other ingredients in Medina, as well as the wine made from wheat, barley, honey, and other ingredients in Yemen. It also included intoxicating drinks that appeared after his time, such as those made from mares’ milk by the Turks and others like them. No scholar distinguished between intoxicants made from mares’ milk and those made from wheat and barley, even though one existed in his time and was known to him, while the other was unknown to him, since no one in Arabia made wine from mares’ milk.

As for this “hashish,” the earliest reports that have reached us place its appearance among Muslims in the late sixth and early seventh centuries AH, when Tatar rule emerged. Its appearance coincided with the rise of the sword of “Genghis Khan.” When people openly committed the sins that Allah and His Messenger had forbidden them, Allah gave their enemy power over them. This accursed hashish was among the gravest evils. In some respects it is worse than intoxicating drink, while intoxicating drink is worse than it in another respect. Besides intoxicating those who eat it until they become stupefied, it causes effeminacy and indifference to sexual misconduct within one’s household. It corrupts the bodily constitution, making a grown man like a saftaja, causes excessive eating, and brings on insanity. Many people have become insane through eating it.

Some people say, “Like henbane, it alters the mind but does not intoxicate.” This is not so. Rather, it produces euphoria, pleasure, and exhilaration like wine, and this is what prompts people to consume it. A little leads to more, just as with intoxicating drink. Those accustomed to it find it harder to give up than wine. Its harm is therefore greater than that of wine in certain respects.

For this reason, the jurists have said that consuming it incurs the prescribed punishment, just as drinking wine does. They differed over its “ritual impurity,” with three views within the school of Ahmad and other schools. Some held that it is impure; others held that it is not. A third view holds that its moist form is impure like wine, whereas its dry form is not. The correct view is that ritual impurity applies to all its forms, just as it applies to wine in both solid and liquid form.

Anyone intoxicated by an intoxicating drink or intoxicating hashish may not approach the mosque until he becomes sober, and his prayer is not valid until he knows what he is saying. In either case, he must wash his mouth, hands, and clothes. Prayer remains an individual obligation, but unless he repents, his prayers are not accepted for forty days, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever drinks wine will have no prayer accepted from him for forty days. If he repents, Allah will accept his repentance. If he returns to drinking it, no prayer will be accepted from him for forty days. If he repents, Allah will accept his repentance. If he returns to drinking it again, it will be incumbent upon Allah to make him drink from the mire of corruption.” He was asked, “What is the mire of corruption?” He replied, “The discharge of the people of the Fire—or the sweat of the people of the Fire.”

falls within their scope. Everything within their scope is mentioned in the Quran and hadith under its general designation. Otherwise, it would be impossible to mention everything by its specific name. Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to all creation, and said:

“Say, ‘O mankind, I am Allah’s Messenger to you all.’”

He also said:

“We have sent you only to all mankind.”

And Allah Most High said:

“He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he might be a warner to all the worlds.”

And He said:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to all the worlds.”

The terms “mankind” and “the worlds” include Arabs and non-Arabs: Persians, Romans, Indians, and Berbers. If someone were to say, “Muhammad was not sent to the Turks, Indians, or Berbers, because Allah did not mention them in the Quran,” he would be ignorant. It would be as though he said, “Allah did not send him to Banū Tamīm, Banū Asad, Ghatafān, or the other Arab tribes,” because Allah did not mention these tribes by their specific names. Likewise, it would be as though he said, “Allah did not send him to Abū Jahl, ‘Utbah, Shaybah, or the others of Quraysh,” because Allah did not mention them by their individual names in the Quran.

Similarly, when He said:

“Intoxicants, gambling, sacrificial altars, and divining arrows are nothing but an abomination of Satan’s handiwork,”

the term “gambling” included forms unknown to the Arabs and unknown to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. All gambling is forbidden by the agreement of the Muslims, even if the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not know of it. Playing chess or other games for stakes, for example, is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims. It constitutes the gambling that Allah has forbidden, although it did not exist in the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Backgammon, too, is a form of the gambling that Allah has forbidden. Yet neither backgammon nor chess is mentioned in the Quran by a

specific name; rather, the term “gambling” encompasses both. The majority of scholars hold that backgammon and chess are forbidden, whether played for stakes or without them.

Likewise, His words:

“Allah does not hold you accountable for your unintentional oaths, but He holds you accountable for the oaths you deliberately bind yourselves to. The expiation is to feed ten poor people from the average of what you feed your families”—up to His words—“when you swear,”

and His words:

“Allah has prescribed for you a way to release yourselves from your oaths,”

include both the oaths Muslims used to swear during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those they came to swear afterward. Thus, if someone swore in Persian, Turkish, an Indian language, or Berber, invoking the name of Allah Most High in that language, his oath would be binding. If he broke it, expiation would be obligatory upon him by the agreement of the scholars, even though oaths in these languages were not among those sworn by Muslims during the lifetime of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

This differs from swearing by created things, such as the Kaaba, angels, shaykhs, kings, and others. These are not among the oaths of Muslims; rather, they constitute associating partners with Allah, as he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever swears by other than Allah has associated partners with Him.”

Likewise, the Most High said:

“And you find no water, then perform dry ablution with earth.”

This encompasses everything called “earth” and every kind of water, whether it existed during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or came into existence afterward. translated_text:
the scholars—even if those waters were unknown to the Muslims during the lifetime of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Likewise, the Most High said:

“Kill the polytheists wherever you find them.”

This encompasses every polytheist, Arab or non-Arab, including the polytheists among the Turks, Indians, and Berbers, even though these were not among those killed during the lifetime of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Similarly, His statement:

“Fight those among the People of the Scripture who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not follow the religion of truth, until they pay the jizyah with willing submission and are humbled.”

This encompasses all the People of the Scripture, even if they were not among those killed during the lifetime of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Those killed in his time were Arab and Byzantine Christians, while he fought the Jews before this verse was revealed. Yet the verse also encompasses Christians among the Copts, Abyssinians, Circassians, al-All, al-Lāss, Georgians, and others.

This and similar examples illustrate how the Quran encompasses everything covered by its wording and meaning, even when it is not mentioned by its particular name. Even supposing that its wording did not encompass something, if that thing shared the relevant meaning of what is mentioned in the Quran and Sunnah, it would be included through comparison and analogy. Thus, Jews, Christians, and Persians fall within the general scope of the verse, and all intoxicants share the relevant meaning of wine made from grapes. And He sent Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, with the Book and the Balance so that people might uphold justice.

translated_text:
and “the Book” is the Quran, while “the Balance” is justice. Sound analogical reasoning is a form of justice, for it does not distinguish between equivalent things, but treats them equally. Thus, when wrongful acts share the characteristic that necessitates prohibition, one is not singled out as forbidden while another is not. Rather, justice requires that they be treated equally. Treating them differently would be contradictory, and the judgment of Allah and His Messenger is free from contradiction. If a physician prohibited a patient from consuming something because of its harmful effects, yet also permitted it to him, he would depart from the principles of medicine. The revealed Law is medicine for hearts, and the prophets are physicians of hearts and religions. Whenever the revealed Law permits something of this kind, there must be a distinguishing feature separating the two, such that what it prohibits has a characteristic not shared by what it permits. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

What punishment is prescribed for someone who consumes hashish?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. This solid hashish is forbidden, whether or not a person becomes intoxicated by it. Becoming intoxicated by it is forbidden by agreement of the Muslims. Whoever deems that lawful and claims that it is permissible is to be called upon to repent; failing repentance, he is to be executed as an apostate. No funeral prayer is to be offered for him, nor is he to be buried in Muslim cemeteries.

“When they commit an indecency, they say, ‘We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to do it.’ Say, ‘Allah does not command indecency. Do you say about Allah what you do not know?’”

Everything that deprives a person of reason is forbidden, even if it produces neither euphoria nor exhilaration, for depriving oneself of reason is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims. As for taking banj without becoming intoxicated or losing one’s reason, it incurs discretionary punishment.

The jurists who have carefully examined the matter recognize that hashish is intoxicating. The wicked consume it precisely because of the euphoria and exhilaration it produces; in this respect, it shares the effects of intoxicating drink. Wine induces agitation and quarrelling, whereas hashish induces lethargy and abasement. In addition, it corrupts the physical constitution and the mind, arouses lust, and causes a loss of protective jealousy—effects that make it worse than intoxicating drink. It only appeared among people with the emergence of the Tatars.

The jurists have differed over its ritual impurity, holding three views. The first is that it is not impure. The second is that its liquid form is impure, while its solid form is pure. The third—and correct—view is that it is impure like wine: hashish resembles excrement, whereas wine resembles urine. Both are among the foul things that Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

Anyone known to consume hashish is like someone known to drink wine, and is worse in certain respects. He is to be shunned and punished for this just as the wine-drinker is, because of the warnings concerning wine, such as the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has cursed wine, the one who drinks it, the one who serves it, the one who sells it, the one who buys it, the one who carries it, and the one who consumes its proceeds.”

And his words:

“Whoever drinks wine, Allah will not accept his prayers for forty days. If he repents, Allah will accept his repentance. If he returns to drinking it, Allah will not accept his prayers for forty days. If he repents, Allah will accept his repentance. If he returns to drinking it, Allah will not accept his prayers for forty days. If he repents, Allah will accept his repentance. If he returns to drinking it a third or fourth time, it is incumbent upon Allah to give him tīnat al-khabāl to drink, which is the discharge from the inhabitants of Hell.”

It is also authentically reported from him in the Sahīh, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

He was asked about these drinks, and, having been endowed with concise, comprehensive speech, he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

The prohibitions in the Quran and Sunnah apply to those who consume it just as they apply to those who consume other forbidden substances.  فَيَجِبُ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ أَنْ يُجْلَدَ الْحَدَّ إذَا ثَبَتَ ذَلِكَ عَلَيْهِ وَحَدُّهُ أَرْبَعُونَ جَلْدَةً أَوْ ثَمَانُونَ جَلْدَةً. فَإِنْ جَلَدَهُ ثَمَانِينَ جَازَ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ وَإِنْ اقْتَصَرَ عَلَى الْأَرْبَعِينَ فَفِي الْإِجْزَاءِ نِزَاعٌ مَشْهُورٌ فَمَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ أَنَّهُ يَجِبُ الثَّمَانُونَ وَمَذْهَبُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد فِي الرِّوَايَةِ الْأُخْرَى عَنْهُ أَنَّ الْأَرْبَعِينَ الثَّانِيَةَ تَعْزِيرٌ يُرْجَعُ فِيهَا إلَى اجْتِهَادِ الْإِمَامِ فَإِنْ احْتَاجَ إلَى ذَلِكَ لِكَثْرَةِ الشُّرْبِ أَوْ إصْرَارِ الشَّارِبِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ فَعَلَ وَقَدْ كَانَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ يُعَزِّرُ بِأَكْثَرِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ؛ كَمَا رُوِيَ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَنْفِي الشَّارِبَ عَنْ بَلَدِهِ وَيُمَثِّلُ بِهِ بِحَلْقِ رَأْسِهِ.

Whenever it causes intoxication, it is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims. This is the drink known as “tilā’” (boiled grape juice), which ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb permitted the Muslims to drink. If, however, it causes intoxication after being boiled until two-thirds has evaporated, it is also forbidden according to Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked about habitual wine-drinking and abandonment of prayer, and the ruling concerning someone who persists in this.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

As for the “wine drinker,” the imams agree that he must receive the prescribed flogging if his drinking is proven. His prescribed punishment is forty or eighty lashes. Administering eighty lashes is permissible by agreement of the imams. If only forty are administered, however, there is a well-known disagreement over whether this suffices.

The position of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and Ahmad—according to one of the two reports from him—is that eighty lashes are obligatory. The position of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad—according to the other report from him—is that the additional forty lashes constitute discretionary punishment, left to the ruler’s judgment. If this is needed because drinking has become widespread, because the drinker persists, or for similar reasons, he imposes them.

‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb used to impose discretionary punishments beyond this. It is reported that he would banish the drinker from his town and disfigure him by shaving his head.

 فَإِذَا لَمْ تُمْكِنْ إقَامَةُ الْحَدِّ عَلَى مِثْلِ هَذَا فَإِنَّهُ يُعْمَلُ مَعَهُ الْمُمْكِنُ:
 فَيُهْجَرُ: وَيُوَبَّخُ حَتَّى يَفْعَلَ الْمَفْرُوضَ وَيَتْرُكَ الْمَحْظُورَ وَلَا يَكُونُ مِمَّنْ قَالَ اللَّهُ فِيهِ: 
{فَخَلَفَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ أَضَاعُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَاتَّبَعُوا الشَّهَوَاتِ فَسَوْفَ يَلْقَوْنَ غَيًّا}
 مَعَ أَنَّ إضَاعَتَهَا تَأْخِيرُهَا عَنْ وَقْتِهَا فَكَيْفَ بِتَارِكِهَا؟
translated_text:
It has been reported through several chains of transmission that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever drinks wine, flog him. Then, if he drinks it again, flog him. Then, if he drinks it again, flog him. Then, if he drinks it a third or fourth time, execute him.”

Thus, he commanded that the drinker be executed on the third or fourth occasion. Most scholars, however, do not regard execution as obligatory; rather, they consider this hadith abrogated. This is the well-known position in the schools of the imams.

Some scholars say that if people will not desist from drinking except through execution, this is permissible. Likewise, another hadith in the Sunan collections states that he forbade them certain kinds of drinks and said:

“If they do not give that up, execute them.”

The correct position is what has already been stated. It is established in the Sahīh:

“A man called Hammār used to drink wine. Whenever he drank, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would have him flogged. A man cursed him, saying, ‘May Allah curse him! How often he is brought before the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him!’ He replied, ‘Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.’”

This indicates that he was flogged despite his repeated drinking.

As for someone who abandons prayer, the imams agree that he deserves punishment. Most of them—including Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad—say that he must be called upon to repent: if he repents, he is spared; otherwise, he is executed. There are two views as to whether he is executed as an unbeliever who has apostatized or as a sinful person, like others guilty of major sins.

If the prescribed punishment cannot be carried out on such a person, whatever measures are possible should be taken: he should be shunned and rebuked until he performs what is obligatory and abandons what is forbidden, and is no longer among those of whom Allah said:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; so they will meet ruin.”

Neglecting prayer here means delaying it beyond its appointed time—so what, then, of abandoning it altogether?

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man owns a mare with a filly following her. Is it permissible to drink her milk?”

He replied:

“It is permissible to drink her milk, provided it has not become intoxicating.”

He—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

“For years, a man has habitually consumed some compound pastes every night before the afternoon prayer. When questioned about this, he said, ‘I find various benefits in them.’ Is this permissible for him?”

He replied:

“If it deprives him of reason, he may not consume it, for everything that deprives a person of reason is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims.”

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Concerning the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—‘Whoever drinks wine, flog him. If he does it again, flog him. If he does it again, kill him’: does this hadith have a basis, and who narrated it?”

He replied:

“Yes, it has a basis. It is narrated through several chains and is regarded as established by hadith scholars. However, most scholars say that it has been abrogated, and they hold several different views about what abrogated it. Some say, rather, that its ruling remains in force. Another view is that the obligation has been abrogated, while the permissibility remains. Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī and others narrated it, and I know of no one who has impugned it. Allah knows best.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man breaks up sorghum and boils it in his pot, then takes it off the heat, adds wheat to it, leaves it until the next morning and strains it. On that day it is not intoxicating, but if he then leaves it for another two or three days, it becomes intoxicating. Is it permissible for him to drink some of it on the first day?”

translated_text:
He replied:

“It is permissible to drink it for up to three days, provided it does not become intoxicating. If it becomes intoxicating, however, it is forbidden by the explicit words of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—whether this happens before or after the three days. Whenever it becomes intoxicating, it becomes forbidden, for it is authentically reported that he said:

‘Every intoxicant is wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“If ‘wine’ is boiled over a fire and reduced by a third, is it permissible to use it?”

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah. Once it has become intoxicating, it is forbidden and must be poured away; cooking does not make it lawful. However, if it is cooked before becoming intoxicating until two-thirds have evaporated and one-third remains, and it is not intoxicating, then it is lawful according to the vast majority of Muslims. If it is cooked before becoming intoxicating until a third or half has evaporated, then, if it is intoxicating, it is forbidden according to the positions of all four imams. If it is not intoxicating, it may be used for up to three days, provided it does not become intoxicating.”
